papers.abstract: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.
authors: Chenjie Zhao, Zhiliang Zhu, Quan Chen, Yuquan Xue, Xingxue Shi, Puyue Wang, Zhiqiang Zhao, Kangye Zheng, Boyang Xu, Mingwei Lin, Dejun Li

Adapts to simulated underwater vehicle dynamics using expert trajectories and predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D paths.
Marine spatial pretraining improves simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%.
Reaches 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials without real-test-environment fine-tuning, versus 47.50% for InternVLA-N1.

papers.abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: https://drift-e2e.github.io/
authors: Emad Aghajanzadeh, Bethany Anne Wong, Leonhard Kunze, Moritz Thoma, Maximilian Forstenh\"ausler, Nael Fasfous, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Pierpaolo Mori, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann
bullets: Integrates a compact (<150M-parameter) language model for visual question answering, scene description, and action commentary.
Projects intermediate driving representations into language-embedding space to support effective reasoning with a lightweight LM.
Distills LM reasoning into surrogate features so planning can operate with either the LM or without it during deployment.
Uses an adjustable reasoning rate to balance computational cost and language-assisted planning.
Reports strong Bench2Drive performance and competitive NAVSIM and AlpaSim results at lower computational cost than VLM-based approaches.

papers.abstract: Semantic 3D mapping is a powerful representation that enables platform agnostic mobile robot navigation in challenging offroad conditions. Current vision foundation models can accurately predict semantics zero-shot on structured scenes but performance is compromised in natural environments. On the other hand, 3D point clouds encode valuable information for discriminating semantics in scenarios where vision foundation models fail. In this work, we propose fitting a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class to act as geometric anchor. Only the points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions are considered when fitting to produce high quality geometric prior distributions. The geometric prior is fused with the vision foundation model prediction to produce the final semantic mapping. The proposed prior improves SAM3 baseline by +6.3 in mIoU and +8.9 in accuracy on the RELLIS-3D dataset, and by +1.7 in mIoU and +2.1 in accuracy on the WildScenes dataset. The source code will be made public upon paper acceptance.
bullets: Vision foundation models struggle with semantic prediction in natural, unstructured offroad scenes.
The method fits a sphericity–elevation distribution for each semantic class using only high-confidence vision predictions.
These class-specific geometric priors are fused with vision foundation model outputs to produce the final 3D semantic map.
The approach improves the SAM3 baseline on RELLIS-3D by 6.3 mIoU points and 8.9 accuracy points, and on WildScenes by 1.7 and 2.1 points, respectively.
The work focuses on offroad semantic mapping and plans to release its source code upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained visual world models generate multi-step action plans from current and goal observations, yet terminal-proximity objectives fail to prevent forbidden-zone traversal or rigid-body collision sliding. Purely visual interfaces may lack analytical dynamics, structured states, or explicit collision geometry, requiring internal prediction of action-conditioned process risk. We propose Risk-Triggered Search (RTS) for frozen Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models. Rather than relying on static state features that cannot distinguish candidate plans sharing an observation, RTS unrolls action-conditioned future latent prefixes in the frozen world model and trains a lightweight risk head with process-violation supervision. To intervene selectively while preserving safe nominal behavior, RTS uses the same predicted prefix-risk criterion as both the search trigger gate and hard feasibility gate: safe nominal plans execute directly, whereas alarms trigger local Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) search to minimize nominal deviation within the feasible set. To prevent isotropic Euclidean minimal modification from shrinking obstacle-directed actions into zero-amplitude stalling, we introduce an amplitude-preserving metric $d_{\mathrm{AP}}$ that retains tangential progression while maintaining a unique zero at the nominal plan. Under unified gating and this unique-zero condition, bypassing safe-state search yields closed-loop trajectories strictly identical to every-step same-kernel search. Evaluated under a process-safety benchmark and Safe Arrival Rate (SAR) metric across five tasks, RTS improves SAR over Direct by 12.67--41.67 percentage points on navigation and articulated control and +2.08/+4.17 pp on Cube/PushT boundary cohorts, maintaining 100% action identity with every-step search while cutting controller time by 17.71%--70.41% across 1,968 paired trajectories.
authors: Xinyu Deng, Bohao Lan, Kunpeng Li, Mingkai Yuan, Weihang Pan, Binbin Lin
bullets: Addresses forbidden-zone traversal and collision sliding in visual world-model planning when explicit dynamics or collision geometry are unavailable.
Unrolls future latent action prefixes in a frozen JEPA world model and trains a lightweight risk head using process-violation supervision.
Uses predicted prefix risk for both search triggering and feasibility gating; risky plans invoke local CEM search, while safe plans execute unchanged.
Introduces an amplitude-preserving deviation metric to retain tangential progress instead of collapsing obstacle-directed actions into stalling.
Across five tasks, improves Safe Arrival Rate by 2.08–41.67 percentage points, matches every-step search action-for-action, and reduces controller time by 17.71%–70.41%.

papers.selection_reason: Integrates a frozen JEPA world model with a risk-triggered search mechanism for safe control, bridging interactive world models and embodied navigation/safe control.
papers.title: Risk-Triggered Search: Behavior-Preserving Safe Control

papers.abstract: Object search in unknown environments requires robots to gather useful observations while avoiding obstacles and accounting for limited sensor visibility. We present SearchDiffusion, a diffusion-based planner that generates position and heading trajectories using a learned dense utility map. The map represents geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress. It conditions trajectory generation and provides an objective for sampling guidance. Sampled map hypotheses provide additional geometric context, while geometric and heading guidance, validity checks, and analytical selection support execution. Across 90 simulated tasks on 24 map layouts, SearchDiffusion achieved 95.6\% target detection at greater computational cost. Ablations show complementary benefits from utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime map hypotheses. In ten physical quadruped trials using OneMap relevance maps, eight were successful under operator assessment, without fine-tuning on real-robot data. These results support combining learned spatial utility with guided trajectory generation for object search under partial observability.
authors: Sausar Karaf, Dmitrii Plotnikov, Alexey Kotcov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Plans robot position and heading trajectories using utility maps encoding accessibility, visibility, and semantic progress.
Uses map hypotheses, geometric and heading guidance, validity checks, and analytical selection during sampling and execution.
Achieved 95.6% target detection across 90 simulated tasks on 24 layouts, at greater computational cost.
Succeeded in 8 of 10 physical quadruped trials using OneMap maps without real-robot fine-tuning.
Ablations found complementary benefits from utility and guidance, while runtime map hypotheses added limited detection benefit.

papers.abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.
bullets: Addresses the need for communication-efficient federated learning beyond perception-only tasks.
Uses multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation.
Evaluated in closed loop on Bench2Drive for both one-shot and multi-round federated learning.
Achieves a Driving Score of 55.85 in one-shot learning and 60.35 after five communication rounds.
Scope: performance is demonstrated on the Bench2Drive evaluation benchmark.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of token-wise consensus distillation. The server dataset is first fed into the calibrated teacher models and the student model to extract features. The teacher features are then mapped into the student feature space using the optimal orthogonal transformation matrices. Next, token-wise consensus is used to compute adaptive weights for teacher feature fusion. Finally, the student model is trained by minimizing the distillation loss between the fused teacher features and student features, together with the supervised driving action loss.

papers.abstract: World models support autonomous driving by evaluating candidate trajectories through predicted future scene evolution. However, accurate future prediction does not ensure road-compliant execution; when all candidates violate road boundaries, re-ranking cannot select a feasible trajectory. We propose Physics-Guided Search Distillation (PGSD), a single-view planning framework that combines future representations and execution feedback for verified beyond-pool repair through three components: (1) Execution-Aware Selection checks ego-vehicle road compliance under simulated execution and selects the highest-scoring feasible trajectory; (2) a Clearance-Aware Search Teacher generates beyond-pool corrections and selects demonstrations with larger minimum road-boundary clearance during execution to buffer imitation errors; and (3) a Future-Conditioned Repair Student predicts one correction from rewarder features and execution feedback for single-rollout verification. The pretrained planner and rewarder remain frozen; no future scenes are generated online. On NAVSIM v1, single-view PGSD achieves 90.97 PDMS, exceeding all compared prior single-view planners and retaining 73.2% of the search teacher's PDMS gain over execution-aware selection. On NAVSIM v2 navhard, it reaches 38.96 EPDMS, improving on WorldDrive by 11.24 points (40.5%). The student replaces up to ten search rollouts with a single verification rollout per repair trigger. HUGSIM Hard examples provide qualitative evidence of zero-shot transfer.
authors: Hongyu Zhang, Xiaoshuai Hao, Heye Huang, Qingwen Meng, Wenjun Shi, Jianao Xu, Xin Hu, Xuanru Jin, Jingyi Zhang, Baicang Guo
bullets: Addresses the failure of trajectory re-ranking when every candidate violates road boundaries.
Combines execution-aware feasible selection, clearance-aware teacher search, and a future-conditioned repair student.
Keeps the pretrained planner and rewarder frozen and performs no online future-scene generation.
Achieves 90.97 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 38.96 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navhard, with reported gains over prior methods.
Replaces up to ten search rollouts with one verification rollout per repair trigger; qualitative HUGSIM Hard results suggest zero-shot transfer.

papers.abstract: Robot navigation requires both an understanding of the scene and an efficient adaptation to new robots, yet current methods rely on expensive LiDAR sensors, long mapping and modular pipelines. We present BEV-Diffusion, a camera-only model that learns a bird's-eye view (BEV) traversability map, its uncertainty and the path in a single network. A frozen DINOv2 backbone encodes consecutive RGB frames, which inverse perspective mapping and Bayesian fusion lift into the BEV, and a ranking loss keeps outdoor traversability graded rather than binary, separating asphalt from grass (median 0.94 vs. 0.75). On this map, a transformer denoiser generates polar waypoints in a few DDIM steps, and uncertainty-aware guidance refines the path and ends it where the map is no longer reliable. At deployment, a metric BEV memory keeps obstacles after they leave the camera view and warm starts each sample from the previous, ego-motion compensated path. Because the planner jointly learns the path, the map, and its uncertainty, it selects routes through terrain it can confidently traverse. In an unseen courtyard, a wheeled-legged robot autonomously traveled 120 m, completing 96% of the route without intervention, compared with 75-88% for the baselines. Even under low-light conditions after sunset, the proposed model completed the route without requiring any intervention. Retraining only the BEV head, about 3% of the parameters, adapts the model to a small legged robot in 2.3 min. Indoors, the memory gets this robot out of maze-like traps: it retains 62-66% of the nearby out-of-view obstacles, against at most 3% for the baselines, and the robot achieves 67-100% task progress, compared with 20-40% for the evaluated baselines.
authors: Iana Zhura, Timofei Kozlov, Dmitrii Plotnikov, Ivan Valuev, Miguel Altamirano Cabrera, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Uses consecutive RGB frames, frozen DINOv2 features, inverse perspective mapping, and Bayesian fusion to build a BEV traversability map with uncertainty.
A ranking loss preserves graded terrain costs, while a transformer denoiser generates uncertainty-guided polar waypoints in a few DDIM steps.
Metric BEV memory retains obstacles outside the camera view and warm-starts planning using the previous ego-motion-compensated path.
In an unseen courtyard, the robot completed 96% of a 120 m route without intervention; it also completed the route after sunset without intervention.
Adapting to a small legged robot required retraining only the BEV head, about 3% of parameters, and took 2.3 minutes; indoor memory-based navigation retained 62–66% of nearby out-of-view obstacles.

papers.abstract: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.
bullets: Compares attention-based object relevance estimates with counterfactual causal relevance.
Analyzes more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using the PlanT 2.0 planning model.
Finds that attention often misses relevant objects and falsely highlights objects with little driving impact.
Attention performs better in simple single-lane, straight-road scenes but degrades on multi-lane roads and intersections.
The results motivate relevance methods that distinguish causal influence from correlation.

papers.abstract: Exocentric cameras, mounted on walls or ceilings in indoor environments, offer wider vantage points and are less easily occluded than robot-mounted cameras, making them an appealing alternative for perception in robot navigation algorithms. Previous methods that use such cameras, however, require their pose and intrinsics to be known before deployment, demanding calibration that is time-consuming, requires specialized personnel, and must be repeated whenever a camera moves or a new room is navigated. We propose Robot-centric Obstacle Maps from Unknown and uncalibrated eXocentric cameras (ROMUX), an agent that navigates a robot toward point goals while avoiding obstacles using exocentric cameras that are both uncalibrated, meaning the system does not require their pose or intrinsic information as input, and unknown, meaning it is not fit to a specific camera during training and does not require pre-deployment fine-tuning. We train a cross-view transformer on large-scale simulation data to predict metric robot-centric obstacle maps from exocentric images, without conditioning image tokens on camera information. A small policy trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) then navigates on the predicted maps toward a goal coordinate relative to the robot. We benchmark our agent in simulation with cameras randomized per episode, and it matches the success rates of a PPO policy that navigates from a robot-mounted camera. Further, ROMUX works with one camera or multiple cameras with partial views and has been transferred zero-shot to a real robot using a camera at varying positions and orientations across various room layouts.
authors: Raul Steinmetz, Raphael Druon, Yusuke Yoshiyasu, Akihisa Ohya, Ayanori Yorozu
bullets: Addresses the costly calibration and camera-specific adaptation required by prior exocentric-camera navigation methods.
Uses a cross-view transformer to estimate metric, robot-centric obstacle maps without camera pose or intrinsic information.
A PPO policy navigates toward robot-relative point goals using the predicted maps.
In simulation with randomized cameras, ROMUX matches the success rate of a robot-mounted-camera PPO policy.
Supports single or partially overlapping multiple cameras and transfers zero-shot to a real robot across camera placements and room layouts.

papers.abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.
authors: Jiazhe Wang, Tianyi Yang, Ruihang Li, Fan Lu, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Lei Yang
bullets: Addresses stale observations and action delays caused by changing driving scenes during model computation.
Runs a Video DiT world model asynchronously on a background GPU to stream predictive surround-view context.
Uses a lightweight freshness carrier and gated key/value bank on a foreground GPU for current visual feedback.
A fast Action DiT combines fresh observations with the latest completed world context without waiting for updates.
Reports strong accuracy-latency results across NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, Waymo E2E, and nuScenes benchmarks.

papers.abstract: To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training. For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement. However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system's capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and its revision mechanism. RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness.
authors: Yang Li, Ziju Han, Aming WU, Zihao Zhang, Sijia Zhang, Yahong Han, Qinghua Hu
bullets: Targets efficient search for multiple objects in unseen environments without task-specific training.
Diagnoses failed searches, requests additional views when observations are insufficient, and generates targeted navigation revisions.
Links later search outcomes to the rules behind revisions, updating diagnosis, observation, and revision planning.
Carries accepted program updates and spatial memory across goals so experience improves future searches.
Benchmark and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate its effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Once deployed on vehicles, end-to-end driving models continuously encounter challenging scenarios, generating valuable human takeover data that capture both model outputs and human behaviors. However, human interventions are often imperfect, as drivers may intervene too late or unnecessarily. Consequently, direct imitation can reinforce late responses or discourage otherwise appropriate maneuvers. To address this challenge, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision. We first construct diverse trajectory candidates by augmenting the plans of the deployed model and shifting recorded human corrective maneuvers earlier in time. We then train a scene-conditioned trajectory scorer to rank these candidates using expert demonstrations and unpaired preference signals from takeover logs. Using this scorer, we selectively replace pre-takeover training targets with higher-scoring candidates while retaining the original targets in normal driving scenarios. Finally, we distill the resulting targets into the driving model without changing its inference architecture. In closed-loop evaluations using real-world scenarios reconstructed with 4D Gaussian splatting, our method achieves the highest overall success rate, outperforming the deployed model, direct imitation learning and trajectory post-optimization. These results highlight a practical path toward efficient updates of deployed driving models using existing fleet logs.
authors: Yangang Ren, Di Zeng, Jun Li, Zirui Li, Chengjiang Zhang, Xiaoqing Ye, Ji Tao, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses late or unnecessary human interventions that can make direct imitation unsafe or overly conservative.
Generates candidate trajectories by augmenting model plans and shifting human corrections earlier.

Closed-loop tests on reconstructed real-world scenarios show the highest overall success rate versus the deployed model, direct imitation, and trajectory post-optimization.

papers.abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.
authors: Johannes Mootz, Mani Amani, Reza Akhavian
bullets: Latent safety filters may reject many safe actions even when calibrated to accept unsafe actions only rarely.
The proposed overlap groups similar latents and actions into cells and measures the share of safe transitions in cells containing both safe and unsafe outcomes.
The overlap is proven to be the minimum fraction of safe transitions any cell-level filter must reject to accept no unsafe transitions in the data.
The framework applies to arbitrary latents and compares safety prediction via a classifier, the world model, or a separate encoder.
In visual navigation, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, rejects the fewest safe actions at the same conformal level, and enables the planner to reach the most goals.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).
authors: Anas Anwarul Haq Khan, Amrin Kareem, Muhammad Umer Sheikh, Biplab Banerjee, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Problem: 2D visual encoders and unreliable monocular depth struggle with long-range distances, altitude selection, and coordinating forward/downward views.
Method: Lift depth from both cameras into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV frame, while aligning visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model during training.
The two components address complementary failure modes: explicit 3D lifting reduces collisions, while implicit geometry alignment improves target completion.
GRID raises target-reaching from 61.5% to 69.5% and task completion after reaching the target from 57.7% to 61.4%, with reported statistical significance.
On TravelUAV, GRID achieves the best success rate across all splits, with relative gains of 9.5%–25.4% over the prior state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of GRID on a real TravelUAV frame, following one token on a utility pole (yellow). Top: explicit 3D lifting (Sec. 3.2). The frozen depth model Φ predicts range maps Dc (on the flat ground below the UAV, range grows radially). The token keeps four depth samples di,s, whose mean would land in empty space. papers.abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) enables fine-grained sensing of spatial relationships between wireless devices. The WiFi Sensor for Robotics (WSR) toolbox demonstrated that WiFi-CSI measurements collected during robot motion, combined with odometry, can be used to synthesize virtual antenna arrays, enabling motion-induced bearing estimation in multi-robot experiments. However, deploying the WSR approach has remained challenging due to its limited integration with standard robotics tools and reliance on deprecated WiFi-CSI acquisition hardware. This work presents an open-source simulation framework that integrates the WSR sensing pipeline within the robotic simulator Gazebo. The framework generates synthetic WiFi-CSI measurements with realistic physical signal properties and leverages realistic robot motion required for motion-induced sensing and downstream localization. It further supports processing both simulated and real WiFi-CSI data for direct comparison and validation. Our aim is to make WSR-style sensing accessible as a modular sensing modality for robotic research. We validate our framework by comparing simulated and real-world experiments using TurtleBot3 robots, and demonstrate its use for bearing estimation and robot localization. This work lowers the barrier to entry for WiFi-CSI-based sensing in multi-robot systems and provides a foundation for integrating WiFi-CSI sensing with multi-modal perception for localization and coordination. All code and experimental details are publicly available at https://github.com/baharhaghighat/DARS_2026_Dijkstra_et_al
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of using WSR sensing due to limited robotics-tool integration and deprecated CSI hardware.
Integrates the WSR pipeline into Gazebo with synthetic CSI based on realistic signal properties and robot motion.
Processes both simulated and real WiFi-CSI data to support direct comparison and validation.
Validated with TurtleBot3 experiments for bearing estimation and robot localization.
Provides a modular foundation for WiFi-CSI-based multi-robot perception, localization, and coordination.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of the functionality of our simulation framework (green and orange) in parallel with that of the WSR toolbox (blue). The framework blocks in green involve implementations in MATLAB, Gazebo, and ROS and those in orange involve MATLAB. The WSR toolbox blocks in blue involve implementations in C++ and Python from [19]. Our simulation framework operates fully independently from the WSR toolbox software package as we directly implement its methods within MATLAB. Three steps are included in our framework: (i) simulating raw CSI and robot odometry data, (ii) computing phase using CSI data, and (iii) running Bartlett’s estimator and Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm to estimate robots’ relative bearing and position.

Fig. 4 3D view of the simulated experiment setup in Gazebo with an indication of the trajectories. The benchmark scenario matching the setup described in [19] only includes R1 to R4, while R5 and R6 are added in the experiments that follow. R4 and R5 are mobile while R1, R2, R3, and R6 are static beacons.

Fig. 3 We use TurtleBot3 Waffle robots in our simulation and real setups to collect data. (a) Real robot with onboard UP Squared SBC, Intel WL5300 NIC, and WiFi antenna. (b) Simulated robot with the WiFi antenna at the model’s center.

papers.abstract: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.
bullets: Studies trajectory prediction from V2X-like histories sampled at 10, 5, 2, and 1 Hz.
Uses an LSTM RNN with only focal-agent history, without maps or neighboring agents, and compares it with CV and CA models.
The frequency-specific RNN’s error increased as sampling dropped, by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz.
Its advantage over the better kinematic model remained 24–30% for straight motion and turns at every frequency; for pedestrians, CV was more accurate.
A 10 Hz-trained model with interpolation nearly matched frequency-specific training down to 2 Hz but was 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz; hypotheses were only partly supported.

papers.selection_reason: Learned trajectory prediction under sparse observations is transferable to robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of symbolic recognizers and methods requiring hard-to-transfer dynamics models.
Learns a trajectory prior and runs a warm-started denoising process for each candidate goal.
Steers samples toward observed motion using a closed-form likelihood gradient, then applies Bayes’ rule to estimate goal posteriors.
Evaluated on simulated robots, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories with four metrics covering distinct failure modes.
Preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs during ambiguous trajectory prefixes, unlike filter- and classifier-based observers that may collapse or become overconfident.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Four metric trade-offs across the five evaluation domains. Each panel scatters one point per (method, domain) for the six methods over the five domains. Colour identifies the method; marker shape identifies the domain (legend below). WORD points carry a thicker outline. The desirable corner is bottom-right in every panel; panel (d) reverses the x-axis so lower Brier still points right.

Figure 2: WORD online inference on a 2-goal synthetic scenario. An agent (green) starts at the bottom of a 10× 10 world and must reach one of two goals separated by a circular obstacle; WORD maintains one denoising chain per candidate goal and updates a posterior as observations arrive. (a) Prior. Before any observation, the score network ϵθ shapes Gaussian noise into two obstacle-aware trajectory clusters, one towards each waypoint, and the goal prior is uniform. (b) Ambiguity. The agent has skirted the lower edge of the obstacle but its heading is still consistent with both goals; both clusters survive and the posterior remains nearly balanced. A filtering baseline would already have collapsed onto one mode here. (c) Observation guidance. Once the agent commits left of the obstacle, the score-guidance term ∇τ log p(Z | τ ) (orange) pins each chain to the observed path; the right cluster must arc awkwardly over the obstacle to remain reachable, and posterior mass shifts toward w1. (d) Commitment. As the agent approaches w1, the surviving chain dominates and the posterior collapses. Pseudocode is in algorithm 1.

papers.abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.
authors: Hoang Pham Cong, Long D. Nguyen, Ho Viet Duc Luong, Nguyen Tran Minh Nhat, Binh P. Nguyen
bullets: Targets decision-relevant missed objects rather than relying only on image cues or uniformly increasing resolution.
Builds a decision-sensitivity field by testing how hypothetical objects at different locations would affect the planner’s draft action.
Repeatedly verifies the sensitivity field and the detections supporting the current action until the action stabilizes.
For two planner classes, it is theoretically equivalent to whole-frame high-resolution perception when crop detections and coverage conditions hold.

Across three driving datasets, it matches the full-resolution action on about 98% of frames using about one-quarter of the pixels, while reducing false braking and recovering more relevant missed objects.

papers.abstract: Drifting, the deliberate control of a vehicle at large sideslip angles, is relevant to both motorsport and recovery from unexpected oversteer. Existing autonomous drifting methods typically determine drift intensity through predefined reference trajectories, optimization objectives, or learned policy rewards, rather than accepting a desired sideslip angle as an explicit input. We propose, to the best of our knowledge, the first generative drift trajectory planner explicitly conditioned on a requested peak sideslip angle. A conditional flow matching model is trained on demonstrated drift laps with hindsight-derived sideslip labels and refined through reinforcement fine-tuning. A control barrier function (CBF) correction is then applied to satisfy model-based road, tire friction, and actuator constraints at the planning waypoints. In closed-loop experiments in the racing simulator Assetto Corsa, a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks the generated plans for six requested sideslip angles from 20 deg to 45 deg, with 30 laps (approximately 75 km) per request. The median peak sideslip angle measured across drift-corner passes follows the requested angle, with a mean absolute error of 1.2 deg across the six conditions. Ablation experiments show that reinforcement fine-tuning improves conditioning accuracy, while CBF correction substantially reduces off-road and spin events.
bullets: Addresses autonomous drifting without relying on fixed trajectories, objectives, or reward-defined drift intensity.
Uses conditional flow matching trained on demonstrated drift laps with hindsight-derived sideslip labels, followed by reinforcement fine-tuning.
Applies control barrier function corrections to enforce road, tire-friction, and actuator constraints at planning waypoints.
In Assetto Corsa closed-loop experiments, nonlinear MPC tracked plans for requested angles from 20° to 45° across 30 laps per condition.
Ablations indicate reinforcement fine-tuning improves angle conditioning, while CBF correction reduces off-road and spin events.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' mobile manipulator robot, developed at the Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Shahid Beheshti University. Hereafter, this platform is referred to as the @Work Robot. The robot targets industrial tasks, with an emphasis on improving efficiency in repetitive or hazardous work environments. It uses a 4-wheel Mecanum drive for omnidirectional movement and a 5-degree-of-freedom manipulator arm with a 3D-printed gripper for object handling and navigation. The electronics consist of custom PCB boards built around ESP32 microcontrollers, together with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX that handles high-level processing and real-time system control. On the software side, Hector SLAM provides mapping and localization, A* handles path planning, and YOLO performs real-time object detection. These modules draw on fused sensor data to deliver robust navigation and reliable collision avoidance. Overall, the system shows effective hardware-software integration, with consistent performance in autonomous navigation, object handling, and task execution in industrial-like settings.

papers.abstract: An agent or robot in a scanned building must locate its camera in rooms that no model saw during training. Point cloud registration methods can align each RGB-D frame with the building's colored point cloud, accurately but at a high cost. We observe that geometric refinement brings nearby initial poses to the same final pose, so the learned component only needs to find the place. Kolibri does this with a graph network of 55,712 parameters that describes 10 cm cubes of points, called cells, by their color, local shape and neighbors. With the same refinement, it matches GeDi on 96 unseen ScanNet rooms (81.4% against 80.3% within 5 cm and 5{\deg}) and on a held-out test of 10 further rooms, in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti. The saved time allows for search without a room label. In one point cloud of 100 rooms, Kolibri loses 1.3 points against knowing the room, while retrieving the room first loses 56.0. In a hospital emergency department scene from a real scan, it localizes 86.5% of the frames rendered from the scan in 384 ms each, where GeDi needs 91 minutes per frame on cubes of the scan for a similar recall. The method needs colors that agree between the frame and the point cloud. On gray frames and across cameras with different color responses, point cloud registration methods keep the lead.
authors: Leonel Aguilar, Bartu Tuncay, Christoph Hoelscher
bullets: Addresses fast localization in previously unseen rooms from colored point clouds.
A 55,712-parameter graph network represents 10 cm point-cloud cells using color, local shape, and neighboring cells.
Matches GeDi on unseen ScanNet rooms: 81.4% vs. 80.3% within 5 cm and 5°; runs in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti.
Efficient search largely removes the need for a known room label, losing only 1.3 points versus room-aware retrieval in a 100-room cloud.
Performance depends on consistent colors between the RGB-D frame and point cloud; gray frames and cross-camera color differences favor registration methods.

papers.abstract: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.
authors: Mohammad Nomaan Husain, Tanja Katharina Kaiser
bullets: Addresses collective estimation when robot observations are noisy and sensor faults vary over time.
Extends the DeGroot-Friedkin model by weighting peers according to retrospective predictive performance.
Supports decentralized, asynchronous communication without requiring sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models.
In simulated collective navigation, it produced more stable estimates and sustained decision criteria more reliably than three baselines, but required longer decision times.
Performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection.

papers.abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.
authors: Muhammad Zain Khawaja, Zaynab El Mawas, Ryota Yamada, Gabriela Cordova, Arseni Lysak, Intisar Chowdhury, Bharat Jayaprakash, Apostolos Georgiadis, Shri Harsha Adapala, Jatin Gautam, Christoph Bank, Alejandra Solarte Uscategui, Atanasko Boris Mitrev, Hassan Ali Ansari, Nishad Sahu
bullets: Targets real-time end-to-end autonomy across advanced driver assistance and robotaxi research.
Uses a temporal bird’s-eye-view architecture with multi-camera perception, HD-map data, route conditioning, temporal fusion, and a recurrent trajectory planner.
The v1.0 release includes checkpoints, training/evaluation code, and an experiment-visualization dashboard.
On KITScenes validation, it reports 0.745 m ADE and 2.020 m FDE over a three-second horizon.
Includes preliminary real-vehicle research, but remains an early release with open-loop evaluation and no validated closed-loop autonomy.

papers.title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis

papers.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.
authors: Weitao An, Chenghao Xu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based end-to-end autonomous driving models have shown strong potential in generating multimodal planning trajectories. However, their performance still depends heavily on trajectory initialization, mode evaluation, and supervision quality. Weakly constrained noisy initialization may introduce infeasible proposals and increase the burden of denoising. Moreover, selecting the optimal mode remains challenging when candidate trajectories are geometrically similar but differ in safety, interaction risk, and progress. To address these issues, we propose FIRE-Drive, a feasibility-informed risk evaluation framework for end-to-end autonomous driving. FIRE-Drive improves diffusion-based planning through dynamic feasible anchor initialization, candidate-specific bird's-eye-view risk evidence, and compact high-quality candidate supervision with lightweight refinement. This design aligns the initial support, risk-aware scoring, and multimodal supervision of trajectory modes under a unified planning objective. It enables the diffusion decoder to focus on refining plausible trajectories while the scorer distinguishes modes using local risk evidence. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 show that FIRE-Drive achieves a Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 with a ResNet34 backbone. Additional closed-loop evaluation on 220 Bench2Drive routes yields a Driving Score of 71.43 and a Success Rate of 42.73%. Component ablations and a scorer comparison under matched candidate inputs support the contributions of feasible initialization, auxiliary supervision, and risk-informed selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/Latte00/FIRE-drive.
authors: Qifeng Xie, Kai-Yuan Feng, Wenkang Wan, Yue Wu, Maoguo Gong, Kai Sheng

papers.abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl
authors: Abdullah Waqar Malik, Hamza Tariq, Adeel Akhtar

An interval branch-and-bound inner layer is formally verified, while a learned outer layer is evaluated on samples.

papers.abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Ying Wu, Chen Jiang, Randy Freeman
bullets: Addresses the limitation of binary safety constraints in safety-critical navigation.
Estimates kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal risks for objects and people.

Uses a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as an online safety filter.
Demonstrated in a simulated restaurant scene; broader real-world performance is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.

papers.abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
authors: Samuel Sch\"onherr, G\"unther Waxenegger-Wilfing, Sascha Ranftl
bullets: Standard PINNs enforce initial and terminal states with weighted penalties, making training sensitive to loss-weight choices.

This converts constrained, multi-objective training into unconstrained single-objective thrust minimization over admissible trajectories.
Numerical experiments show improved convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
The approach leverages the low-dimensional boundary structure of trajectory optimization problems.

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

papers.abstract: This paper presents FlowRRT, a kinodynamic planner for agile monoped hopping on discrete terrain. Steering for kinodynamic RRT on complex dynamical systems currently relies on motion primitives or closed-loop policies, limiting the diversity of motions or the planning speed. Distilling a trajectory optimizer avoids both, but existing methods regress a single solution per query, which fails on monoped hopping, where the feasible action set is narrow and disconnected. Our key insight is to treat steering as set-valued and predict the distribution of feasible actions instead. A multi-start MPPI expert collects the entire feasible set of each query offline, and conditional flow matching distills it into a generative sampler. With this sampler, FlowRRT coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and finds non-greedy maneuvers that are hard for reactive policies to discover. Benchmarks across different terrains show higher success rates and substantially shorter planning times than sampling-based baselines. On terrains with inclined platforms, FlowRRT reaches $80\%$ success within $1$~s, versus $24$~s for RL-RRT and $77$~s for SST. Sim-to-sim tracking in MuJoCo confirms accurate execution under full-order dynamics.
authors: Yue Qin, Denglin Cheng, Jingyu Liu, Yanran Ding
bullets: Addresses kinodynamic planning challenges caused by narrow, disconnected feasible action sets in monoped hopping.
Uses multi-start MPPI to collect feasible action sets offline, then applies conditional flow matching to learn a generative steering sampler.
Coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and discovers non-greedy maneuvers beyond reactive policies.
Outperforms sampling-based baselines in terrain benchmarks, including 80% success within 1 s on inclined platforms versus 24 s for RL-RRT and 77 s for SST.
MuJoCo sim-to-sim tracking confirms execution under full-order dynamics.

papers.abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.
authors: Shivin Mangal, Divyansh Chawla, Anshu Garg, Isshaan Singh
bullets: Models bird movement as pollution-aware reinforcement learning grounded in environmental outcomes rather than human or synthetic preferences.
Combines Xeno-canto bird-call metadata, geographic state boundaries, spatial discretization, and a precomputed AQI matrix.
Uses structured AQI lookup instead of repeated real-time API queries to improve training and execution efficiency.
Compares DQN with Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration; the abstract reports stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance for DQN.
Scope is a simulation-based framework for ecological decision modeling, not a direct account of real bird trajectories.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.
authors: Baiting Luo, Shatadal Mishra, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar
bullets: Addresses the cost of repeated history encoding and iterative video generation in driving-oriented video foundation models.
Uses causal autoregressive temporal modeling to incrementally update visual context from a single front camera.
Computes future features in one forward pass to condition trajectory generation, avoiding iterative video generation.
Applies reinforcement learning to optimize driving rewards and improve the policy.
Achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1; it also performs well in continuous dynamic driving while retaining visual history.

papers.abstract: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.
authors: Alejandro Casado-P\'erez, Marija Popovi\'c, Daniel Guti\'errez-Reina, Sergio L. Toral., Samuel Yanes
bullets: Multi-ASV monitoring must reconstruct heterogeneous oil-spill fields from sparse, noisy measurements under time and energy constraints.
The study evaluates Evidential Deep Learning, Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and Gaussian Processes within closed-loop IPP using five planners.
Across 60 physics-based maps, the information model explains 80% of final reconstruction-error variance, compared with 1% for the planner among deep models.
EDL achieves the lowest error and highest IoU under every planner, is best calibrated, and runs in 3.9 ms per step.
Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error increases, highlighting the need for uncertainty models robust to planner-collected data.

papers.abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between ring-free, front-facing hybrid solid-state LiDAR and methods designed for spinning 360° LiDAR.
Traces each scan curve and detects two geometric cues: height steps and range fold-backs.
Introduces HySoLiD-Drive, a benchmark with 100 labeled and 7,000 unlabeled real-driving frames from two vehicles.
Reports 0.907 road IoU and 0.896 ground IoU, with over 0.96 precision and roughly 22 ms per frame on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Formation maneuver control enables a multiagent system to cooperatively navigate through constrained environments in collective motion. While various formation controllers exist, they rely heavily on high-quality and dynamically feasible reference trajectories provided a priori, making formation motion planning (FMP) essential. To address the computational challenges for high-dimensional joint trajectories faced by conventional constrained optimization-based solutions, this paper introduces a hybrid optimization-generative framework with a focus on affine formations, which provide the necessary spatial flexibility. By formulating the planning task as a constrained Maximum-a-Posteriori estimation, we decouple multiagent objectives to leverage pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors for dynamic feasibility, obstacle avoidance, and smoothness. We then interleave the generative process with projected gradient descent (PGD) to strictly enforce affine geometric constraints with safety guarantees. Simulations demonstrate that our framework generates highly smooth, collision-free plans that are readily trackable by common distributed controllers and outperforms state-of-the-art planners in various metrics.
authors: Zhonggang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Raj Thilak Rajan
bullets: Targets the computational difficulty of planning high-dimensional joint trajectories for formation motion.
Formulates planning as constrained maximum-a-posteriori estimation using pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors.
Interleaves diffusion sampling with projected gradient descent to enforce affine formation constraints and safety.
Simulations show smooth, collision-free, controller-trackable plans with strong performance across multiple metrics.
Scope: focuses on affine formations and simulation-based evaluation.
