papers.abstract: Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.
authors: Shaobo Yang, Zichen Ai, Ziyang Ma, Qian Yang, Bin Fang
bullets: Expert actions show meaningful temporal dependence: ordered demonstrations outperform shuffled ones.
LG-DKGP combines recent and long-range action history with a neural continuation and temporal Gaussian-process residual.

The planner reaches 87.07% macro success, compared with 71.03% for INTACT, 61.66% for PRISM, and 58.66% for LeWM.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable future prediction in latent space without pixel reconstruction. However, latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans. We present ActWorld-JEPA, a joint-embedding formulation for candidate-based driving. Where Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction, then combines the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention; Relational Residual Reranking ($R^3$) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, yielding bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. This formulation connects latent prediction to candidate selection using only observed context and proposed trajectories at inference. Benchmark-specific implementations report 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback, and 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively. The nuScenes evaluation reports a mean $L_2$ error of 1.20 m and a predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1--6 s. This work provides an effective path from JEPA's predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.
authors: Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Caiyan Jia, Lei Yang, Lin Liu, Yuchen Liu, Ziyang Liu, Zirui Li, Gang Wang, Peiliang Wu, Li Wang, Yadan Luo, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the gap between latent future-prediction consistency and the relative quality of candidate driving plans.
Uses Plan-Conditioned JEPA to predict future latent states from scene context and global/step-wise trajectory intentions.
Applies Relational Residual Reranking to model plan–future agreement and discrepancy, producing gated corrections to base planning scores.
Reports 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 91.6/42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest/navhard, and 1.20 m mean L2 error with 0.76% predicted collision rate on nuScenes.
Inference uses only observed context and proposed trajectories; the reported selector is calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback.

papers.abstract: We study robot navigation in indoor environments from fixed exocentric cameras (infrastructure-mounted, external to the robot). We show that standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which succeeds with onboard cameras, fails to learn this navigation end-to-end in our setup. This failure results from the perspective mismatch between exocentric observations and egocentric action and goal formulations, which is too complex to resolve from the reward signal alone. To address this, we propose Viewpoint-Invariant Navigation from Exocentric Cameras (VINE). VINE uses an obstacle map estimation network, trained with supervised learning, that takes exocentric images, camera pose, robot pose, and room dimensions as input and produces a viewpoint-invariant obstacle map. This map can be used either by a PPO policy or by a planner such as A*. VINE's map estimation performs better than perspective mapping approaches, handles cameras placed across a wide range of positions and orientations without view-specific tuning, requires only approximate camera pose estimates (noise with a standard deviation of 30cm per axis in x, y, and z and about 20{\deg} of rotation error on average), is robust to intrinsic variation, and extends to two-camera setups with partial coverage. Despite operating from cameras randomized in position during evaluation, VINE surpasses the navigation success rate of PPO with an onboard camera in simulated environments.
authors: Raul Steinmetz, Jair Augusto Bottega, Ayanori Yorozu, Akihisa Ohya
bullets: Standard PPO fails end-to-end because exocentric observations mismatch egocentric actions and goals.
VINE estimates obstacle maps from images, camera and robot poses, and room dimensions using supervised learning.
The maps support either PPO policies or classical planners such as A*.
It works across varied camera positions and orientations, tolerates approximate poses and intrinsic variation, and supports partially covering two-camera setups.
In simulation, VINE outperforms PPO using an onboard camera despite randomized camera placement at evaluation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of VINE. The figure shows one of the two options for the controller, in which the map is warped to the robot’s egocentric frame (green) using the robot’s pose and used by a reinforcement-learned policy (red) to select actions, while in the other option a planner such as A* acts directly on the global map. Within a camera setup, VINE handles randomized camera poses without retraining.

Fig. 3. Qualitative results of VINE with the PPO controller in the Random Camera Double setup. papers.abstract: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.
authors: Fabian Deuser, Peter Mortimer, Robin-Nico Kampa, Anna B\"o{\ss}end\"orfer, Mirko M\"ahlisch, Martin Werner, Norbert Oswald
bullets: Targets ground-to-aerial localization when GNSS is unreliable, especially in forests, fields, and rural tracks.
Provides 9,356 georeferenced scenes near Munich across four seasons, pairing aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB and 3D LiDAR.
Includes paved/unpaved terrain labels and seasonal variation to study terrain structure and appearance gaps.
Fine-tuned state-of-the-art baselines degrade substantially off-road, while the proposed RGB–LiDAR baseline improves localization performance.
Data and baselines are publicly released for future research.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured off-road terrain, providing a valuable resource for evaluating navigation and perception methods in challenging environments.
papers.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain
papers.tldr: GOOSELoc introduces a multimodal benchmark showing that cross-view localization methods struggle in seasonal, unstructured off-road environments and benefit from combining RGB imagery with LiDAR.

papers.abstract: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($\kappa = 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($\kappa = 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.
authors: Abdalmalek Aburaddaha, Zaid A. El Shair, Ali Al-Bustami, Samir A. Rawashdeh
bullets: Pothole detectors locate defects but generally do not assess severity or recommend actions; single-image severity estimation is inherently ambiguous.

The five-stage offline pipeline applies perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro classification with composite risk scoring, and warning generation.

Geometric grounding substantially changes warnings: it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier, increases critical-tier assignments by 109%, and is preferred 3.5:1 over image-only warnings in a blind study.

Severity agreement is weak with both human references and measured depth, although predictions preserve the ordering of measured depths; the categories should be interpreted as visual perceptions, not depth estimates.
The system costs USD 0.105 per scene and is intended for large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; maneuver suggestions are advisory and not validated vehicle guidance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the five-stage modular pothole hazard assessment framework. Stage 1 applies perspective transformation to raw dashcam imagery. Stage 2 performs zero-shot pothole segmentation using SAM. Stage 3 extracts deterministic geometric features from segmentation masks. Stage 4 performs VLM-based severity classification grounded in geometric context and computes composite risk scores. Stage 5 generates natural language warnings with maneuver recommendations. Structured outputs are passed sequentially between stages.

Fig. 5. Warning urgency distribution across all 1,119 scenes for the imageonly and hybrid methods. The hybrid pipeline shifts a substantial portion of high-urgency assignments to medium while increasing critical-tier assignments.

Middle: warning produced by the image-only baseline, which describes the scene in generic terms. Fig. 7. Qualitative warning-generation example for a high-hazard scene. Top: dashcam image with annotated pothole bounding boxes. Middle: warning produced by the image-only baseline. Bottom: warning produced by the multimodal hybrid pipeline, which combines the same visual input with the deterministic geometric feature vector. The hybrid output localizes hazards to wheel paths, recommends a specific steering offset, and reports a composite risk score.

papers.title: Pothole Risk Assessment with Geometrically Grounded Vision Language Models

papers.abstract: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.
authors: Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Filip Rybansky, Quoc Vuong, Frank Guerin, Andrew Gilbert
bullets: Introduces sub-action detection, requiring explicit recognition of hand roles and manipulated objects during high-level actions.
Adds FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention module that emphasizes action-relevant visual cues without changing the underlying vision or language encoders.
Uses MetaLoss, a masked object-weighted loss that prioritizes visually grounded terms.
Introduces BiScopeCap-100K, a densely captioned egocentric video dataset with hand-role, object, action, and spatial metadata.
Improves action, hand-role, and object recognition across evaluated Video-LLM backbones, with the strongest aggregate performance among tested configurations on BiScopeCap.

papers.abstract: This work addresses the problem of finding a concealed object in an environment by unifying formalisms for partially observable environments with multi-modal priors drawn from a mix of ontologies, semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs. We propose a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP (CA-MOMDP), a Bayes-adaptive setting where uncertainty is over both object locations and which nodes can conceal them, held as a hypothesis with a bounded ontology prior and resolved only by interaction. We define a hierarchical transition system (HTS) to abstract the environment into room and object nodes that can be planned over via our CA-MOMDP. We further propose a COMBS-score: a multi-modal fusion of a human informed semantic network, LLM, and VLM, to initialize the belief over object locations, which grounds our abstractions and reduces reliance on a single model. Belief is maintained via Bayes' rule, which never lets a look rule out a closed container. We prove a present target is found in a bounded number of searches under exact perception and that its location is never ruled out given missed detection under noisy perception. We ablate each component to demonstrate their significance. Across five simulator configurations, from a gridworld to Matterport3D with a real detector, COMBS finds 92-100% of in-distribution and 92-100% of out-of-distribution targets, matches or beats the baselines in processing speed, significantly outperforms a per-step LLM policy at lower cost on the larger scenes, recovers more out-of-distribution placements than a TidyBot ranking, and matches an LLM-only prior at a fraction of its per-decision latency. COMBS is the only standalone method that can declare a target absent at a stated error level, and the per-step LLM policy offered a termination action abandons 12-22% of targets that were present, against 1.6-3.2% for COMBS on the same episodes.
bullets: Models uncertainty over both object locations and which environmental nodes may conceal them using a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP.
Plans over room and object nodes through a hierarchical transition system.
Fuses human-informed semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs to initialize location beliefs, then updates them with Bayes’ rule.
Across five simulated settings, finds 92–100% of in- and out-of-distribution targets and generally matches or outperforms comparison methods.
Can declare a target absent at a stated error level; it abandons fewer present targets than a per-step LLM policy.

papers.title: COMBS: Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search
papers.tldr: COMBS combines Bayesian search, hierarchical environment abstractions, and multimodal priors to efficiently find concealed objects while avoiding false conclusions that objects are absent.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians' psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from $10.0\%$ to $1.33\%$, at a mean travel-time cost of $0.68$ s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies $2.11\%$ of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus $22.84\%$ with generic-obstacle handling.

papers.abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.
bullets: Imperfect detections make both search-location and stopping decisions uncertain.
The method models target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors in a Bayesian active-search framework.
Ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses evaluate these representations and their update mechanisms across detector configurations.
Target belief and its updates are critical, especially as false detections and missed detections become more prevalent.
The work informs world-model design for embodied agents operating under uncertain observations.

papers.abstract: Compositional diffusion planners extend short-horizon trajectory models to long-horizon goal-conditioned planning by generating and stitching multiple local trajectory chunks. However, in multimodal environments, local plausibility is not sufficient for global consistency: independently initialized chunks may denoise toward incompatible overlap modes, producing plans that are individually feasible but incoherent after stitching. Existing remedies typically add search, guidance, pruning, or graph-based structure at inference time, increasing computational cost or relying on task-specific machinery. We instead investigate graph-structured dependence among chunk-wise initial diffusion noises as a lightweight coordination mechanism for compositional trajectory planning. We propose \textbf{M}arginal-Preserving \textbf{C}oupled \textbf{D}iffusion \textbf{C}omposition (MCDC), a training-free inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners. Instead of sampling chunk noises independently, MCDC constructs coupled Gaussian initializations whose per-chunk marginals remain exactly standard Gaussian, as required by the pretrained denoiser, while neighboring chunks receive positively correlated noise components. This preserves the standard-Gaussian initialization marginal of each chunk while biasing adjacent chunks toward compatible overlap-mode choices. We prove exact marginal preservation and show, under a simple multimodal overlap model, that positive coupling increases the probability of compatible mode selection. On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently improves over independent compositional diffusion sampling while retaining nearly the same inference time, and achieves a favorable success--cost trade-off compared with search-based composition methods.
authors: Hengrui Zhang, Qiyu Wang, Yuhu Cheng, Brooks Paige, Xuesong Wang
bullets: Problem: Independently sampled chunks can select incompatible overlap modes, making globally stitched plans incoherent in multimodal environments.
Method: Couple neighboring chunks’ initial Gaussian noises with positive correlations while preserving each chunk’s exact standard-Gaussian marginal.

Contribution: A training-free, lightweight inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners, with proofs of marginal preservation and improved compatibility under a multimodal overlap model.

Results: On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently outperforms independent sampling, with nearly unchanged inference time and a favorable success–cost trade-off versus search-based methods.

papers.abstract: Existing methods for predicting surrounding vehicles' forward occupancy may under-approximate the ground-truth occupancy, exposing the ego vehicle to collision risk, or produce overly conservative regions that unnecessarily restrict feasible space and cause planning failures. To address these issues, we propose FloCOS, a conditional flow-matching framework that predicts compact forward occupancy sets with high occupancy coverage. FloCOS represents the forward occupancy set as a time-varying union of half-space convex polygons parameterized by temporal basis coefficients. Conditional flow matching captures the conditional distribution of these coefficients to govern the temporal evolution of the convex components, trained under coverage and union-area losses that penalize missed occupancy and excess area. For downstream trajectory optimization, the predicted nonconvex union is directly incorporated into hyperplane-based collision-avoidance constraints. Evaluations on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset show that FloCOS generates compact forward occupancy sets with high coverage and achieves a higher interaction completion rate than evaluated baselines. Real-world vehicle experiments further confirm its ability to support collision-free planning in interactive scenarios.
authors: Chuansheng Dong, Yinxiao Zhan, Zongdian Li, Peng Hou, Jin Wang, Jiayu Fan
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between missed occupancy, which increases collision risk, and overly conservative regions, which hinder planning.
Represents occupancy as a time-varying union of half-space convex polygons parameterized by temporal basis coefficients.
Uses conditional flow matching with coverage and union-area losses to model occupancy evolution while limiting excess area.
Directly integrates the predicted nonconvex union into hyperplane-based collision-avoidance constraints.
On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and in real-world experiments, it supports improved interaction completion and collision-free planning.

papers.abstract: The RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition (SPARC) is a new competition under development of the RoboCup Rescue Robot League that uses the Unitree A2-W as a common robot platform. SPARC aims to make research on artificial intelligence for autonomous rescue robots accessible to a broader research community, including groups without expertise in developing and maintaining custom robot hardware. By providing a capable standard platform and established benchmark environments, researchers can focus on autonomous navigation, perception, manipulation, and embodied AI for challenging disaster-response scenarios. This paper introduces the SPARC competition, its benchmark environment, and the Unitree A2-W standard platform. Furthermore, we present the first open SPARC datasets collected during the IEEE ICRA 2026 Legged Robot Challenges and RoboCup Rescue 2026, release an open-source software stack for autonomous navigation, and provide initial simulation assets representing RoboCup Rescue test environments. Together, these resources aim to lower the barrier to entry for autonomous rescue robotics and facilitate reproducible research and collaborative development on a common hardware platform.

papers.abstract: Titan is a compelling target for future deep space exploration, while its extreme Earth-Titan distance and complex environment make continuous ground-in-the-loop planning impractical. Existing planning methods, primarily developed for Earth-observation scenarios, have limited generalizability to uncertain deep space conditions and adaptability to time-varying mission states. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization (PCM-PPO) method for Titan autonomous mission planning. A Titan-specific discrete-time Markov decision process is established to characterize mission feasibility and resource constraints. A system dynamics and geometric model is incorporated to enhance physical representation, including central gravity, J2 perturbation, third-body attraction, and downlink occultation. To accommodate opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension, PCM-PPO organizes predefined and opportunity targets through a fixed-capacity target pool and represents the mission state with a target-wise state matrix and a global state vector. A physics-constrained action mask constructs an admissible decision domain from current mission states, guiding policy learning toward physically executable decisions and avoiding infeasible exploration. An integrated training strategy facilitates policy optimization under coupled constraints. Comparative, ablation, and uncertainty experiments validate the effectiveness of PCM-PPO. PCM-PPO provides a feasible and interpretable scheme for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes.

bullets: Addresses the impracticality of continuous ground-in-the-loop planning for distant Titan missions.

papers.abstract: Vision-based high-speed navigation requires a trajectory planner that can reactively generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from onboard visual observations. Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to vision-based trajectory planning, as it enables the optimization of sequential decision-making policies in complex environments. However, model-free policy gradient methods rely on sample-based policy gradient estimation, which yields noisy gradient estimates and inefficient training. To this end, we propose a framework for learning trajectory planning policies using the analytic policy gradient (APG) method and use it to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11\,m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors.
authors: Jinwoo Lee, Geunsik Bae, Changseung Kim, Jiwoo Kim, Woojae Shin, Hyondong Oh

Achieves comparable or better performance than baselines in simulation, reaches up to 11 m/s in real-world flight, and transfers to a skid-steer robot.
Scope: demonstrated on differentially flat robotic systems, including quadrotors and skid-steer ground robots.

papers.abstract: Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge. We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data. First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length. Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin. We validate our framework on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.
authors: Fabian Jenelten, Deepana Ishtaweera, Pablo Garcia, Liana Margolese, Igor Bogoslavskyi, Luca Buonocore, Jan Migliazza, Aleksandrs Ecins, Annika Wollschlaeger, Dario Bellicoso, Gabriel Nelson, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter
bullets: Encodes trails as semantic terrain layers used for both training and onboard deployment.
Jointly optimizes local navigation and locomotion without traditional twist or pose command interfaces.
Combines a frozen vision foundation model, lightweight semantic/confidence decoding, and LiDAR into a semantic elevation map running at 30 Hz.
Autonomously traversed all sections of a kilometer-long unstructured mountain-bike trail, exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s.
In simulation, failed up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Approach overview. (A) Deployment: The policy, parametrized as Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with three hidden layers, observes proprioceptive states, an operator-triggered stand command, and a semantic height scan. Joint action targets are computed at 50Hz to control the rear wheel velocity, the fork angle, and the two DOFs of the torso. (B) Training: Our learning framework utilizes synthetic trails or high-fidelity digital twins and applies to both trail racing and parkour. (C) Semantic pipeline: An incoming RGB image passes through a frozen DINOv3 model and a frozen upsampler to produce high-resolution per-patch features. A lightweight trainable decoder maps these features to a per-pixel segmentation mask. A parallel reconstruction head, scored by cosine similarity to the original features, yields a per-pixel confidence score. A coefficient assignment operation converts the segmentation mask into a traversability image. Finally, an elevation mapping pipeline fuses traversability and confidence scores with odometry and point clouds at 30Hz.

Figure 5. Hardware overview. (A) The modified UMV robot in a track-stand position showing the three different visual sensors. The robot has four actuated DOFs: the rear wheel, the fork, and the lower and upper torso joints, whereas the front wheel is unactuated. (B) The field-of-view of the cameras when the robot is in a resting position.

Figure 2. Autonomous trail racing and dynamic parkour. (A) The UMV autonomously navigates a mountain bike trail in Zurich at speeds exceeding 5m/s, relying exclusively on onboard perception and computation. The robot masters diverse obstacles, including roots, rocks, waves, and tabletop drops (first and second row). The policy jointly combines control and local navigation, while the two-layered grid map encodes a traversable path (third row). (B) With only the episode length and mesh as tuning degrees, the identical learning pipeline generalizes to agile parkour: A single policy navigates a slalom segment, accelerates up a ramp at 5m/s, clears a 1.2m long gap, lands on a five-step staircase, and executes a track-stand, all within an 8 s window.

Figure 7. Indoor parkour and indoor racing. (A) MoCap-assisted indoor parkour. The parkour track features a slalom segment, a ramp for lift-off, and a staircase for landing. (B) Autonomous indoor racing using onboard perception. The UMV navigates a high-contrast circuit utilizing only full onboard compute and perception, completing 130 consecutive laps over a duration of 891 s. (C) Telemetry of the indoor racing experiment. The left plot illustrates the median base velocity with ±1 standard deviation. The right plot displays a 2D positional trace of all laps overlaid with a velocity heatmap. Red markers denote five phase positions (0: starting location, and 1: full lap). (D) Confidence-weighted map fusion during indoor racing. Top: With confidence-weighted fusion. Bottom: Low-confidence observations from high-speed turns progressively corrupt the map.

Figure 4. Mesh generation. (A) The procedural generation of mountain bike meshes is divided into four stages. First, a cross-section polygon is swept along a 4D sweeping path (x, y, z, and yaw). papers.abstract: We present DroneDiffusion, a perception-aware diffusion planner for local 3-D UAV trajectory generation that explicitly models and avoids failure zones caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces. A vision-language perceptual safety estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that highlights regions of degraded sensing. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is conditioned on this map together with the onboard RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity to generate egocentric 3-D trajectories. To enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time without retraining, we apply training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D Euclidean signed distance field. The model is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on a real drone. Reliability conditioning raises the mean perceptual reliability along generated trajectories to 0.71, compared with 0.63 for a geometric baseline, while guidance halves the collision rate of the learned prior from 14.7% to 7.8%. Perceptual safety conditioning and geometric guidance are therefore complementary: treating sensor reliability as a first-class signal reduces incursions into unreliable regions while maintaining competitive navigation performance.
authors: Ivan Valuev, Iana Zhura, Valerii Serpiva, Miguel Altamirano Cabrera, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Targets navigation failures caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces.

Trained only in simulation but deployed zero-shot on a real drone.
Reliability conditioning increased mean trajectory reliability from 0.63 to 0.71, while guidance reduced collision rate from 14.7% to 7.8%.

Right: scene and reliability tokens enter the U-Net bottleneck through two sequential cross-attention blocks, which keeps appearance and perceptual-reliability reasoning separate.

papers.abstract: Safe trajectory tracking (STT) aims to enable autonomous vehicles to follow a reference trajectory accurately while avoiding collisions. This problem is particularly challenging for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) in highly dynamic environments. Existing non-learning-based STT methods often use simplified vehicle and interaction models to meet real-time requirements, which may result in suboptimal tracking accuracy. Although Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) can help address this limitation, widely used Lagrangian DRL methods often suffer from unstable training because increasing Lagrange multipliers amplify policy-gradient magnitudes. To address these issues, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for STT, called STT Control Epigraph Form RL (STTC-EFRL). In this framework, the STT problem is formulated as an epigraph-form min-max optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we develop a learning mechanism that uses a decreasing scalar related to the epigraph to adjust the policy gradient descent direction without increasing the gradient magnitude, thereby improving training stability. We also develop a computationally efficient ray-casting method to compute a polyhedron scaling factor for safety quantification. Experimental results, including Vehicle-in-the-Loop tests, show that STTC-EFRL achieves higher tracking accuracy than the considered non-learning-based baseline and more stable training than widely used Lagrangian DRL methods, while satisfying safety requirements in connected environments.
authors: Xiaoke Yang, Jin Chen, Yafei Wang, Qi Zhang, Ming Li, Haiwen Wu, Chengliang Yin, Yong Zhang
bullets: Targets accurate trajectory tracking while avoiding collisions in highly dynamic connected environments.
Formulates safe trajectory tracking as an epigraph-form min–max optimization problem.
Uses a decreasing epigraph-related scalar to adjust policy-gradient directions without amplifying gradient magnitudes.
Introduces an efficient ray-casting method to compute a polyhedron scaling factor for safety quantification.
Vehicle-in-the-Loop experiments report higher tracking accuracy than a non-learning baseline and more stable training than Lagrangian DRL methods while meeting safety requirements.

papers.abstract: Learning safe policies that generalize to unseen environments is difficult under bounded actuation, where an unsafe decision may become unrecoverable. Conventional control barrier function (CBF) filters enforce only instantaneous safety and ignore future recoverability. We propose SAFTER (Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability), which embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter into Soft Actor-Critic training. SAFTER unifies current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input admissibility into a single differentiable certificate. Its CBF condition yields an exact minimum-intervention projection without iterative online optimization. In quadruped navigation, SAFTER reaches 90% training success with 30.6% fewer transitions than Vanilla SAC and 34.1-35.1% fewer than current-state CBF-filtered SAC baselines. Across unseen simulated environments, SAFTER improves success by up to 42.4 and 61.4 percentage points over the state-of-the-art methods CBF-RL and SEA-Nav, respectively, and achieves 73.3% and 76.7% success on two real-world navigation maps. Ablations identify accurate differentiation through the safety filter as a key contributor to robustness, in which replacing the projection Jacobian with the identity approximation reduces success rate in a High-Shift environment from 61.4% to 6.2%. These results show that recoverability-aware filtering serves as both a runtime safety mechanism and a learning mechanism for sample-efficient, robust policies.
bullets: Addresses unsafe, potentially unrecoverable actions under bounded actuation and unseen environments.
Integrates current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input limits into one differentiable certificate.
Uses a closed-form backup-CBF filter with exact minimum-intervention projection, avoiding iterative online optimization.
In quadruped navigation, reaches 90% training success with fewer transitions and substantially improves success in unseen simulated environments and two real-world maps.
Accurate differentiation through the safety projection is critical; an identity Jacobian approximation sharply reduces performance in a high-shift setting.

papers.abstract: GAMBIT is an opening chess move in which a player sacrifices a piece, typically a pawn, to gain a positional advantage later in the game. Analogously, in multi-robot coordination, individual robots may need to forgo locally reward-maximising behaviours to improve overall team performance. Such self-sacrificial behaviours are difficult to capture with manually designed heuristics, particularly in dense, interaction-rich environments. Focusing on double-integrator continuous dynamics, this work studies how to learn such coordinated heuristics over motion primitives for multi-robot trajectory execution. Our framework, GAMBIT, first learns coordinated motion-primitive selection through imitation learning and subsequently fine-tunes the policy through reinforcement learning. We further introduce a safeguarded rollout mechanism with backup trajectories that guarantees collision-free execution at all times. Experiments demonstrate that GAMBIT substantially outperforms a range of baselines, including centralised motion planners and decentralised reactive planners, while exhibiting strong scalability. In particular, it coordinates over a thousand robots with planning latency below a few hundred milliseconds in continuous domains.
bullets: Addresses coordination in dense, interaction-rich environments where locally optimal robot actions can harm team performance.
Uses imitation learning to initialize coordinated motion-primitive selection, followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning.
Introduces safeguarded rollouts with backup trajectories to guarantee collision-free execution.
Outperforms centralized and decentralized planning baselines and scales to over a thousand robots with sub-second planning latency.
Scope: multi-robot systems with continuous double-integrator dynamics; the abstract does not specify experimental datasets or detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. GAMBIT framework overview. We aim to learn a coordination-aware GNN policy that provides heuristic preferences over motion primitives. The framework consists of (a) imitation pretraining and (b) RL fine-tuning. The former step learns from demonstration trajectories by treating motion-primitive selection as a classification task. The latter uses multi-agent RL to maximise multi-robot navigation performance through our safeguarded rollout mechanism. The resulting policy, combined with the safeguarded rollout, enables collision-free execution while retaining high scalability.

papers.abstract: Adverse weather and poor illumination remain major challenges for robust ego-trajectory planning in mobile autonomy. 4D radar offers reliable sensing under adverse conditions and direct radial-velocity measurements. However, sensing robustness does not necessarily translate into robust downstream planning, while existing 4D radar benchmarks focus primarily on perception rather than trajectory planning. We present Radar2Plan, a modular benchmark for open-loop ego-trajectory planning using real-world 4D radar data. Radar2Plan connects sensor encoders, scene representations, and planning heads through common interfaces, enabling controlled comparisons between different sensor and planner configurations. Using DSERT-RoLL and MAN TruckScenes, we evaluated seven combinations of camera, 4D radar, and LiDAR in four representative planning baselines and 12 weather and illumination conditions under a unified protocol. To our knowledge, Radar2Plan is the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating real-world 4D radars for autonomous driving planning. Experiments show that 4D radar alone supports competitive ego-trajectory planning and robust performance under adverse conditions. Sensor-configuration comparisons further demonstrate its complementary value to other modalities, while revealing dependencies on sensor combination and planning architecture. The modular design also supports additional datasets, sensing modalities, and planners, providing a flexible foundation for future research on radar-based autonomous driving planning.
bullets: Addresses the gap between robust 4D-radar sensing and downstream trajectory-planning evaluation, especially in adverse weather and poor illumination.
Evaluates camera, 4D radar, and LiDAR configurations with four planning baselines across 12 weather and illumination conditions using real-world datasets.
Finds that 4D radar alone supports competitive planning and improves robustness under adverse conditions.
Shows radar’s complementary value depends on the sensor combination and planning architecture.
Provides extensible interfaces for comparing sensor encoders, scene representations, and planning heads, and for adding future datasets, modalities, and planners.

papers.abstract: Risk-aware planners score paths on uncertain elevation maps using the path cost's mean and standard deviation. Modeling rigid contact, however, requires computing a maximum over several uncertain cells. First-order propagation loses accuracy here by differentiating at only a single cell, while Monte Carlo sampling requires a full path evaluation per draw. We compute the moments of that contact maximum in closed form using Clark's pairwise recursion. By tracking each contact's covariance against the shared map cells, we propagate the smooth remainder using exact Gaussian quadratic-form identities. A contest-depth calibration, fitted once on two design traverses, closes the aggregate standard-deviation shortfall that remains. On 317 held-out rover path segments, scored against a Monte Carlo reference from the same belief, every pre-registered criterion was met. The corrected Clark fold cuts the median error of the mean from linearization's 2.3% to 0.19% and attains the lowest error in the conditional value at risk (CVaR) at the 90% level of every method tested. A benchmark plan costs just 5.5 microseconds on a GPU. These accuracy gains concentrate at contested contacts. While they seldom change which path is chosen on this terrain, the fold still selects the reference-best path in 98% of decisions against linearization's 93 to 96%. On a second dataset the mean transfers, though the risk number does not.
bullets: First-order propagation is inaccurate for contact maxima, while Monte Carlo requires costly full-path evaluations.
The method computes contact-maximum moments with Clark’s pairwise recursion and propagates the remaining smooth terms using Gaussian quadratic-form identities.

On 317 held-out rover segments, median mean error fell from 2.3% with linearization to 0.19%, and the method achieved the lowest 90% CVaR error among tested methods.
It selected the reference-best path in 98% of decisions versus 93–96% for linearization, though risk estimates did not transfer fully to a second dataset.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models provide expressive priors over trajectories, but adapting these priors to test-time constraints requires maintaining feasibility and consistency across successive control decisions. We introduce Persistent Particle Planning (P3), a sequential Monte Carlo framework for diffusion control that maintains a weighted population of candidate plans across replanning steps. At each control step, P3 shifts and partially re-noises the candidate trajectories, refines them under the latest observation, and uses constraint-aware weighting and resampling to select among alternative continuations without retraining the diffusion model. We consider denoising and replanning as one Feynman--Kac particle system and analyze it under an idealized repair. We prove that the re-noising depth controls how reliably a kept plan stays on its route, and that keeping a rare, well-separated route takes far fewer plans than rediscovering it by sampling from scratch. Experiments under multiple test-time constraint configurations show that population reuse reduces route switching and improves success without constraint violations. Because P3 refines earlier plans instead of redrawing them, it also needs fewer denoising iterations per replan. On maze-navigation tasks, it plans faster than both regenerated populations and methods that correct a single sampled plan by constrained optimization. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/p3-username/p3-anon.
bullets: Maintains weighted candidate trajectories across replanning steps using shifting, partial re-noising, constraint-aware weighting, and resampling.
Unifies denoising and replanning as a Feynman–Kac particle system and analyzes route retention under an idealized repair.
Theoretical results link re-noising depth to route persistence and show efficient preservation of rare, well-separated routes.
Experiments find less route switching, higher constraint-compliant success, and fewer denoising iterations than regenerating plans or correcting one plan by optimization.
On maze navigation, P3 plans faster than the compared baselines; scope is demonstrated under multiple test-time constraint configurations.

papers.abstract: Emerging mission classes such as on-orbit servicing, satellite inspection, and active debris removal require trajectory design methods that are adaptable to a variety of mission scenarios. We present a diffusion-based trajectory generation approach for rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) that enables flexible configuration of mission constraints. First, individual energy-based diffusion models are trained to satisfy distinct constraints such as approach cone and sensor line-of-sight from a set of optimized trajectories. Then, at inference time, the learned energy models can be composed with one another, or with an analytically defined energy field, to enforce specific constraint combinations. We validate this framework with the composition of a learned approach cone model and a learned sensor line-of-sight model, as well as a learned approach cone model and synthetic obstacle avoidance model, both of which yield constraint satisfaction rates that are within 1 percentage point of the single-constraint models or higher. These results indicate that our compositional diffusion framework can provide a modular approach to RPO trajectory design and enable reconfiguration for new constraint combinations without requiring model retraining.
bullets: Targets adaptable trajectory design for rendezvous and proximity operations, including servicing, inspection, and debris removal.
Trains separate energy-based diffusion models for constraints such as approach cones and sensor line-of-sight.
Composes learned constraint models at inference time, including with analytical obstacle-avoidance energy fields.
Combined models achieve constraint satisfaction within 1 percentage point of, or better than, corresponding single-constraint models.
Scope is demonstrated on approach-cone, line-of-sight, and synthetic obstacle-avoidance constraint combinations.

papers.abstract: In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has progressed to whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination, which depends on the locomotion controller accurately executing velocity commands from the navigation policy. However, carrying an object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking. Persistent tracking biases can accumulate into position and heading deviations, increasing the risk of collisions and navigation failure. To address this problem, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under asymmetric upper-body loads. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to modulate actor features for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations. Cross-load tracking consistency training compares loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to promote consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads. Real-world experiments demonstrate collision-free goal reaching in all 40 tested navigation trials under unilateral hand loads with a fixed mapless navigation policy.
authors: Xianghui Wang, Aoran Fu, Liyou Luo, Shanze Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses persistent velocity-tracking and directional biases caused by carrying an object in one hand.
Uses estimated-wrench modulation of actor features to compensate for asymmetric loads while preserving reflected-action correspondence.
Trains consistency between loaded and unloaded conditions under identical velocity commands.
Simulation results show improved tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads.
Real-world tests achieved collision-free goal reaching in all 40 navigation trials with unilateral hand loads and a fixed mapless policy.

papers.abstract: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.
authors: Eduardo Figueiredo, Adrien Banse, Qi Heng Ho, Raphael Jungers, Morteza Lahijanian, Luca Laurenti
bullets: Targets high-probability goal reaching and unsafe-state avoidance under nonlinear dynamics and distributional uncertainty.
Uses optimal transport to learn high-confidence ambiguity sets containing the true system distributions.
Efficiently propagates and safety-checks these sets while growing a sampling-based forest of search trees.
Proves correctness with prescribed confidence and probabilistic completeness under feasibility and distributional assumptions.
Demonstrates strong performance on several robotic benchmarks while retaining formal guarantees.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.
authors: Yu Zhao, Hongyi Duan, Ming Yin, Hongyuan Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongzhi Wang, Xiubo Liang
bullets: Addresses delayed failures, tail risk, and unstable candidate rankings in end-to-end autonomous driving.
Uses candidate-conditioned latent future rollouts to estimate distributions of long-horizon outcomes.
Ranks candidates with a tail-risk-aware, perturbation-robust decision criterion rather than deterministic point scores.
Evaluated on NAVSIM-v1, NAVSIM-v2, and closed-loop HUGSIM, where it reports state-of-the-art performance and more robust candidate selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the RiSE-Drive pipeline. Multi-view observations are encoded, and the proposal generator produces 𝐾 ego-trajectory candidates. A future-condition generator predicts 𝐿 branch-specific condition codes that parameterize plausible downstream evolutions. For each candidate–condition pair, RiSE-Drive initializes a latent consequence state, propagates it along the trajectory, and decodes one branch-level long-horizon outcome sample. The resulting branchwise consequence traces are pooled over time and across branches and mapped to ordered outcome quantiles by a distribution head. The final ranking score combines the mean estimate, lower-tail CVaR, and cross-condition instability, thereby favoring candidates that remain reliable under plausible future deviations rather than merely optimal under a single nominal forecast.

Each column shows two temporal snapshots of one representative case. Magenta denotes the RiSE-Drive plan, green the human future trajectory, orange dashed the ego history, and blue the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles. Across all four cases, RiSE-Drive produces smooth, route-consistent, and interaction-aware behaviors while remaining close to safe human driving in conflict-prone regions.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth foundation models make it tempting to replace depth sensors on mobile robots with a single RGB camera. We show that, used off the shelf, this is unsafe: in a simulated indoor navigation benchmark, a standard Nav2 stack driven by Depth Anything V2 (metric) collides in 63\% of 120 episodes, because the model systematically over-estimates the distance to nearby obstacles. We propose a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into \emph{safe depth}. A 0.58\,M-parameter head on top of the \emph{frozen} depth model predicts, per pixel, a log-depth correction $\mu$ and an uncertainty $\sigma$, trained with a $\beta$-weighted Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The navigation stack consumes the one-sided bound $\hat d_{\text{safe}}=d\,e^{\mu-k\sigma}$, where $k$ is set by conformal calibration on a held-out world, and uncertainty also decides which pixels may be treated as floor. The correction halves the depth error (AbsRel $0.262\rightarrow0.134$) and reduces near-range over-estimation from 59.8\% to 12.0\%. In navigation, safe depth raises the success rate from 37\% to 70\% and lowers collisions from 63\% to 3\%, close to the 2\% of ground-truth depth. A constant safety margin calibrated to the same pixel coverage reaches only 30\% success because it freezes the robot; uncertainty-aware safety wins 52 of 56 discordant paired episodes against it. Gains hold on glass, texture-less walls and dark regions.
bullets: Off-the-shelf Depth Anything V2 depth caused collisions in 63% of 120 simulated navigation episodes, mainly by over-estimating nearby obstacle distances.
A lightweight 0.58M-parameter head predicts per-pixel log-depth corrections and uncertainty while keeping the depth model frozen.
Conformal calibration converts predictions into a one-sided safe-depth bound, with uncertainty also guiding floor-pixel selection.
Safe depth reduced AbsRel from 0.262 to 0.134 and collisions from 63% to 3%, while raising navigation success from 37% to 70%.
The approach outperformed a constant safety margin and retained gains on glass, texture-less walls, and dark regions.

papers.abstract: Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model. We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making. To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.
authors: Yuchen Yang, Ming Ding, Xinyu Wu, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Targets photorealistic, metrically consistent world models for continuous LiDAR–inertial–visual SLAM.
Calibrates LiDAR–camera extrinsics offline, then jointly refines keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters using rendering and LiDAR projection objectives.
Reconstructs a globally optimized map from refined keyframes without online constraints.
Relocalizes through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP initialization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement.
Across one self-collected and five public sequences, reports 14.3–19.9 dB gains over the online map, about 9 dB higher PSNR than Gaussian-LIC2, and 86–100% held-out relocalization success.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview. The online track 1O runs an IESKF over LiDAR, inertial, and visual measurements against a compact Gaussian tracking reference, and keyframes accumulate under the five-channel contract into the shared keyframe schema. The offline track 2O consumes the keyframe schema: joint optimization refines keyframe poses and map, after which global reconstruction reinitializes the Gaussians into the final 3DGS model. The calibration refinement 3O is an independent process: the extrinsic is estimated once per sensor rig by direct-method calibration and reused by both tracks. The bypass relocalization path 4O matches descriptors against the relocalization database upon tracking loss and hands the refined pose back to the front end.

papers.abstract: End-to-end navigation in cluttered environments relies on compact visual representations to support collision avoidance and goal-directed motion. Existing methods typically learn these representations jointly with the policy or through observation reconstruction, which does not explicitly specify what information the representation should preserve. Moreover, they are usually evaluated with a single downstream policy learner, although the benefit of a representation may depend on how the policy is learned. It therefore remains unclear how different representation-learning objectives affect downstream navigation performance and robustness. This work proposes DeRep, a navigation-oriented representation-learning method that combines local bird's-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction. To compare representation objectives under controlled conditions, we pretrain encoders with a common architecture and freeze them during downstream learning. We evaluate the representations using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with PPO. DeRep achieves the lowest linear policy probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction alone across all six tested PPO conditions. In imitation learning, both reachability-based objectives achieve higher mean success rates than reconstruction alone, with similar mean success rates between the reachability-only and joint objectives. These results demonstrate consistent benefits of incorporating reachability supervision into depth representation pretraining across different downstream learning methods and evaluation conditions. We further deploy the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning, demonstrating its capability for zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.
bullets: Addresses the unclear relationship between representation-learning objectives and downstream navigation robustness in cluttered environments.
Combines local bird’s-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction; encoders are pretrained with a shared architecture and frozen during evaluation.
Tests representations with a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and PPO reinforcement learning.

DeRep has the lowest linear-probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction-only pretraining across all six PPO conditions; reachability-based objectives also improve imitation-learning success.
A PPO policy using the frozen DeRep encoder transfers without fine-tuning in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor, demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: Existing cooperative end-to-end driving works at Class A (status-sharing) of the SAE J3216 classes of cooperative driving automation (CDA): vehicles exchange what they perceive, not what they intend, so each plans alone when to go, which limits cooperation and leads to deadlock when both vehicles yield or to collisions when both go. We present When2Go, a cooperative end-to-end driving system that learns when to go by sharing intent under CDA Class B or higher. Each vehicle broadcasts its LiDAR detections with forecast motion as instance tokens, together with its plan and intended trajectory. The receiver draws the fused detections, forecasts and partner plans into a route-time conflict map, the occupancy along its route over the planning horizon, on which a planner scores candidate speed profiles. Where two intended trajectories conflict, an order gate, a precedence network distilled from a right-of-way rule, decides who goes first; both vehicles evaluate it on the same messages and so reach the same order. When2Go imitates the rule-based expert of V2Xverse, which sees the simulator's ground truth; stops that When2Go cannot observe within its 2 s planning horizon are relabelled, so that it does not learn to wait without an observable cause. For our runs only, the benchmarks' PID controller steers by When2Go's waypoints instead of the route, and its forced push of long-waiting vehicles is off. With one model, When2Go sets the state of the art on three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks: 97.8 and 90.7 driving score on InterDrive without and with traffic (best published 90.1 and 78.9), 70.0 on the public V2Xverse protocol (best of sixteen rerun methods 59.1) and 88.2 on MDrive (best rerun 85.1), with 95.0% of its vehicles collision-free (87.7%).
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Tianle Zhu, Zhipeng Bao, Yiping Li, Handong Yao
bullets: Addresses the limits of perception-only cooperation, which can cause mutual yielding deadlocks or collisions when vehicles proceed simultaneously.
Vehicles share LiDAR detections, predicted motion, plans, and intended trajectories as instance tokens.
A route-time conflict map represents predicted occupancy along the ego route; a planner evaluates candidate speed profiles.
An order gate based on a distilled right-of-way precedence rule gives vehicles a consistent crossing order.
Achieves reported state-of-the-art driving scores across three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks, with 95.0% of vehicles collision-free.

papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
authors: Rumi Loghmani, Bozhang Song, Victor Alvarado, Aliyah Redding, Amir Barati Farimani

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Mingzhe Li, Bruno Castro da Silva
bullets: Addresses the failure of local safety filters when constraints invalidate an entire behavior mode.
Steers the generator’s behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margins.
Uses a path-space control-barrier-function quadratic program to correct only residual violations.
Provides finite-time recovery guarantees and reduces the burden on path-level correction.
Experiments in navigation and robot end-effector planning show preserved safety, better goal reaching, and less correction than path-level filters.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Experimental domains and test-time safety constraints. Each row shows one planning domain: 2D point-navigation, Maze2D, and Franka 3D end-effector planning. The first column visualizes the original scene and multimodal demonstration dataset, where multiple behaviors can reach the same goal. The remaining columns show three test-time safety constraints imposed on the same pretrained planner. Green circles denote starts, orange stars denote goals, and red shaded regions denote unsafe sets. These constraints test whether a method can preserve safety and goal reaching when certification requires more than local path repair.

Figure 3: Latent steering provides the warm start needed for path-space repair. Stage I performs behavior-level selection by steering the latent and changing the decoded rollout before certification; Stage II then applies path-level CBF repair to remove residual violations. The second row removes Stage I and applies the same path-space correction directly, corresponding to SAFEFLOWMATCHER. Without the latent-steered warm start, the local corrector remains tied to the original rollout and fails to produce a goal-reaching safe path. With Stage I, the corrected trajectory starts from a better behavior and Stage II only needs to repair the remaining local violation.

Figure 1: Latent Barrier Steering separates behavior selection from path repair. A vanilla flow-matching planner may generate a goal-reaching but unsafe rollout under a new constraint. A path-space CBF corrector such as SAFEFLOWMATCHER can enforce safety locally, but may produce a trajectory that is safe while no longer reaching the goal when the selected behavior mode is blocked. LBS first steers the behavior latent from z0 to z+ toward a safer rollout, then applies path-level CBF repair only for residual violations, yielding a trajectory that is both safe and goal-reaching.

papers.abstract: Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents' DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training.
authors: Pedro Antonio Alarcon Granadeno, Jane Cleland-Huang
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics.
Represents each agent with an online Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box whose safety margin depends on state, uncertainty, and response characteristics.
Uses geometric interaction features and a physically interpretable reward to guide learning-based policies.
Across four environments, reports a 2.6% mean total failure rate and collision-based failure of at most 2.3% under tested distribution shifts.
Scope: robustness is demonstrated for the evaluated environments and out-of-distribution actuation and uncertainty conditions.
