papers.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

A task generator creates parameterized 3D and image-based environments with automatic rewards and termination signals for RL.
LoRA RL on generated navigation tasks improves in-domain and cross-category performance, raising native GTA V task performance from 15% to 23%.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors in long-horizon navigation and the limitations of failure-insensitive imitation learning and costly physical RL.
Alternates world-model refinement and policy improvement in a recursive self-improvement loop.
Uses imagined action outcomes for group-relative policy optimization and behavioral novelty/prediction error to build a grounded self-curriculum.
Experiments report gains over training baselines and prior methods, with real-world trials supporting practical applicability.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of translating distant navigation goals into coherent local decisions in large, complex environments.
Maintains persistent medium-horizon subgoals and relevant experience through a navigation memory module.
Uses an action-conditioned world model to predict candidate movement outcomes in a visual sandbox.
A vision-language reasoner evaluates predictions, while real observations update memory and revise actions or subgoals.
Evaluations report stronger gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

papers.abstract: Safe robot control often requires combining long-horizon performance optimization with hard state and input constraints, but existing approaches tend to address this tradeoff partially. Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) methods such as model predictive path integral (MPPI) are effective in handling nonlinear and nonconvex environments, yet their finite-sample rollouts and unconstrained weighted-average update can return an unsafe control. Deterministic nonlinear MPC can explicitly incorporate constraints, but its real-time safety and performance depends strongly on warm starts and local convergence. Hamilton--Jacobi reachability (HJR) provides rigorous safety certificates, but offline value-function computation remains practical only for reduced-order models. We propose ReSQ-MPPI, a reachability-informed generation--refinement architecture that combines these complementary strengths. An HJR value function computed offline for a reduced-order model guides online MPPI sampling toward safe, promising trajectory candidates. The MPPI solution is then refined by a small number of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations in a full-order MPC problem. A key observation is that the standard MPPI inference step is an unconstrained weighted least-squares problem; ReSQ-MPPI replaces it with a constrained MPC refinement that recovers the MPPI update when it is feasible and minimally modifies it otherwise. Simulations in cluttered navigation and autonomous racing environments demonstrate that ReSQ-MPPI improves safety and performance over standalone MPPI, MPC, and reachability-filtered sampling-based control baselines.
bullets: Targets the tension between long-horizon optimization and hard state/input constraints in safe nonlinear control.
Uses an offline Hamilton–Jacobi reachability value function from a reduced-order model to guide online MPPI sampling.
Refines MPPI’s weighted-average update with a few sequential quadratic programming iterations in a full-order constrained MPC problem.
The constrained refinement preserves the MPPI update when feasible and minimally changes it when necessary.
Simulations in cluttered navigation and autonomous racing show improved safety and performance over several baseline controllers.

papers.abstract: For ground robots operating in outdoor environments, understanding the properties of the underlying terrain is essential for ensuring reliable operation. In most perception-based studies, this problem is formulated as categorical classification with a fixed number of classes defined during training. We propose an approach that enables new surface classes to be added as trainable vectors, which can subsequently be used to address higher-level tasks. By employing a learning paradigm based on predicting the robot's next state in time and using attention blocks, we improved classification accuracy to 98.56% on the Belyaev-Kushnarev dataset and 94.8% on BorealTC.
bullets: Targets reliable outdoor ground-robot operation through improved surface understanding.
Uses next-state prediction as the learning objective, combined with attention blocks.
Represents newly introduced surface classes as trainable vectors rather than requiring a fixed class set.
Reports classification accuracies of 98.56% on Belyaev-Kushnarev and 94.8% on BorealTC.

papers.abstract: Ensuring high returns while providing strong safety guarantees in offline imitation learning (IL) is a fundamental challenge: existing approaches either rely on explicitly specified cost functions, which are difficult to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or require expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are often too costly to collect. We introduce dual-expert imitation learning, which leverages two complementary data sources: (i) safety-compliant demonstrations that faithfully follow safety guidelines but may be suboptimal, and (ii) performance-oriented demonstrations that achieve high returns but may violate safety guidelines. To address this problem, we propose DexDICE (Dual-expert offline imitation learning via stationary DIstribution Correction Estimation). Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, enabling agents to exploit high-return behaviors while remaining within safety-compliant regions. We prove that the ideal solution satisfying this constraint exactly has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability. We evaluate DexDICE on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and validate it on a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained directly from human teleoperation demonstrations, where it substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.
authors: Seokin Seo, Sung Kuk Shyn, Minji Seo, Yisoo Lee, Jongmin Lee, Hongseok Yang, Kee-Eung Kim
bullets: Addresses offline imitation learning when safe, high-performing demonstrations are unavailable and explicit safety costs are difficult to specify.
Uses dual-expert data: safety-compliant demonstrations and performance-oriented demonstrations.
Combines DICE-style stationary distribution correction with safe support constraints rather than conventional distribution constraints.
The ideal constrained solution is proven to have zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability.
Evaluations on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and real-world mobile-robot navigation show strong baseline performance and robustness to scarce or degraded data.

papers.abstract: Autoware is an open-source autonomous driving software platform widely adopted by researchers and industry developers. Originally developed primarily for public-road applications, including passenger vehicles, taxis, and buses, Autoware is increasingly being extended to off-road environments such as construction and agricultural sites. Construction sites, however, differ fundamentally from public roads and challenge many assumptions underlying conventional autonomous driving systems. They are characterized by unstructured terrain, airborne dust, continuously evolving site conditions, and construction-specific objects. This paper presents lessons learned from ongoing efforts to extend an Autoware-based autonomous driving system to large dump trucks operating at construction sites. We identify gaps between public-road and off-road construction applications across the sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules of the Autoware stack. We then discuss potential solutions for addressing these gaps, with particular emphasis on ongoing LiDAR-based perception pipeline development and findings from field testing. Finally, we propose a roadmap toward end-to-end autonomous driving for construction vehicles.
bullets: Construction sites introduce unstructured terrain, dust, changing conditions, and specialized objects that violate public-road assumptions.
The authors identify gaps across Autoware’s sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules.
Potential solutions are discussed, with emphasis on developing a LiDAR-based perception pipeline.
Field-testing lessons inform the proposed path toward end-to-end autonomy for construction vehicles.

papers.abstract: Inertial odometry is a compelling approach to state estimation for agile quadrotor flight due to its affordability, low weight, and robustness to perceptual degradation. However, relying only on integrated inertial measurements is impractical, as sensor errors and time-varying biases lead to significant pose drift. Although recent advances have enabled inertial odometry for drone racing, existing approaches show limited generalization to trajectories not seen during training. This work improves generalization by adopting a body-frame representation and incorporating body-frame torque dynamics into the learning pipeline. The learned model predicts short-horizon relative displacements, which are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for quadrotor pose estimation on unseen trajectories. An additional evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets, with whole trajectory shapes held out of training, confirms a lower velocity error on every held-out set and shows that the torque input is most informative when it is derived from the rotor signals. Code, data pipeline and trained models are publicly available.
bullets: Addresses pose drift and poor generalization in inertial odometry for agile quadrotors.
Uses body-frame representations and incorporates body-frame torque dynamics into learning.
Predicts short-horizon relative displacements and fuses them with IMU data in an Extended Kalman Filter.
Outperforms the prior state-of-the-art on unseen trajectories and achieves lower velocity error across four held-out public datasets.
Rotor-signal-derived torque is the most informative torque input; code, data pipeline, and models are available.

papers.abstract: Autonomous 3D exploration with UAVs requires efficient target selection under limited flight time and onboard computation. In conventional Euclidean-distance-based frontier pipelines, geometric distance may poorly represent the actual collision-free travel cost in cluttered environments, leading to inefficient frontier choices. This paper presents a lightweight path-aware frontier re-ranking method for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. The method first retains a small top-N set of promising frontier candidates using a lightweight utility function and then applies time-bounded RRT* planning to estimate their feasible path costs for re-ranking. The path generated for the selected frontier is further reused for navigation to reduce redundant global planning. Experiments in three warehouse-like environments show that the proposed method consistently produces shorter exploration trajectories than conventional frontier baselines, with traveled-distance reductions of up to 14.1%, while reducing exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments and remaining competitive in the third. The method maintains map detail comparable to the conventional OctoMap-based baseline, demonstrating an effective trade-off between exploration efficiency and mapping quality.
authors: Duc Manh Do, Thanh Nguyen Canh, Ngoc Minh Do, Mai Thanh Thai, Xiem HoangVan
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between Euclidean frontier distance and actual collision-free travel cost.
Keeps a small top-N frontier set, estimates feasible path costs with time-bounded RRT*, and re-ranks candidates accordingly.
Reuses the selected path for navigation, reducing redundant global planning.
In three warehouse-like environments, it reduced traveled distance by up to 14.1% and exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments.
Preserved map detail comparable to an OctoMap-based baseline, with competitive performance in the third environment.

The exploration module detects frontier voxels, clusters them into frontier candidates, and selects the best frontier (vbf ) by evaluating candidates according to their estimated collision-free path costs. The reusable-path mechanism stores and reuses the feasible path generated during frontier evaluation (Pbf ), thereby reducing redundant planning and accelerating subsequent navigation.

papers.abstract: Modern object detectors can predict keypoints as per-object geometric features, but keypoints are inherently vulnerable to occlusion and truncation. Object edges can provide complementary information, often remaining observable even when partially occluded or when their defining endpoints leave the field of view. We therefore introduce object keyline detection, the task of predicting a fixed, semantically ordered set of infinite lines per object instance. Unlike the outputs of general line-segment detectors, each keyline is associated with an object instance and identified by a semantic index, providing a line-level analog of keypoints. To solve this task, we extend YOLO with keyline prediction parameterized in continuous Hesse-normal form $[\rho,\cos\theta,\sin\theta]$, and introduce Object Keyline Similarity (OKLS), which serves as an evaluation metric, target assignment signal, and regression loss. We instantiate this formulation on runway perception in vision-based landing, a motivating example containing semantic linear features that remain partially observable throughout the approach. Experiments show that our representation achieves the highest detection accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations, and keylines integrate directly into standard YOLO heads as additional output channels without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.
authors: Leander Fritsch, David R\"ugamer, Alexej Klushyn
bullets: Keylines provide complementary geometric cues when keypoints are occluded, truncated, or outside the image.
Each object predicts a fixed, semantically ordered set of instance-associated lines, unlike generic line-segment detectors.
The method extends YOLO with continuous Hesse-normal-form line parameters and introduces Object Keyline Similarity for evaluation, assignment, and regression.
For runway perception, the proposed representation achieved the best accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations.
Keyline outputs integrate into standard YOLO heads without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.

papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.
authors: Etor Arza, Luca Girardi, Gabriel Maquignaz, Javier Paez, Stefan Leutenegger, Stefano Mintchev, Kostas Alexis
bullets: The method jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque–deflection response of two passive folding arms.
Candidate designs are evaluated in contact-based traversal simulations, with success rate guiding iterative improvement.
The prototype narrows from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm opening at a 2 m/s reference speed.
It tolerates approach-angle errors up to 30° and folds through a 40 cm confined passage.
Compared with a rigid twin, it adds only 2 mm position RMSE and under 1% electrical power during contact-free flight.

papers.abstract: Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle's motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements. We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%-39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%. Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24-42 and 30-44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.
authors: Chinmay Mundane, Amith Manoharan, Arun Kumar Singh
bullets: Defines traversability as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair executes a path while satisfying trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements.
Predicts closed-loop trajectory distributions with a latent-space flow-matching model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features, vehicle attitude, and wheel-ground contacts.
In 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT lowers safe-path rejection to 2.2% and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%.
When integrated into a receding-horizon planner, EGT reduces navigation failures and goal-reaching time relative to two baselines.
The simulation-trained model demonstrates zero-shot transfer to real-world outdoor experiments.

papers.abstract: Global planners for ground vehicles usually approximate the vehicle by a disk, trading safety against conservativeness, while exact-footprint checking pays for every candidate motion, pose, and footprint edge. We present TPS-A*, a lattice planner whose edges are kinematically feasible trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators, built on certified collision checking in trajectory parameter space. A grid precomputed per footprint returns, in one pass over the local obstacles, a certified free distance along every candidate trajectory, so the per-node collision cost is independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count. We prove that this grid never overestimates the free distance of the continuously swept, possibly non-convex footprint, and state the planner's guarantees: collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to its lattice abstraction. Goals with or without heading are reached exactly by Reeds-Shepp shots certified as trajectories of the same generators. An exact independent test finds no collision in its paths. On 300 cluttered worlds, with the true footprint and the same goal pose for all planners, it solves every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of three milliseconds on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X, on par with hybrid A*, 45\% of whose paths overlap obstacles, and nearly sixty times faster than a state-lattice planner, the only other collision-free one; with position goals, eighty-nine times faster than hybrid A*. It matches hybrid A* in automated parking and on narrow doorways, docks a non-convex fork footprint that no convex model admits, and drove a real robot across a university campus among people.
authors: Jose Luis Blanco-Claraco, Shravan S. Rai, Fernando Ca\~nadas-Ar\'anega, Jos\'e Luis Torres-Moreno, Jos\'e Carlos Moreno-\'Ubeda
bullets: Uses a lattice of kinematically feasible trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators.
A precomputed per-footprint grid certifies free distance for all candidate trajectories in one obstacle pass, independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count.
Provides collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to the lattice abstraction, with exact Reeds–Shepp goal connections.
In 300 cluttered worlds, it solved every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of 3 ms; an independent test found no collisions.
Supports non-convex footprints, including a fork shape that convex models cannot dock, and was demonstrated on a real robot among people.

papers.abstract: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.
authors: Gian Luca Ascari, Isidoro Tamassia, Ying Jiao, Luc De Raedt, Giuseppe Marra
bullets: Addresses the lack of long-term safety guarantees in probabilistic logic shielding without requiring a complete environment model.
Learns a model-free critic from one-step shielding signals to estimate whether an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty.
Evaluated on safe navigation tasks in LogiCity.
Achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of step-level PLS and other safety-oriented RL baselines.

papers.abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.
authors: Jingjia Teng, Yang Li, Wenjie Huang
bullets: Targets safe cooperative merging in mixed traffic, especially under dense conditions.
Uses latent-context and action-conditioned models to infer directed behavioral influence, with uncertainty-aware interaction graphs.
Shapes cooperation rewards using signed influence and marginal team utility, while assigning responsibility through excess tail risk versus a safe reference policy.
Applies conditional diffusion for future-response risk estimation and trust-region optimization with adaptive, agent-specific safety requirements.
In highway-env experiments across three traffic densities, high-density success increased 66.04% and crash rate decreased 56.23% versus the best evaluated baselines for each metric.

papers.abstract: We focus on the problem of high-speed multi-robot navigation in cluttered spaces with tight spatial constraints. A key challenge is balancing safety with agility, as existing methods often trade one for the other (slowing down near a bottleneck to avoid collisions versus failing to swerve in time at high speeds), especially for car-like systems. Our approach belongs to the family of formation control methods, in which Ackermann-steering agents coordinate while navigating tight spaces. However, current formation control techniques rely on rigid, pre-defined shapes and transitions that depend on initial conditions, the environment, and vehicle dynamics, and are impractical to maintain at high speeds. For example, agents passing through a small gap must first form a square, transform into a line using analytical equations, and then return to a square. In contrast, our approach is inspired by a droplet of water that continuously adapts its shape to the space it flows through without slowing down. We propose a hierarchical algorithm in which, at the high level, a reinforcement learning policy produces a dynamic, blob-like elliptical patch that morphs its shape in real time, squeezing, stretching, and orienting itself around obstacles and through tight spaces. At the low level, the robots are controlled via distributed model predictive control (DMPC) to stay inside the patch, which acts as a soft forcing function, while avoiding collisions with each other. We evaluate our approach, FastFunnels, on simulated F1TENTH racing cars across 14 scenarios with N=1 to N=6 robots, averaged over 20 trials each. FastFunnels achieves an 89% completion rate at 7.73 m/s, while all baselines either fail to complete the track or succeed only at very low speeds (0.07-1.79 m/s, about 40% completion rate).
bullets: Targets the safety–agility trade-off in high-speed multi-robot navigation through tight spaces.
Uses a hierarchical design: reinforcement learning generates a morphing elliptical formation patch, while distributed MPC keeps robots inside it and prevents collisions.
Avoids rigid, pre-defined formations and discrete shape transitions that are difficult to maintain at speed.
Evaluated in simulation with 1–6 F1TENTH cars across 14 scenarios and 20 trials per scenario.
Achieved 89% completion at 7.73 m/s; baselines completed about 40% of trials at only 0.07–1.79 m/s or failed entirely.

The elliptical funnel patch dynamically adapts its shape and orientation at every control step acting as a soft forcing function to guide the agents fluidly through bottlenecks and narrow gaps at high speed, much like how water flows around rocks and bends. We have tested with N = 6 robots but FASTFUNNELS can scale up to 12 robots as well (beyond N = 12 not tested).

Figure 4: FASTFUNNELS on two Traxxas UDRs (1/7th scale) in a 15m narrow corridor with three obstacles. (middle) FASTFUNNELS passes the same track and another track (bottom) in 1.5 seconds at 10m/s by widening the funnel to 1.9 meters between the walls and closing it to 1.0 meters at the block.
Figure 3: FASTFUNNELS (red curve) at its lowest speed is still several orders of magnitude faster than the second-fastest approach.

Table I: Quantitative results across varying team sizes. FASTFUNNELS completes all 20 trials of 14 scenarios at an average of 40% higher completion rate while being 7.69× faster than the fastest baseline. (See Section VI-C for more details).

papers.selection_reason: Learned RL-based dynamic formation control for agile multi-robot navigation in narrow spaces, fitting learned robot navigation.
papers.title: FASTFUNNELS: Agile Multi Robot Navigation in Narrow Spaces via Adaptive Dynamic Funnels
papers.tldr: FastFunnels enables car-like robots to navigate narrow, cluttered spaces at high speed by continuously adapting a shared formation shape around obstacles.

papers.abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Zixuan Wang, Weisong Shi
bullets: Dense BEV grids waste computation on regions the vehicle will not traverse.
A coarse scene encoding predicts path-related heat, then selectively refines high-heat cells under a fixed budget.
The mixed-resolution BEV covers the full scene and requires neither an HD map nor a navigation command.
With 10% refinement, it uses 28% of BEV queries and 66% of encoder time versus a full fine grid, while achieving lower reported errors on nuScenes and NAVSIM navtest.
The approach is evaluated on two benchmarks and is intended for path-focused, efficient end-to-end driving.

Both encoders read the shared image features and the ego motion embedding and the coarse memory of the previous keyframe. The full grid baseline encodes 10,000 cells of 1.024 m in one pass with the same encoder architecture.

papers.selection_reason: Path-adaptive BEV refinement for end-to-end autonomous driving; fits learned navigation policies and token/cell selection for efficiency.
papers.title: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: BEVCast reduces BEV computation by refining only cells near the predicted driving path while maintaining or improving planning performance.

papers.abstract: Long-term object search requires learning where objects usually appear from repeated but uneven observations of a changing environment. We formulate retrospective open-vocabulary memory as probabilistic inference from censored observations, where the key idea is to reason with evidence per opportunity: a detection or non-detection should influence belief only in proportion to the robot's opportunity to observe the corresponding location. We introduce ECROM, which uses this principle to estimate long-term prevalence for concepts specified only at query time and converts the resulting belief directly into an active-search prior. To evaluate this problem, we introduce a controlled long-term benchmark in ten HM3D homes that independently varies object placement and observation opportunity across repeated traversals. ECROM improves support-level AP on held-out queries by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric. The benchmark, dataset, and code will be open-sourced. Project page: https://jiaming.im/ecrom/
bullets: Addresses learning object-location prevalence from repeated, uneven observations.
Models detections and non-detections as censored evidence weighted by observation opportunity.
Supports concepts specified only at query time and converts beliefs into active-search priors.
Evaluated on a controlled benchmark spanning ten HM3D homes with varied placements and observation opportunities.
Improves support-level AP by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System overview. (2) At query time, open-vocabulary detector responses are lifted to supports and combined with opportunity to infer the long-term prevalence posterior p(θj | Hj , q) (Section 4.3). (3) The resulting belief guides budgeted active search and is updated after each executed view (Eq. 8).

papers.abstract: Existing approaches to offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) struggle with long-horizon tasks. Discounting shrinks value differences between distant states until they fall below the function approximation error, leaving the agent with no signal for ranking states. Temporal abstraction, which treats k environment steps as a single transition, restores this signal at long range, but no single fixed k suits all state-goal distances: large k preserves value differences across long temporal distances while collapsing distinctions between nearby states, and small k does the reverse. We make this trade-off explicit and introduce Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA), which conditions a single value function on k. GITA trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, so scales assigning larger positive advantages to a state-goal pair contribute more strongly to its update. GITA does not need to choose between local resolution and long-range signal; it retains both without committing to a single k. On OGBench, GITA outperforms a broad range of offline GCRL baselines, raising average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL. It also improves over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA, by 7 percentage points (14% relative).
bullets: Offline GCRL struggles on long-horizon tasks because discounting weakens value differences between distant states.
A fixed temporal abstraction scale k creates a trade-off: large k helps long-range planning, while small k preserves nearby-state resolution.
GITA conditions one value function on k and trains a single policy using advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values.
On OGBench, GITA improves average success by 25 percentage points over HIQL and 7 points over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA.
The approach avoids committing to a single temporal abstraction scale, though its reported scope is offline GCRL on OGBench tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed multi-scale temporal abstraction framework. Left: a shared value function conditioned on k learns multiple abstraction scales. Right: scale-specific advantages set the relative contribution of each k value, inducing an implicit soft assignment when training the shared high-level policy.

The strip beneath each panel indicates the factor with the highest correlation in each distance regime; the best factor consistently grows with distance, but its range differs across environments. Inset shows the learned value V h k (s, g) as a function of geodesic distance.

Figure 7: Scale-specific AWR weights across navigation and stitching tasks. Mean clipped exponentiated high-level advantage, min{exp(βhAh), 100}, as a function of geodesic state–goal distance for different abstraction factors k. From top to bottom: large-navigate, giant-navigate, large-stitch, and giant-stitch. Curves show the mean across seeds and shaded regions indicate one standard deviation. Each plot contains the corresponding maze morphologies.

Normalized value function V (s, g; k) on pointmaze-large-navigate, evaluated at every navigable cell for k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 13, 21}. The star marks the fixed reference state. As k increases, the value-sensitive region expands over longer distances while local resolution progressively degrades.
Figure 5: Maze layouts. OGBench provides the medium, large, and giant layouts considered in our experiments, with progressively longer state-goal distances.

Figure 6: OGBench datasets exhibit distinct trajectory structures. Representative trajectories from the OGBench offline dataset variants in the large maze. The navigate dataset contains long goal-directed trajectories, stitch consists of shorter local trajectory segments that must be combined to solve long-horizon tasks, and explore contains high-coverage but highly suboptimal behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA) for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, a key technique for long-horizon robot navigation.
papers.title: Learning Multiple Timescales for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: GITA improves offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning by learning across multiple temporal abstractions, preserving both long-range guidance and local state distinctions.

papers.abstract: This paper explores a reward-based policy to achieve zero-shot transfer between source and target environments with completely different observation spaces. While humans can demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies often struggle to adapt to a new environment and require a considerable amount of samples for successful transfer. Instead, we propose a novel reward-based policy only conditioned on rewards and actions, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations. We discuss the challenges and feasibility of a reward-based policy and then propose a practical algorithm for training. We demonstrate that a reward policy can be trained within three different environments, Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing, and transferred to completely different observations, such as different color palettes or 3D rendering, or Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim, in a zero-shot manner. We also demonstrate that a reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.
bullets: Targets the poor adaptation of observation-based deep policies when source and target observations differ substantially.
Introduces a reward-based policy that avoids dependence on environment-specific visual observations.
Presents a practical training algorithm and discusses the feasibility of reward-only conditioning.
Demonstrates zero-shot transfer across Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing settings, including visual changes and Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim.
Shows that the reward-based policy can also guide training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.

papers.abstract: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework to enable fast adaptation of interactive policies in a multi-agent system (MAS). Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to rapidly adapt to new tasks/environments using a bi-level optimization mechanism. However, existing meta-RL generally focuses on single-agent systems. Extending these frameworks and algorithms to multi-agent systems poses additional challenges, as tasks are characterized by not only the environment but also agents' strategic interactions. To address these challenges, we model multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems as Markov games (MGs) and develop a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. A new concept, called meta-NE, is defined to describe the desired solution concept in a meta-MARL problem. Sufficient conditions for the equivalence between a meta-NE and a stationary point of the gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm are established. Our evaluation on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrates that the proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines, validating the effectiveness of our framework.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting policies across multi-agent tasks that vary in both environments and agent interactions.
Models multi-agent reinforcement learning problems as Markov games distributed across tasks.
Introduces meta-NE as a solution concept for meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Establishes sufficient conditions linking meta-NE solutions to stationary points of a gradient-play meta-MARL algorithm.
Evaluations on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrate faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a meta-MARL framework for fast adaptation of interactive policies in autonomous driving, a core application of Embodied AI.
papers.title: Meta-Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Fast Adaptation of Interactive Policies with Applications to Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: A meta-MARL framework enables multi-agent policies to adapt rapidly to new strategic interaction settings, with autonomous-driving experiments showing faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk. We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation. A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects. The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop. Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.
bullets: Targets outdated scene knowledge caused by changes between robot visits.
Uses probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view selection near the path and uncertain or changing objects.
Integrates perception with hierarchical-task model predictive control, using arm redundancy while prioritizing base-trajectory tracking.
Real-world tests report improved map consistency, lower task-dependent map entropy, and reduced navigation risk versus passive and non-task-aware baselines.
Validated in simulation and real-world sequences with controlled semi-static scene changes.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Our mobile manipulator setup. The system consists of a Universal Robots UR10 arm mounted on a Clearpath Robotics Ridgeback omnidirectional base. Two synchronized Orbbec Femto Bolt RGB-D cameras are installed, with one mounted on the base and the other mounted on the hand. An onboard laptop runs all the perception, planning and control algorithms.

Fig. 1: A snapshot of the proposed active perception and navigation framework for high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulators in action. Equipped with a hand camera, the robot operates in cluttered, semi-static environments. papers.abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different \textit{ex-vivo} porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4\% and 72.5\% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70\% success in 90-degree turns and 60\% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.
bullets: Addresses weak texture, specular highlights, deformable anatomy, and contact-rich interactions that challenge conventional and learning-based navigation.
Uses an RGB-D-E Action Chunking Transformer with RGB, estimated relative depth, and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to emphasize fold ridges and geometric cues.
Predicts overlapping action chunks and fuses them through temporal ensembling for continuous, smooth robot control.
In ex-vivo porcine colons, success rates were 85.4% in straight segments, 72.5% in curved segments, 70% in 90-degree turns, and 60% in double-bend sequences.
Triple-bend experiments further demonstrate feasibility, though performance scope is limited to ex-vivo evaluation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration demands that robots continuously evaluate candidate viewpoints based on their expected information gain and execution cost. Sampling-based planners estimate this gain by volumetric raycasting and, due to its computational cost, evaluate candidates under an assumption of mutual independence, ignoring the overlap between viewpoints along the same path. This work presents a GPU-accelerated method for computing path-dependent marginal information gain, where instead of storing and merging the observed unknown voxels along each candidate path, previous observations are represented using depth buffers. Candidate rays are projected into the depth buffers of their ancestors to identify observation overlap and exclude regions expected to be observed. The planning tree is evaluated in depth order to maintain the dependency between viewpoints and their optimized yaws, while candidate nodes and rays at each level are processed in parallel on the GPU. The proposed method stays within 5-10% of the exact marginal gain computed using voxel hash maps, with speed-ups of up to 118x on a desktop GPU and 28x on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The method was integrated into two sampling-based exploration planners and evaluated in three simulation environments, where marginal gain reduced the time to 95% coverage in five of the six evaluated planner-environment combinations. Real-world experiments also showed a 30% reduction in the time to 95% coverage, as well as earlier exploration termination times.
bullets: Addresses the cost and inaccuracy of assuming independent information gain between viewpoints on the same path.
Projects candidate rays into ancestor depth buffers to detect overlapping observations without storing voxel sets.
Processes planning-tree levels and candidate rays in parallel on GPUs while preserving viewpoint dependencies and optimized yaw choices.
Achieves gain estimates within 5–10% of exact voxel-hash-map computation, with speedups up to 118× on desktop GPUs and 28× on Jetson Orin NX.
Integrated planners reached 95% coverage faster in most simulation cases and showed a 30% real-world reduction in coverage time.

papers.abstract: We focus on legible robot motion generation in social navigation settings. Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently infer the robot's intent. While mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, social robot navigation presents a new challenge: the robot must clearly convey its intent while ensuring human safety in dynamic pedestrian environments where human attention is often divided. With the goal of enabling robots to generate legible motion in dynamic and constrained spaces, we investigate how the choice of representation and the level of human attention shape navigation performance and human impressions. Focusing on the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, we conduct two controlled user studies involving alternative legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 (N = 45) investigates the role of intent representation, showing that passing-side legibility, particularly when adaptively updated, leads to smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than destination-based and non-legible baselines. Study 2 (N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion allows for smooth human motion even under distraction, even if this is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI.
bullets: Legible motion must communicate intent while maintaining safety in dynamic, constrained pedestrian environments.
Two controlled user studies evaluated alternative legibility formulations within a shared model predictive control framework.
Passing-side intent, particularly when adaptively updated, was perceived as more competent and less demanding than destination-based and non-legible motion.
Legible motion enabled smoother human movement under distraction, although subjective ratings did not always show the same effect.
The findings support interaction-level intent representations for coordinating robot–human navigation.

papers.title: Rethinking Legibility in Social Robot Hallway Navigation: Impact of Intent Representation and Human Distraction

papers.abstract: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.
authors: Chibueze Praise Onyenweaku, Toyibat Adele, Sikirulahi Opeyemi Abdulkareem, Obed Honour Eje
bullets: Apparent pedestrian height remains relatively stable under occlusion, while monocular depth shifts toward the nearer occluding surface.
The method uses only the ordering of these cues, avoiding focal-length, body-height, and depth-scale calibration when depth errors are approximately a gain.
It requires no training or occlusion annotations and can check the depth-model assumption without labels.
It detects heavy occlusion with AUC 0.909 on KITTI, 0.819 in synthetic CARLA scenes, and remains effective within fixed distance ranges.
Several tested architectural approaches did not generalize beyond training distributions, highlighting the value of annotation-free signals.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.
authors: Pranay Samineni, Adam Thorpe, John Chubick, Anand Balakrishnan, Christian Ellis, Swarat Chaudhuri, Ufuk Topcu

papers.abstract: Ground robots operating in temperate forests suffer from systematic LiDAR occlusions caused by tree trunks, creating persistent blind regions that degrade traversability estimation. In this paper, we propose FOSCo-Net, a self-supervised voxel completion framework that learns to reconstruct occluded geometry from a single scan using temporally accumulated observations as automatic supervision, and we evaluate cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs. FOSCo-Net consistently improves reconstruction quality and traversal safety, with a gated skip decoder achieving the most reliable performance and significantly reducing false obstacle predictions compared to baselines.
bullets: Addresses persistent LiDAR blind regions caused by tree trunks in temperate forests.
Reconstructs occluded voxel geometry from a single scan using accumulated observations as automatic supervision.
Evaluates cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs.
A gated skip decoder provides the most reliable reconstruction and reduces false obstacle predictions versus baselines.
Scope: ground-robot LiDAR perception and traversability estimation in forest environments.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.

papers.abstract: Inspired by the coordination of global motion and local shape adaptation in snakes, elephant trunks, and octopus arms, we propose a unified planning and control framework for mobile continuum robots in cluttered and confined environments. Existing approaches often address high-level path planning and local motion control separately, limiting coordinated base-arm motion, kinematic consistency, and collision avoidance. Our framework integrates long-horizon trajectory planning with real-time geometric refinement under kinematic and environmental constraints. The global layer combines A* search with minimum-jerk planning to generate smooth reference trajectories. The local layer uses a geometry-consistent inverse kinematics solver and Riemannian optimization to coordinate mobile-base motion and continuum deformation while avoiding obstacles. We evaluate the framework through simulated pipe-traversal tasks with multiple baseline planners and real-world experiments involving navigation among dense obstacles and manipulation in confined spaces. Results demonstrate improved motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability, supporting coordinated whole-body motion of mobile continuum robots in constrained environments.
authors: Duo Tang, Ping Deng, Sophie Armanini, Yajing Shen, Toshio Fukuda, Cosimo Della Santina, Peng Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitations of separately planned base motion and local arm control, which can cause kinematic inconsistency and poor obstacle avoidance.
Combines A* search with minimum-jerk planning for smooth, long-horizon reference trajectories.
Uses geometry-consistent inverse kinematics and Riemannian optimization for real-time coordination of mobile-base motion and continuum deformation.
Evaluated in simulated pipe traversal and real-world dense-obstacle and confined-space manipulation tasks.
Reports improved motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability compared with multiple baseline planners.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near--far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7\% (flat LeWM) to 63.0\% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.
bullets: Flat JEPA Euclidean goal costs may fail to distinguish states by temporal proximity, especially at long offsets.
T2G trains a lightweight metric on offline trajectory latent triples using a margin-ranking loss, without rewards or policy labels.
The metric replaces Euclidean planning costs while keeping the JEPA encoder and predictor frozen.
Diagnostics show stronger temporal contrast and improved near–far ranking on AntMaze and FourRoom.
Across four benchmarks, average success rises from 32.7% to 63.0%, matching or surpassing hierarchical H-JEPA baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of T2G metric training. A latent triple (zt, zt+k, zt+k+∆) is sampled from an offline trajectory, where the near and far states are separated from the anchor by k and k+∆ steps, respectively. The three encoder blocks denote the same frozen JEPA encoder applied to the corresponding observations. T2G evaluates the learned temporal distances from the anchor to the near and far latents and optimizes the metric with a margin ranking objective, so that the near state is closer to the anchor than the far state by at least a margin m. Only the metric network and its scale are updated, and the world model remains frozen.

Figure 4: Overview of T2G planning. The current observation o1 and goal observation og are encoded into latents z1 and zg by the frozen JEPA encoder. A solver optimizes an action sequence a1:H , and the frozen predictor rolls out the resulting latent trajectory z1→z2→· · ·→zH . Each predicted latent is scored by its learned temporal distance to the goal, dθ(zt, zg), and the solver updates the actions to minimize the aggregated cost. The updated actions are executed and planning is repeated from new observations in a receding-horizon loop, while the encoder, predictor, and solver remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Marine surface vehicles (MSVs) have attracted considerable attention for their commercial, scientific, and military applications. Owing to their favorable performance-to-cost ratio, shipboard cameras are widely used to detect and recognize potentially hazardous situations across diverse operational scenarios. However, visual perception is inevitably degraded by restricted conditions, including irregular motion of the imaging platform, adverse weather, and long imaging distances. To improve situational awareness and navigation capabilities, complementary sensors, such as the automatic identification system (AIS), radar, and light detection and ranging (LiDAR), etc., have become essential shipboard equipment. Multi-sensor fusion can provide richer perceptual information and help ensure navigational safety of MSVs in restricted visibility. This article reviews recent progress from intelligent vision to vision-centered multi-sensor fusion for newcomers and researchers in intelligent ship navigation and intelligent waterborne transportation system (IWTS). After introducing the generation of quality-degraded images in restricted visibility, we will review intelligent vision methods for four key issues, i.e., shipboard video stabilization, visual perception enhancement, object detection and tracking, and navigable area segmentation. We then examine vision-centered multi-sensor fusion methods, including infrared-visible image fusion, radar-vision fusion, LiDAR-vision fusion, AIS-vision fusion, and other multi-sensor fusion scenarios. Open-source datasets and safety-critical applications are also summarized and discussed. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future research directions. The collected maritime datasets are available at https://github.com/MAPGroup/Datasets and will be regularly updated.
authors: Ryan Wen Liu, Fengchuan Song, Tianxiang Wang, Guobei Peng, Youngrong Kim, Xian Zhong, Hooi-Siang Kang, Maohan Liang, Junzhi Yu, Shanliang Yao
bullets: Restricted visibility caused by platform motion, adverse weather, and long distances degrades camera-based maritime perception.
Reviews four vision tasks: video stabilization, visual enhancement, object detection and tracking, and navigable-area segmentation.
Covers fusion of vision with infrared, radar, LiDAR, AIS, and other complementary sensors.
Summarizes open-source maritime datasets, safety-critical applications, open challenges, and future research directions.
Dataset resources are provided through the MAPGroup repository and are intended to be regularly updated.

papers.abstract: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, 53% of contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28.5% of test episodes. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, ZipDrift is collision-free in all 600 test episodes and matches the best evaluated candidate, whereas an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor crashes in 4.0% (16.0% with inconsistent expert labels) and critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget in 2.0%.
bullets: Short-horizon MPC is fast but myopic, and optimal cost corrections can be multimodal when multiple maneuvers are viable.
A deterministic regressor may average these modes or depend on inconsistent expert tie-breaking.
ZipDrift uses a one-step drifting generator trained from candidate cost evaluations, without differentiating through the optimizer.
A learned critic ranks a few generated corrections, while MPC enforces dynamics and constraints.
In the benchmark, ZipDrift had 0% collisions versus 4.0% for an idealized regressor and 2.0% for critic-ranked random candidates.

papers.abstract: Adaptive sampling can substantially improve the value of sparse ocean observations by directing mobile robots toward measurements that are most informative for an evolving environment. Recent learned generative ocean models can produce high-resolution forecasts and ensembles at substantially lower computational cost than traditional numerical models, creating an opportunity to use rich predictive forecasts directly in closed-loop robotic sampling. However, these models do not natively provide the explicit uncertainty representations assumed by classical informative-planning methods, and their forecasts often evolve in learned latent spaces rather than directly in physical ocean variables. We develop a multi-robot closed-loop adaptive sampling framework that uses a single learned generative model for forecasting, uncertainty estimation, planning, and measurement assimilation. The model forecasts an ensemble in latent space, decodes it to physical ocean states, and uses ensemble statistics to construct A- or D-optimal sampling objectives. We select sampling locations subject to robot reachability under predicted currents. The collected measurements are assimilated back into the latent state using observation-conditioned diffusion sampling. Across 120 test scenarios A- and D-optimal sampling generally outperforms static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines while adding little planning overhead. Our experiments uncover several scenarios in which model uncertainty diverges from forecast error, motivating future work in uncertainty quantification.
bullets: Addresses sparse ocean observations and the lack of explicit uncertainty estimates in generative forecasting models.
Generates latent-space ensembles, decodes them to physical states, and derives A- and D-optimal sampling objectives from ensemble statistics.
Plans reachable robot locations under predicted currents and assimilates measurements through observation-conditioned diffusion sampling.
A- and D-optimal strategies generally outperform static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines with little additional planning overhead.
Some scenarios show divergence between model uncertainty and forecast error, highlighting a limitation in uncertainty quantification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Method overview. At each timestep, our method (1) forecasts an ensemble of ocean states in a learned latent space, (2) decodes the ensemble to a physical representation of ocean state, (3) uses ensemble spread to estimate uncertainty and assigns robots to informative, reachable sampling locations using A- or D-optimality with greedy assignment, and (4) assimilates the resulting observations via observation-conditioned diffusion sampling to update the latent state for the next cycle.

On MAB, error concentrates around the shelf-slope front and a warm-core eddy, and the spread highlights many of the same structures. CCS errors are finer-grained and more broadly distributed; spread–error alignment is weaker on average across its temperature ICs, although the example shown here is relatively well aligned (r = 0.44).

papers.abstract: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.
authors: Changyeon Lee, Kelin Yu, Zheng Wei, Shuna Ni, Ruohan Gao
bullets: Addresses the limited study of olfactory sensing in embodied AI beyond semantic odor perception.
Extends Habitat-Sim with FDS-based 3D odor transport and dispersion in photorealistic indoor scenes.
Covers gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization as source-seeking tasks.
Provides a multimodal reinforcement-learning policy that integrates visual and olfactory observations over time.
The policy outperforms diverse baselines, offering a reference point for future research.

papers.abstract: We propose MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that equips diffusion-based trajectory planners with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety specifications. Building on the single-agent construction that embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, we: (i) formalize joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets; (ii) derive centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures with provable invariance under mild assumptions; (iii) address local-trap and deadlock phenomena via time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs; and (iv) develop a lightweight benchmarking suite including a multi-agent Maze2D domain. Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines, while retaining planning quality. We provide algorithms, proofs, and reference implementations.
authors: Kiran Ravish, Ankita Kushwaha, Preeti, Pawan Kumar
bullets: Models joint safety using per-agent and pairwise control barrier-function constraints.
Provides centralized and communication-aware decentralized constrained denoising procedures with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees under mild assumptions.
Uses time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs to mitigate local traps and deadlocks.
Introduces a lightweight benchmark suite, including a multi-agent Maze2D domain.
Experiments report fewer safety violations than unconstrained diffusion baselines while retaining planning quality.
