papers.abstract: This paper presents a scalable optimal-transport-based framework for terminal distribution matching in multi-agent systems. While optimal transport provides a natural way to measure distributional mismatch and assign agents to a desired spatial distribution, global discrete transport can become computationally expensive for large-scale systems. We address this bottleneck by partitioning agents and target samples into spatially corresponding blocks and solving smaller local transport problems. Under a mass-balance condition, the resulting restricted coupling remains feasible for the global problem and provides an upper bound on the Wasserstein cost. The local assignments generate target locations for finite-horizon agent control, applicable to both linear and nonlinear dynamics. By alternating local assignment and control, we establish a cycle-to-cycle descent guarantee for the resulting transport surrogate. The proposed framework therefore enables scalable terminal distribution matching while retaining a rigorous connection to the Wasserstein objective. The technical soundness of the proposed results is validated through simulations.
bullets: Partitions agents and target samples into spatially corresponding blocks to replace one expensive global transport problem with smaller local problems.
Under a mass-balance condition, the restricted local coupling is feasible globally and upper-bounds the Wasserstein cost.
Uses local assignments to generate target locations for finite-horizon control under linear or nonlinear dynamics.
Alternating assignment and control yields a cycle-to-cycle descent guarantee for a transport surrogate.
Simulations validate the technical soundness of the framework.

papers.tldr: A partitioned optimal-transport framework enables scalable multi-agent matching to target distributions while retaining guarantees related to Wasserstein cost.

papers.abstract: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,\theta)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc's offline refinement from $T=35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc's published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23-32 pp under wheel odometry and 35-43 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches 100% SR@1m at 9-10 cm median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at 0.90-0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.67-0.92 with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.
bullets: Uses dominant wall orientations to generate a small set of pose candidates and masked normalized cross-correlation to match observed free space to a known floor plan.
Combines a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter with consensus readout, while allowing the depth front-end to remain interchangeable.
Matches or exceeds competing back-ends across reported Gibson, Bonn LiLocBench, and Hilti-Trimble evaluations.
Improves Bonn pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23–32 percentage points with wheel odometry and 35–43 points with ground-truth motion.
On construction-floor sessions, achieves 0.90–0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions, extending to all five with learned wall isolation.

papers.abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
authors: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reliable outdoor, long-range navigation despite GNSS noise and weak vision-language instruction execution.
Uses a vision-language orchestrator to interpret turn-by-turn maps, satellite imagery, and camera views into atomic commands.
A trace predictor converts each command into an image-space path, which a reinforcement-learning policy follows.
In simulation, it remains robust to GNSS noise and produces about ten times fewer crosswalk and sidewalk violations than point-goal baselines.
A wheeled-legged robot completed missions up to 1.37 km across urban, rural, and campus environments, including stairs and construction sites.

papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Junzhe Wang, Jinqing Zhang, Qingjie Liu
bullets: Existing rollout-based evaluators are costly and accumulate prediction errors over the planning horizon.
RFWorld builds a shared scene memory and trains it with lightweight temporally supervised readout to encode future-relevant information.
At inference, candidate trajectories sparsely query the shared memory instead of generating candidate-specific future states.
This reduces computation by roughly the planning horizon multiplied by the number of candidates.
Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive report state-of-the-art performance and more planning-aligned representations.

papers.abstract: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.
authors: Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Saimouli Katragadda, Yuze Du, Zijun Sha, Guoquan Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-level VLA planning and the physical safety requirements of real-world legged-robot navigation.
Combines a high-level VLA planner with state estimation, in-situ 3D perception, and signed distance fields to produce executable trajectories.
Uses a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with discrete exponential barrier-function constraints for collision avoidance under stated assumptions.
The platform-agnostic system is compatible with different VLM/VLA models and is evaluated on both humanoid and quadrupedal robots.
Real-world experiments demonstrate versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language navigation.

papers.abstract: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in https://github.com/startracker0/htce.git
authors: Xiaoran Xu, Yupeng Wu, Tianyu Xue, Xuanran Dong, Yifan Xu, Xiaoshan Yang, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses mismatched region naming and observation granularity while preserving meaningful anchors, branches, and endpoints.
Uses feature and topology subdivisions with semantically constrained reductions to create comparable route sequences and structural signatures.
Retrieves prior successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching to guide a frozen vision-language policy.
Losslessly merges 17.7–23.6% of distinct route descriptions while retaining full task performance.
Achieves the best reported SR and SPL across HM3D and MP3D settings, with gains of up to 4.9 SR points and 2.8 SPL points from structured retrieval.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
bullets: Addresses the sequential decoding and memory-bandwidth costs of autoregressive VLA policies on embedded aerial platforms.
Uses a compact RGB-D ViT, non-reconstructive JEPA-style latent prediction, a five-head predictor ensemble, and two-step conditional flow matching for velocity/yaw-rate chunks.
DAgger training alone achieved only 11.1–21.1% success across six checkpoints; behavior cloning failed on all 60 missions despite low open-loop error.

A map-free shield using depth memory, barrier constraints, field-of-view limits, and path backoff increased one policy’s success from 21.1% to 52.2% and reduced crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, with more timeouts.
Code, a trained 72.6 MB policy, and the benchmark dataset are publicly released; results are limited to PX4 software-in-the-loop simulations in procedurally generated forests.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Aero-VPA deployment architecture. The inference loop (top) runs once per camera frame and produces a velocity and yaw-rate chunk Ct through five sequential network evaluations; the safety filter applies the uncertaintydependent attenuation α(σ̄), the braking envelope vsafe, and the validity horizon Ht. The executor (bottom) evaluates the newest valid chunk at its chunk-local time, converts it to NED setpoints, and streams them to PX4 over microXRCE-DDS; it engages the braking fallback when a fallback is requested or no valid chunk is available. The runtime shield (orange, added in version 2) filters every setpoint against a 15 s depth memory or flies recovery manoeuvres itself; the setpoint it dispatches is fed back as āt (dashed). In the evaluation of Section 6 the companion-computer software ran on a cloud GPU against PX4 SITL (Section 4.6).

Figure 2: Mode automaton of the runtime shield. In FLY the policy’s executor runs and the shield filters each setpoint. In BACKOFF, NUDGE and HOLD (orange) the executor is paused, and the shield’s own setpoint, passed through the same filters, is dispatched and fed back as āt. The radius r = 0.55m is the barrier’s zero; a backoff that ends without an active waypoint returns to FLY.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.
authors: Yang Chen, Bin Wen, Danyang Peng, Hong-Jie You, Zi-Qiao Shang, Lan-Zhe Guo
bullets: Targets embodied and web agents’ difficulty with multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints.
Provides TextWorld for symbolic temporal planning, SimWorld for grounded topological path planning, and DualWorld-VQA for perception, scene understanding, and planning diagnostics.
Finds a gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning: agents miss optimal task sequences and produce infeasible grounded actions.
Shows that perception and topology understanding alone do not reliably support constrained planning.
Datasets and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.
authors: Anh Thuan Tran, Xiyun Song, Yubin Zhou, Heather Yu, Jana Kosecka, Liang Peng
bullets: Addresses in-view scene changes, where moving objects may be transient distractors or persistent changes.
Uses per-pixel uncertainty to construct a Gaussian dynamicity field and prune transient geometry.
Identifies persistent changes through geometric contradictions weighted by rendered depth uncertainty.
On Bonn and Co-Fusion, outperforms baselines on full images and changed regions while maintaining comparable speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. System overview. Given monocular RGB frames (a), SettleSplat estimates depth, then tracks and maps with the DROID-W backbone (b) while learning per-Gaussian dynamicity field δ that prunes transient distractors. During refinement (c), geometry contradiction score g, derived from the rendered map and estimated depth and weighted by the rendered depth uncertainty, is integrated with the tracking uncertainty into reliability map r. Frames before the settlement frame K are weighted by W = r2, while later frames supervise the settled scene without masking.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on Bonn (rows 1–3) and Co-Fusion (rows 4–6), covering moving, adding, and removing objects. Red boxes show the change regions. At old object locations, baselines leave ghosting artifacts, while SettleSplat reconstructs the updated scene cleanly. For added and moved objects, SettleSplat preserves appearance and detail, whereas the baselines blur or miss them. For removed objects, SettleSplat is competitive with other baselines while reducing ghosting.
Table 2. Novel view synthesis results on the CoFusion dataset, evaluated on the full image and within the change region. Best and second-best results are highlighted.
Table 4. Runtime comparison with dynamic-scene methods. We report the tracking speed in frames per second and the average mapping time per optimization iteration. Best results are in bold.

papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit-evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74-147 Hz, 5.9-17.5x faster than the JAX reference hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.7-16x faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.
bullets: Targets the exponential cost and traditionally offline nature of HJ backward reachable tube (BRT) computation for safety-critical autonomy.
Implements the WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs HJI scheme in CUDA for 2D–4D dynamics, including an in-kernel multi-agent label-propagation extension.
Runs benchmark BRT computations at 61–147 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada and at 54–66 Hz on a Jetson AGX Thor.
Matches reference results in FP64, including reproducing the Air3D BRT within 0.04% of the reference cell count.
Demonstrates a six-quadcopter wildfire-response simulation with a capture-basin Voronoi tessellation computed in 4.0 ms per control tick.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Closed-loop wildfire-response fleet under time-varying, non-uniform wind. Six homogeneous quadcopters defend a 20 × 20 km region (cruise a = 20m/s) against three fires. The joint HJ capture-basin Voronoi tessellation, computed via in-kernel label propagation from each drone’s current position, is refreshed at every 10Hz outer-loop tick. Colored basins are each drone’s 10-minute reachable region; red diagonal hatch marks cells unreachable within the horizon by any drone. White curves are basin bisectors. Triangles mark drones en route (with the MM :SS predicted-arrival countdown); inverted triangles, returning; circles, patrolling at home. Red X marks a burning fire, gray X a suppressed fire. (a) Initial state: drones at homes, basins anisotropic with the prevailing NE wind. (b) The Center drone en route to Fire #1 (NE region); its basin has followed it east through the domain. (c) Fire #2 (SW region) en route during the gust, with the wind rotated. (d) Late phase (t = 700 s), wind rotated further: a pocket in the upwind direction is unreachable in the 10-min window.

Fig. 1. FP64 single-call wall-clock at the largest matched grid for the six distinct dynamics: our CUDA solver, the hj_reachability JAX-GPU reference, and our PyTorch reimplementation of the identical WENO5+TVDRK3 scheme compiled with torch.compile, on an NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada; medians of gated runs (5 ours, 3 JAX, 5 torch.compile). Ours is 2.0–4.6× faster than JAX and 1.3–1.4× faster than torch.compile; the largest gains over JAX appear on the drifter and 4D cases, where the fused per-stage kernels, in-kernel BRT clamping, and host-static CFL step remove the most per-step work relative to JAX/XLA’s per-stage materialization. (The drifter_obs and pe_4d_walls postprocessor variants reuse the drifter_const / pe_4d stencil, so they duplicate those timings; their accuracy is in Table II. JAX-CPU wall-clock is in Table III.)

papers.selection_reason: Fast GPU solver for reachability, relevant to safety in robot navigation and control.
papers.title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
papers.tldr: A CUDA-optimized Hamilton-Jacobi reachability solver enables formally certified safety computations to run in real time within robot control loops on GPUs and embedded hardware.

papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pretrained backbones has become standard practice in multi-sensor computer vision---yet two questions remain open: which pretrained weights transfer best to multi-sensor setups, and can in-domain pretraining outperform off-the-shelf solutions? Frameworks like MultiMAE demonstrate the utility of masked autoencoding in a multi-modal context, but rely entirely on dense, model-derived modalities. It is unclear how robustly these methods translate to real-world applications that use physical sensors, where the aggregation of diverse public datasets for large-scale pretraining inherently introduces modality sparsity. To investigate this systematically, we curate a multi-sensor autonomous driving collection of $2.82M$ images from 16 publicly available datasets, incorporating both physical hardware modalities (RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event) and model-derived modalities (Stereo Depth, Segmentation). We use this collection for in-domain pretraining based on the MultiMAE approach. We adapt MultiMAE's loss formulation to accommodate sparse samples, and study the effect of an enforced encoder bottleneck for modality alignment and of additional losses specific to dense reconstruction (SSIM and FFT). We then systematically compare against common pretrained backbones (ViT, MAE, DINO and MultiMAE) across downstream sensor fusion tasks. We find that MultiMAE is a surprisingly strong out-of-the-box baseline, transferring effectively even to modalities it has never seen, while our targeted modifications yield incremental but consistent improvements on multi-sensor transfer and overall robustness.
authors: Fabio Montello, Ronja G\"uldenring, Lucas Mogensen Sandby, Christoffer Koo {\O}hrstr{\o}m, Lazaros Nalpantidis
bullets: Curates 2.82M images from 16 public autonomous-driving datasets spanning RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event, stereo depth, and segmentation.
Pretrains on this heterogeneous collection with a MultiMAE-based approach adapted for modality-sparse data.
Studies encoder bottlenecks for modality alignment and SSIM/FFT losses for dense reconstruction.
Compares ViT, MAE, DINO, and MultiMAE backbones across downstream sensor-fusion tasks.
Finds MultiMAE transfers effectively even to unseen modalities; targeted modifications improve transfer and robustness incrementally and consistently.

papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies multimodal initialization for multi-sensor autonomous driving, relevant to sensor fusion and pretraining strategies for navigation.
papers.title: Do Pretrained Backbones Transfer to Physical Sensors? A Systematic Study of Multimodal Initialization Across the Sensor Stack
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that MultiMAE transfers well across physical and derived sensors, while sparse-modality adaptations provide consistent additional gains in multi-sensor robustness.

papers.abstract: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the ``why'' behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.
authors: Luca Castri, Gloria Beraldo, Nicola Bellotto
bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting causal data and training robots directly in human-populated environments.
Preserves the high-level causal structure learned in simulation while adapting its parameters to real-world observations.
Runs efficiently onboard a mobile robot for navigation in shared human environments.
Reportedly enables rapid sim-to-real transfer and significantly outperforms non-causal baselines in successful and safe navigation.
Scope: adaptation relies on an invariant causal structure and a limited set of new real-world observations.

papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
authors: Abdulla Nasir Chowdhury, Gulpi Qorik Oktagalu Pratamasunu, Kazuhiro Fukui
bullets: Benchmarks 10 point-cloud classifiers across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion using confirmatory hypothesis tests.
Rotation-invariant models provide the strongest pose robustness but rank near the bottom for noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains.
A simple embedding-level invariance loss transfers narrowly, improving targeted corruption families when baseline headroom exists.
On independently designed corruptions, the best standard and rotation-invariant models perform similarly; invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model.
Wider rotation augmentation leaves standard backbones with a consistent, angle-independent accuracy gap under full-sphere rotations; the benchmark and analysis tools are released.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a statistical benchmark for rotation-invariant point cloud architectures, relevant to robust 3D perception for robotic navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.tldr: Rotation-invariant architectures excel under pose changes but sacrifice noise robustness; targeted invariance training can narrow this gap without a clear overall winner.

papers.abstract: Computing distances between sets is important in many robotic applications, such as motion planning and control. In many applications, derivatives of the distance are needed as well. It is well known that the Euclidean distance is not always differentiable, which create issues to algorithms that need a derivative. In this paper, we introduce NESDF, the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function between two general (with mild regularity assumptions but possibly non-convex) sets. This metric is still not differentiable, but it allows us to introduce a generalization, $h$-NESDF, which has a smoothing parameter $h$ such that the metric is infinitely differentiable for all $h>0$ and that reduces to the NESDF when $h$ goes to $0$. The metric is amenable to GPU parallelization, and thus can be computed efficiently. We show extensive simulation results to evaluate its viability in motion planning.
authors: Vinicius Mariano Gon\c{c}alves, Pedro Antonio de Souza Campos Rodrigues
bullets: Addresses the nondifferentiability of Euclidean set distances, which can hinder derivative-based robotics algorithms.
Introduces NESDF, a normal Euclidean signed distance for general, possibly non-convex sets under mild regularity assumptions.
Generalizes NESDF to h-NESDF with smoothing parameter h>0, yielding infinite differentiability and recovering NESDF as h approaches zero.
Designed for efficient GPU-parallel computation.
Extensive simulations evaluate its viability for motion planning.

papers.title: h-NESDF: An Infinitely Differentiable Signed Distance Between Two Sets with Robotic Applications
papers.tldr: h-NESDF provides an infinitely differentiable, GPU-friendly signed distance between general sets for gradient-based robotic motion planning and control.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: The challenge requires training only on synthetic LiDAR while evaluating on unseen real roadside LiDAR and synthetic-cloud realism.
Recovering the correct coordinate frame increased the combined score from 0.3520 to 0.5147.
Per-class NMS prevented suppression of closely grouped pedestrians, raising detection mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295.
Modelling real-cloud null returns at (0, 0, 0), absent from synthetic data, improved distributional realism.
The final entry achieved a combined score of 0.7457, with detection mAP 0.4382 and realism score 0.9251.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on Sim2Real V2X LiDAR detection for autonomous driving, addressing specific sensor alignment and post-processing issues for real-world navigation.
papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A diagnostic-focused Sim2Real V2X LiDAR pipeline substantially improved detection and realism by fixing coordinate-frame errors, using class-specific NMS, and modelling null returns.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: Targets detection trained only on synthetic LiDAR and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, alongside synthetic-data realism scoring.
A parameter-free geometric refinement addressed small-object localization, yielding a reported 86% relative pedestrian AP gain.
Fixing a post-processing rule that removed valid predictions produced the largest detection improvement: 335% relative on the Van class.
Analytical examination of realism metrics identified one component as a closed-form function of nine summary statistics.

The proposed submission methodology combines independently controlled class-wise experiments, enabling pre-submission score prediction and transparent reporting of negative results and data provenance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Sim2Real LiDAR detection for roadside navigation, focusing on geometric refinement and distributional alignment for real-world deployment.
papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A PointPillars-based Sim2Real roadside LiDAR system improves challenge performance through geometric localization refinement, post-processing repair, and analytical realism optimization rather than a new detector architecture.

papers.abstract: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.
authors: Yueyang Liu, Lance Kennedy, Andreas Z\"ufle
bullets: Addresses staypoint fragmentation caused by spatial noise and prolonged signal dropouts.
Uses a dynamic centroid, an n-step lookahead heuristic, and temporal bridging to tolerate drift and missing observations.
Estimates parameters without annotated ground truth through consensus-based structural agreement.
Evaluated on the ExtraSensory dataset against Trackintel’s sliding-window baseline.
Reports higher F1-scores and improved computational efficiency than the baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a robust algorithm for staypoint extraction in trajectory data, a foundational task for mobility analytics and agent localization/navigation relevant to embodied agents.
papers.title: SSPE: Robust Sequential Staypoint Extraction in Degraded Trajectory Data
papers.tldr: SSPE robustly extracts meaningful staypoints from noisy, temporally incomplete trajectories using dynamic state tracking, lookahead, temporal bridging, and unsupervised parameter selection.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in congested environments requires both collision avoidance and coordinated passage. We introduce neuromorphic decision dynamics (NDD), a decentralized, event-based controller, that provides navigation in congested spaces with guarantees on safety, liveness, robustness, and scalability. NDD makes safe-and-live deconfliction a controllable, locally tunable emergent property of local agent interactions, without requiring communication, preassigned priorities, models of neighbors' objectives or future actions, or estimates of group size or global network properties. By design, NDD couples the dynamics of internal decision and attention states with changing physical states and locally observed relative motion. Each agent continuously modulates its speed along its prescribed path, responding as soon and as much as conflict resolution requires. Agents self-organize into disjoint, locally engaged groups that resolve conflicts concurrently. When any group's conflict becomes safety-critical, decision-action feedback destabilizes collective indecision, and coordinated conflict-resolution emerges that stabilizes a safe traversal order within the group. Order persists as conflicts clear, but groups may split or merge as agents autonomously adapt to new conflicts and those with resolved conflicts resume their nominal motion. We derive explicit conditions on sensing range, feedback gains, response time scales, and actuation limits that guarantee collision avoidance and traversal-order formation in finite time with no deadlock or livelock for finite, heterogeneous agent populations of arbitrary, changing size. Computational cost scales with the number of local interactions sensed by each agent. Large-scale simulations, comparisons with existing approaches, and hardware experiments demonstrate NDD in complex congested scenarios and validate its scalability.
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance and coordinated passage without communication, priorities, neighbor-intent models, or global population estimates.
Couples internal decision and attention dynamics with physical state and locally observed relative motion, allowing agents to modulate speed along prescribed paths.
Agents self-organize into local conflict groups that resolve interactions concurrently; feedback breaks indecision and establishes a safe traversal order in finite time.
Provides explicit conditions for sensing, feedback, response times, and actuation that guarantee safety, liveness, and no deadlock or livelock for finite heterogeneous populations.
Simulations, comparisons, and hardware experiments demonstrate operation in complex congested scenarios and support scalability; computational cost depends on sensed local interactions.

(A) The dashed rays extend the currently measured velocity directions and are instantaneous heading projections; the physical paths may subsequently smoothly curve. The intersection of the rays defines the geometric crossing point 𝒒𝑒c and crossing angle 𝛼𝑒. papers.title: Neuromorphic Decision Dynamics for Deadlock-free Safe Navigation in Congested Environments
papers.tldr: NDD is a decentralized, event-based navigation controller that enables heterogeneous agents to safely and deadlock-free resolve conflicts in congested environments using only local sensing and motion adaptation.

papers.abstract: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io
authors: Gaoyue Zhou, Yvonne Wu, Zichen Jeff Cui, Nicolas Ballas, Mido Assran, Lerrel Pinto, Yann LeCun
bullets: Addresses compounding prediction errors and search complexity in long-horizon planning.
Uses a high-level model to sample feasible state transitions and a low-level inverse-dynamics model to realize them.
Enables fine-grained control without rigid macro-actions or fixed latent skills.
Synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, including in unseen configurations.
Improves performance by 38.5% over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion planners and by 135% over single-level world-model MPC across three navigation and manipulation suites.

papers.abstract: Autonomous wheelchairs can improve the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments by providing greater independence. However, reliable navigation especially in human environments is a major challenge due to factors such as dynamic obstacles, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, and the users' need to complete multiple stops along the way before reaching their final destination. This paper presents a hybrid path planning framework for multi-goal navigation in dynamic environments. The framework integrates the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for global task ordering with the Potential Field (PF) method and heuristic local planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) to achieve collision-free navigation. Within this hybrid framework, TSP determines the visiting order of intermediate stations, PF transfers global path information, and local planners avoid obstacles while guiding the robot to the stations. The local planners generate feasible paths that allow the robot to follow the global trajectory and reroute to avoid static and dynamic obstacles. For this purpose, two algorithms have been developed: (i) TSP-PF-RRT and (ii) TSP-PF-A*. The performance of the proposed algorithms are evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded scenarios that contain heterogeneous dynamic and static obstacles. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid framework enables efficient multi-goal navigation while maintaining safe operation in dynamic environments with humans, with TSP-PF-RRT achieving fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances.
authors: Damla Leblebicio\u{g}lu, Rachel Barume, Ta\c{s}k{\i}n Pad{\i}r

Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded environments evaluate performance with heterogeneous static and dynamic obstacles.

papers.abstract: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.
authors: Jasmine Ratchford, Raffaele Romagnoli, Mark H. Klein
bullets: Uniform knot placement can waste control points or poorly capture rapidly varying trajectory regions.
The method learns local trajectory-variation characteristics directly from the system’s initial condition.
These predictions construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator.
The goal is to meet a prescribed approximation accuracy with fewer control points.
The abstract describes the approach and objective but does not report specific experimental results or limitations.

papers.abstract: This paper extends an existing framework for the coordination of mobile agents in unknown worlds, by considering the possibility of dynamic instability. In the original problem, known as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) (arXiv:2512.09495), the multi-agent system must establish a communication network which completely covers an initially unknown constrained space. However, the POCGAGP fails to account for the unpredictability often seen in real-world deployment. To address this, the dynamic case (DPOCGAGP) introduces two settings which can influence the mobile network during deployment: Agent Loss and World Change, which represent dynamic changes to the world. Within this study, we present advancements to two state-of-the-art algorithms, the Centralized Agent-Directed Exploration for Network Coverage (CADENCE), and its decentralized analogue, DADENCE, to provide solutions in these cases. We then compare their performance against another state-of-the-art benchmark algorithm, and show that the adapted algorithms outperform across our benchmark test set, which comprises over 4500 test cases of varied size and structure.
authors: Hugo Gandhi, Edwin Meriaux, Antonio Lor\'ia
bullets: Extends the POCGAGP framework to dynamic settings called DPOCGAGP.
Models two disruptions: Agent Loss and World Change.
Adapts CADENCE and DADENCE for dynamic network coverage.
Evaluates the methods on more than 4,500 varied benchmark cases.
Reports that both adapted algorithms outperform a state-of-the-art benchmark across the test set.

papers.abstract: Accurate BEV map prediction is a critical component of autonomous driving systems, enabling downstream planning and control. Recent approaches such as Mask2Map achieve strong performance by predicting vectorized, instance-level map elements directly from multi-view images. However, existing BEV map prediction models operate largely independently of object-level scene understanding, despite the fact that traffic participants frequently occlude or implicitly encode information about road geometry. In this work, we propose a multitask architecture that jointly predicts BEV maps and 3D objects, explicitly enabling information exchange between the two tasks. Building upon Mask2Map, we introduce an object detection branch and incorporate cross-task feature fusion at both the BEV feature level and the instance-query level via deformable attention and cross-attention mechanisms. This design allows map instances to leverage object context while remaining robust to occlusions caused by traffic participants. Experimental results on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently improves BEV map prediction accuracy, with particularly significant gains of 21% mAP in scenes containing heavy object occlusion.

bullets: Targets the limited object-level scene understanding of existing BEV map prediction methods.

Exchanges information through BEV-level deformable-attention fusion and instance-query cross-attention.
Improves map prediction on nuScenes and Argoverse 2, with a reported 21% mAP gain under heavy object occlusion.

papers.abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.
authors: Markus Gallacher, Vu Anh Minh Le, Matteo Trobinger, Davide Vecchia, Carlo Alberto Boano, Gian Pietro Picco
bullets: Wearer-induced NLOS from the human body can substantially degrade UWB ranging but remains understudied.
The work evaluates machine-learning and lightweight radio link-indicator classifiers, and proposes hybrid methods combining both.
Performance—including ranging impact from misclassification—varies substantially across channels and PHY settings.
Energy costs differ sharply: some methods provide only marginal accuracy gains while using up to 39.6× more energy.
A recommender tool helps select classifiers under user-defined accuracy, runtime, and energy constraints; the dataset and tool are publicly released.

papers.abstract: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360{\deg} multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360{\deg} multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. Evaluations span 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning architectures.

The benchmark targets work-zone geometry and regulatory diversity missing from existing datasets.

papers.abstract: Achieving safe navigation in confined dynamic environments remains a challenging problem, as robots must balance navigation efficiency with safety. Existing actor--critic MPC architectures typically employ differentiable MPC layers, but this way cannot readily accommodate explicit state constraints, making it intractable to involve collision avoidance within learning-based planning. To address this issue, we propose an actor--critic model predictive control framework with state constraints. We first use vertices to represent the robot and obstacles, and half-spaces to represent the workspace. Based on these, the nonlinear robot dynamics is locally linearized and the hyperplane-based collision avoidance constraints are convexified into the differentiable MPC layer, and then the actor exploits closed-loop feedback to adjust the MPC objective parameters that shape local motion behavior, while the critic evaluates long-term task performance. We further relax the convexified constraints with bounded and penalized slack variables to form an elastic quadratic program, accommodating cases where the local constraint approximations cannot be satisfied simultaneously. Simulation tests and experiments, involving dynamic collision avoidance for multi-robot in narrow cases, illustrate the advantages of the proposed framework in adaptively adjusting the learned policy and improving navigation efficiency over existing approaches while maintaining the motion safety.

Introduces bounded, penalized slack variables in an elastic quadratic program for locally infeasible constraints.
Simulations and experiments on dynamic multi-robot collision avoidance in narrow spaces show improved navigation efficiency while maintaining safety over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Robotic exploration can reduce human exposure to hazardous environments by autonomously searching unknown areas for objects of interest while constructing a complete, risk-aware map. However, existing autonomous exploration approaches typically prioritize geometric coverage or information gain, without explicitly coupling semantic object detection and the risk associated with operating near potentially hazardous objects. Moreover, many systems have been demonstrated primarily in simulation or controlled environments, leaving limited validation of risk-aware semantic exploration in complex, unstructured field settings. To address this gap, we propose SAFARI, a framework that treats object detection as a native channel of a unified probabilistic map, thereby jointly informing exploration and planning with both geometric and semantic evidence. We evaluated SAFARI in 11 missions across three field sites on a quadruped platform. The framework achieved an average coverage of 98.7% of the accessible mission area, without operator intervention for 97.6% of mission time, and detected objects with characteristic dimensions as small as 15cm. Lastly, through ablation studies and a detailed analysis of system behavior, we show that object-size awareness and safety-aware path planning are crucial for effective hazardous-object search.

papers.abstract: Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible free space and reachable commands depend on each robot's geometry and dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output normalized commands that disregard these differences, or compensate through per-robot training and distillation. World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the mapping from commands to body-specific motion. On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner's observations only through the camera ego-motion. This letter proposes Hourglass, an hourglass-shaped architecture that factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at this interface: a body-agnostic world model and each robot's differentiable ego-dynamics, which map commands to that ego-motion, are coupled only through it. The world model is trained on data pooled across embodiments and camera mounts; each robot's ego-dynamics is a reduced-order template with identified physical parameters. A generalist parameter-conditioned policy is learned once at this junction: each imagined step rolls out the template and then the world model, and imagination training through each robot's template makes the policy body-aware. On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines on the same world model by 3.8--10.6 percentage points in success rate and matches per-robot specialists without dedicated training, while approaching its parameter-conditioned MPPI teacher within 1.4--2.8 points without an online map. After three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers zero-shot to a real skid-steer robot unseen in training, navigating unseen indoor scenes.

papers.abstract: Centralized multi-agent path planning with cooperative localization in GPS-denied environments is generally computationally intractable when formulated in full belief space due to tightly coupled uncertainty dynamics. Prior work typically approximates belief dynamics or restricts inter-agent coupling. This work examines a multi-agent planning problem in which a primary agent must reach a goal in minimum time subject to a chance-constrained collision-avoidance requirement and a terminal bound on localization uncertainty. We obtain a tractable surrogate of the underlying belief-space problem by optimizing over the mean-state trajectories of all agents and propagating covariance for terminal constraint evaluation only. We propose CONSORT (Cooperative Navigation with Support-Optimized Routing and Trajectories), a discrete-to-continuous pipeline combining hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based trajectory refinement. Across 50 randomized scenarios, the planners separate as the terminal uncertainty bound tightens, with CONSORT solving 80% of scenarios where the strongest baseline solves 54%, at comparable path length. In marine simulations, with the plans executed under feedback control on an independently developed factor-graph estimate, the trajectories remain collision-free and their terminal uncertainty falls within 6% of the planner's prediction.
authors: Tony Zhang, Ryan Bartholomew, Kalliyan Velasco, Joshua Mangelson, Brady Moon
bullets: Targets minimum-time navigation with chance-constrained collision avoidance and bounded terminal localization uncertainty.
Uses mean-state trajectory optimization, with covariance propagated only for evaluating the terminal uncertainty constraint.
Combines hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based continuous trajectory refinement.
Solved 80% of randomized scenarios versus 54% for the strongest baseline at comparable path length.
Marine feedback-control simulations remained collision-free, with terminal uncertainty within 6% of predictions.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed as heterogeneous fleets with diverse kinematic and actuation capabilities. While graph control barrier function (GCBF) methods provide a scalable framework for decentralized safe control, existing approaches typically assume homogeneous robot dynamics. Methods that directly encode robot classes can distinguish known types, but do not represent state-dependent motion capabilities or naturally transfer to unseen robot models. To address this challenge, we propose the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point operational space. This formulation provides a common geometric representation of safety across heterogeneous robots while retaining their model-specific dynamics and admissible control constraints. To enable zero-shot transfer, we introduce the Radial Capability Field (RCF), a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of each robot's state-dependent finite-horizon reachable velocity set. Conditioning the shared graph barrier and decentralized policy on the RCF enables them to adapt to changes in robot state, kinematic constraints, and control limits without relying on predefined robot identities. We jointly train the barrier and policy using proactive safety labeling and neural CBF-QP supervision, and evaluate them on mixed teams containing both seen and unseen robot models. Experiments demonstrate scalable safe coordination and zero-shot transfer to robot models and capability variations withheld during training. Physical-robot experiments further demonstrate zero-shot deployment to unseen kinematic models without retraining.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Janghyun Cho, Jeehyun Lee, Changjoo Nam, Yiwei Lyu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing GCBFs, which generally assume homogeneous dynamics or predefined robot classes.
Uses a shared second-order reference-point space to represent safety while preserving each robot’s dynamics and control constraints.
Introduces the Radial Capability Field, a fixed-dimensional encoding of each robot’s finite-horizon reachable velocity set.
Jointly trains the barrier and policy with proactive safety labels and neural CBF-QP supervision.
Experiments show scalable coordination and zero-shot transfer to unseen robot models and capability variations, including physical-robot deployment without retraining.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in heterogeneous multi-robot teams faces two coupled challenges: differences in robots' braking and turning capabilities limit how each robot can respond to an approaching neighbor, while simultaneous interactions require a single control action to satisfy multiple collision-avoidance constraints. Together, these challenges can make local safety constraints incompatible with a robot's admissible controls, leaving a decentralized safety controller without a feasible action. We propose a Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter (CA-BRF), based on the insight that navigation actions should preserve access to a certified recovery maneuver. First, we construct a backup-recoverable set in a shared Cartesian operational space by evaluating whether prescribed backup maneuvers maintain pairwise safety until the robots come to rest. Each maneuver respects the corresponding robot's kinematic and actuation constraints, making the recovery certificate capability-dependent. Second, CA-BRF filters candidate controls by selecting admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions while coordinating the selection across simultaneous interactions. This preserves backup recoverability while retaining as much of the candidate action as possible and ensures that all pairwise recovery conditions are satisfied by a single executable control for each robot. Together, we establish recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed-loop system even when the nominal safety-constrained optimization becomes infeasible. The validity and effectiveness of the proposed CA-BRF are validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments of robots with five different kinematic classes.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Yanze Zhang, Wenhao Luo, Yiwei Lyu
bullets: Addresses infeasibility caused by differing braking/turning capabilities and multiple concurrent collision-avoidance constraints.
Builds a shared-space backup-recoverable set by checking whether constrained backup maneuvers maintain pairwise safety until stopping.
Coordinates admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions across simultaneous interactions.
Establishes recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed loop, including cases where nominal safety optimization is infeasible.
Validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments spanning five kinematic classes.

papers.abstract: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.
bullets: Fixed-conservativeness filters trade performance inside their operational design domain (ODD) against safety margin outside it.
The proposed filter-agnostic pipeline uses policy confidence to modulate filtering at runtime.
High confidence permits better performance where filter assumptions are valid; low confidence adds margin beyond the ODD.
Preliminary F1TENTH simulations show the approach combines strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog's alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans' eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.
bullets: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share spaces with companion animals, motivating welfare-informed navigation.
Researchers designed a laterally arcing pass-by maneuver triggered at the dog’s alert distance, based on canine communication and legible-motion theory.
In a naturalistic home evaluation with one companion dog, the maneuver produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline.
Repeated stopping and reorienting made the maneuver discontinuous and potentially less legible, becoming a stressor itself.
The pilot reframes cross-species navigation around animal legibility and the validity of proxy stimuli.

papers.abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
bullets: An opponent’s group-level response can serve as a shared “tell,” revealing information unavailable to individual members.
Precommitting to response rules determines how much the opponent can hide and can prevent losses when the opponent prioritizes its own objectives.
In a solved Gaussian setting, deliberately limiting how much information the team uses can recover the truth while preserving the opponent’s concealment cost.
An exact test characterizes when this information-recovery result holds in finite games.
Trust allocation matters: private randomization, differentiated responses, or a small trust discount can protect against deception.
