papers.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
bullets: Supports waypoint, discrete local, pixel-based, and object-directed navigation actions.
Lets agents ask for clarification or assistance when facing ambiguity or difficulty.
Stores observations and dialogue by location to improve future visits.
Evaluated across eight benchmarks spanning four navigation task families and multi-day physical navigation.
Reports strong performance, including 100% first-visit SR across four 100-episode sets and improved R2R revisit SPL from 82.23% to 93.31%.

papers.abstract: Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach target objects in complex environments. Humans often rely on low-cost yet informative schematic maps, such as rough sketches or directional annotations. We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework. Our lightweight data-generation pipeline turns 2D floorplans into navigation training environments, yielding Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes and noise-controllable schematic maps. ScheNav turns rough schematic guidance into exploration and stopping decisions by using SchemaField, a learned spatial module that fuses the guidance with accumulated observations and predicts spatial value fields. The framework updates these fields as exploration proceeds, with trajectory-based training and a cross-frame consistency objective supporting coherent guidance across changing viewpoints. ScheNav learns to use schematic guidance entirely from simulated floorplans and transfers this ability to unseen embodied environments. Experiments show improved navigation success and path efficiency across schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, together with tolerance to the tested schematic perturbations and omissions. Together, these results demonstrate that rough schematic guidance offers a practical way to improve embodied navigation.
bullets: Addresses object-goal navigation in complex environments using low-cost schematic maps such as sketches, goal ellipses, and directional pointers.
Introduces Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with navigation episodes and controllable schematic-map noise.
Uses SchemaField to fuse schematic guidance with accumulated visual observations and predict spatial value fields for exploration and stopping.
Trains with trajectory-based learning and cross-frame consistency to maintain coherent guidance across viewpoints.
Experiments report improved navigation success and path efficiency, with tolerance to tested schematic perturbations and omissions.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The ScheNav framework. Schematic guidance at any level, a schematic map, ellipses, a pointed direction, or none, is encoded by SchemaField, the only learned component our framework introduces: a schematic-fusion transformer fuses the guidance with the observed map from the map memory, and a distance decoder and a corridor decoder predict the two value fields from the fused embedding in a single forward pass. Two rule-based components read the fields. The Goal Verification module compares the distance-field value at goal instances detected in the map memory against a threshold τstop, and the decision transformation scores frontier candidates with the corridor field and gates stopping, emitting a waypoint or a stop. Map memory, frontier extraction, and execution are supplied by the host navigation system, and each new observation closes the loop.

Figure 3. Furnished-RPLAN construction pipeline. Starting from an RPLAN vector floorplan, a vision-language pipeline proposes and extracts a machine-readable furniture layout. The resulting furnished environment is used to generate navigation episodes, paired schematic guidance, and the local observations consumed by ScheNav.

Figure 1. Overview of schematic-guided navigation. A human provides imperfect schematic guidance, such as a rough sketch or a pointed direction. ScheNav grounds the guidance in the agent’s observations and predicts a value field that rises toward the goal. Guided by the predicted field, the agent reaches the goal along an efficient route in an environment it has barely explored.

Figure 4. Closed-loop trajectories on one episode under decreasing guidance. The five panels show our four input conditions and unmodified UniGoal on the same episode, rendered on a textured top-down view of the scene. papers.abstract: Vehicle-infrastructure cooperation can complement onboard sensing with broader and more informative observations of the traffic environment, providing valuable support for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing cooperative driving methods mainly exploit roadside information to enhance the representation of the current scene, while the future consequences of prospective driving actions are rarely modeled explicitly. This limits the ability of the planner to anticipate how its decisions may interact with the evolving traffic environment. To address this issue, we propose V2X-WAM, a cooperative world action model that tightly couples cooperative scene understanding, action generation, and future-world reasoning. V2X-WAM constructs a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle- and infrastructure-side observations, while compressing infrastructure information into a compact quantized message for efficient communication. Based on the resulting cooperative representation, a multimodal planner generates prospective trajectories, which explicitly condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow prediction. The predicted world consequences are then fed back to refine the planned trajectory, forming a closed interaction between action and future-world evolution. Experiments on a large-scale real-world cooperative driving dataset demonstrate that V2X-WAM consistently improves planning accuracy and safety over representative end-to-end cooperative driving methods, while achieving stronger future-world prediction and substantially lower communication overhead. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed design.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing V2X methods mainly represent the current scene without explicitly modeling action consequences.
Builds a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle and infrastructure observations, with infrastructure data compressed into a quantized message.
Uses a multimodal planner whose candidate trajectories condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow predictions.
Feeds predicted future-world consequences back into trajectory planning, creating a closed action–world interaction loop.
Experiments show improved planning accuracy and safety, stronger future-world prediction, and substantially lower communication overhead; ablations support the design.

papers.abstract: We study a constrained sequential decision problem for detecting regions of interest from noisy online measurements collected by a team of energy-constrained mobile sensors. The sensor motion is restricted to a precomputed set of feasible paths that satisfy mobility constraints, limited available energy by requiring return to charging stations, and avoidance of known obstacles. We cast the resulting active path selection as a multi-armed bandit problem and propose an iterative search algorithm that adaptively assigns paths using confidence bounds computed from the collected data. We also propose a graph-based method to construct low-cardinality path covers under the team's constraints. We establish finite-time and anytime probabilistic correctness guarantees for the proposed algorithm, derive non-asymptotic upper bounds on the times required to detect all regions of interest and to label all nodes, and show that these bounds match algorithm-independent lower bounds up to constant factors for a broad class of problem instances. Using numerical simulations, we illustrate the behavior of the proposed approach and the effect of path redundancy and team size on search performance.
bullets: Models constrained path selection from noisy online measurements as a multi-armed bandit problem.
Uses confidence-bound updates to adaptively assign feasible sensor paths.
Constructs low-cardinality path covers while respecting mobility, energy, charging, and obstacle constraints.
Provides finite-time and anytime correctness guarantees plus non-asymptotic detection and labeling bounds.
Simulations examine how path redundancy and team size affect search performance.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has predominantly relied on open-loop imitation learning for training, which presents two limitations. First, expert demonstrations show only one behavior per scenario, so the model cannot learn alternative valid behaviors and, in turn, cannot adapt to user-specified preferences at test time. Second, noise or ambiguity in these demonstrations can produce inconsistent, unreliable supervision for the end-to-end models. Driving is inherently multi-modal: multiple different behaviors can be valid responses to the same scene, and this diversity arises largely from speed rather than path. We introduce a planning paradigm that learns the path through imitation while scoring a set of candidate speeds across multiple criteria with a learned function supervised by physically grounded safety constraints. We realize this paradigm as Closed-Loop Aware Planning for Autonomous Driving (CLAP-AD), a plug-in planning head that integrates with existing end-to-end driving models and, to our knowledge, is the first to enable explicit test-time control over their speed selection without speed-conditioned training. On Bench2Drive-Speed, CLAP-AD sets a new state of the art Speed-Adherence Score of 82.53, topping TFv6, the strongest baseline on this metric, by 12.9 points while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance. On Bench2Drive, it improves driving score by +28.5 and +32.7 over UniAD and VAD, and on NAVSIM v2, built on real-world driving data, EPDMS by +6.1 over its backbone. Project page: https://clap-ad.github.io
bullets: Addresses limited behavioral diversity and noisy supervision in open-loop imitation learning.
Learns paths through imitation while scoring candidate speeds using multiple criteria and physically grounded safety constraints.
Works as a plug-in planning head for existing end-to-end driving models without speed-conditioned training.
Achieves state-of-the-art speed adherence on Bench2Drive-Speed and improves driving performance on Bench2Drive and NAVSIM v2.
Scope: the approach focuses on behavioral multimodality arising primarily from speed rather than path.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the CLAP-AD planning head. The architecture consists of an Ego-Path block that takes ego detection and motion queries as input and predicts a feasible driving path. The Collision block encodes surrounding agents’ detection and motion queries, fuses them with the predicted path representation, and uses learned collision queries to produce collision scores. Similarly, the Traffic Light and Stop Sign blocks employ dedicated queries that attend to their respective detection features together with the path embedding to generate their speed scores.

papers.abstract: Autonomous micro-mobility vehicles (MMVs) such as wheelchairs, scooters, and bicycles have the potential to improve mobility access and support safe low-speed transportation in pedestrian-shared spaces. Achieving MMV autonomy will require realistic, predictable MMV motion. However, many existing autonomous vehicle stacks rely on simplified kinematic models that fail to capture key MMV characteristics such as tire slip, friction, and wheel layouts, limiting realism and gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we explore differentiable formulations of dynamics models for autonomous micro-mobility systems. We first construct DiffKBM, a differentiable version of the kinematic bicycle model (KBM). Then, we introduce DiffGM3, a differentiable formulation of the General Micro-Mobility Model (GM3), a unified tire-based dynamics formulation for micro-mobility vehicles that supports a wide range of MMV configurations. DiffKBM and DiffGM3 enable end-to-end differentiable optimization through MMV dynamics, making them suitable for integration into differentiable autonomy stacks. We evaluate these dynamics models in both open-loop and closed-loop settings: (1) open-loop trajectory matching, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are integrated as a dynamics layer within DiffStack and optimized to reproduce real-world MMV trajectories, and (2) closed-loop autonomous navigation, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are paired with a differentiable MPC controller in CrowdNav pedestrian scenarios. In the open-loop setting, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in reproducing trajectories with improvements in ADE and NLL across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle modes, and reductions in planning loss for bicycle and motorcycle trajectories. We also find that, in closed-loop settings, DiffGM3 improves on DiffKBM's CrowdNav performance by producing 55\% fewer collisions and a 75\% lower discomfort frequency for the bicycle mode.
bullets: Targets limitations of simplified vehicle models that omit tire slip, friction, and diverse wheel layouts.
Constructs DiffKBM, a differentiable kinematic bicycle model, and DiffGM3, a differentiable general micro-mobility dynamics model.
Evaluates both models in open-loop trajectory matching and closed-loop navigation with differentiable MPC in pedestrian scenarios.
DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle trajectory evaluations.
For bicycle navigation, DiffGM3 yields 55% fewer collisions and 75% lower discomfort frequency than DiffKBM.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Overview of the DiffMPC pipeline integrated with DiffKBM or DiffGM3. At each timestep, the environment provides a state estimate xt , which is passed to the optimizer with the goal position and surrounding pedestrian states pedst . The optimizer proposes a control sequence u0:T−1 and uses either DiffKBM or DiffGM3 parameterized by learnable parameters ρKBM or ρGM3 to roll out predicted future states x0:T . A cost function is defined with learnable cost weights ρC. Because both the dynamics and the cost function are differentiable, gradients can be back-propagated through the prediction and cost modules to enable end-to-end learning of MMV dynamics parameters. The first control action u0 is applied to the environment, and the process repeats in a receding-horizon loop.

Fig. 2: DiffGM3 contains several differentiable components with sets of learnable parameters ρlean,ρtire, and ρVI. First, the steering control input δ is converted into tire-specific steering angles δi. This, along with the MMV’s previous longitudinal velocity vx, lateral velocity vy, and yaw rate r, is used to calculate tire velocities. Meanwhile, longitudinal and lateral accelerations, ax and ay, are used to transfer load among the tires, and the previous lean angle γ and roll rate γ̇ are used to determine the next lean angle. In addition to wheel angular velocity Ω, the results from these modules are inputs to the tire brush model, where forces and moments are computed. The outputs for each tire are integrated into the vehicle dynamics to obtain longitudinal, lateral, and yaw acceleration. Finally, the resulting position is calculated with Euler integration. This fully differentiable formulation allows gradients to backpropagate to each module so parameters can be tuned on MMV trajectory data.

Fig. 5: Closed-loop Navigation in Pedestrian Crowds Comparison between DiffGM3 Bicycle and DiffKBM: We show two unique scenarios each for DiffGM3 and DiffKBM. Longer pedestrian paths reflect the longer navigation time taken by the MMV to avoid moving pedestrians to reach its goal. Scenario 1: DiffGM3’s route reflects its ability to use real-world kinematics to avoid pedestrians when necessary, while DiffKBM’s simple kinematics forces it to attempt to fit right in between two pedestrians, resulting in a collision. Scenario 2: While both models reach the goal, DiffGM3’s longer route demonstrates less discomfort and higher minimum distance from pedestrians relative to DiffKBM’s direct route.

Fig. 3: Open-loop Trajectory Matching Comparison between the DiffKBM and DiffGM3: (a) On bicycle trajectories, DiffGM3 is able to stay on path because it has learnable parameters to prevent overturning. However, in some cases, it stops before the goal as shown by the red arrow, leading to a higher goal cost in the planning loss function. (b) On the other hand, the DiffKBM reaches its goal but veers off the ground-truth straight path, as indicated by the red arrow. This is due to the DiffKBM’s lack of support for realignment in its formula for yaw. (c) For a scooter, DiffGM3 is able to steer the scooter to its goal while avoiding other agents. (d) On the same trajectory, the DiffKBM causes the ego agent to turn towards another agent and slow down, preventing it from reaching its goal.

Fig. 1: DiffKBM implements wheelbase L as a learnable parameter in the steering component. The resulting turning rate θ̇ along with velocity are used in Euler integration to obtain the position. By making KBM end-to-end differentiable, we are able to tune L for an MMV with unknown wheelbase length.
TABLE I: Physical Parameters in the tire brush model.
TABLE II: Input Variables in the tire brush model.

TABLE V: Closed-loop Pedestrian Crowd Navigation Performance Comparison between DiffGM3 and DiffKBM: DiffGM3 prioritizes safety and demonstrates significantly fewer collisions across all vehicle configurations relative to DiffKBM. Specifically, in the baseline comparison between the two bicycle models, DiffGM3 produces 55% fewer collisions, with a 3% better success rate. DiffGM3’s incomplete rate and slower navigation time can be explained by its tendency to avoid collisions by veering away from the goal, resulting in situations where the vehicle is unable to arrive at the goal within the time limit. This also explains why DiffGM3’s discomfort frequency is 50%-75% better than DiffKBM’s across all modes. Moreover, DiffKBM’s faster navigation times are primarily the result of collisions ending the scenario early.

TABLE IV: Open-loop Trajectory Matching Evaluation Results: DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in ADE (Bicycle: - 1.16%, Scooter -9.84%, Motorcycle: -2.37%) and NLL (Bicycle: -3.02%, Scooter -2.05%, Motorcycle: -4.75%) on all modes. For planning loss, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM on bicycle (-4.16%) and motorcycle (-28.9%) trajectories, but performs worse on scooters (19.39%).

TABLE III: DiffGM3 parameters optimized using IMPTC trajectories. Align gain kalign and damping coefficients dyaw,droll help to stabilize the MMV and reduce oversteering. Moments of inertia Iz, Ix, and tire parameters are tuned because they are not easily measurable.

papers.abstract: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.
authors: Hooman Hamze, Benjamin Houshmand, Deepthi Pathare, Erik B\"orve, Morteza Haghir Chehreghani, Nikolce Murgovski
bullets: Targets the challenge of balancing safety constraints with efficient long-horizon decisions for heavy-duty trucks.
Combines finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, with a pre-trained RL model that estimates terminal costs.
Evaluated in simulation with reactive surrounding traffic against zero-terminal-cost MPC, base-policy rollouts, and pure RL.
The hybrid approach achieved zero collisions and the lowest cost among the evaluated configurations.

papers.abstract: Monocular RGB tracking is useful for robots operating near people, but perception errors affect binary stop/proceed decisions in ways that geometric accuracy metrics do not capture. We examine how much decision error arises from the safety rule versus perception. We prove that lateral-only distance is a lower bound on planar distance: with accurate positions, it cannot miss dangers identified by the planar rule, but it produces unnecessary stops. We introduce a two-factor Shapley attribution separating rule and perception contributions, and further distinguish missed detections from localization errors. Experiments use ETH and UCY pedestrian videos with simulated stationary robots, disjoint calibration and evaluation pedestrians, and time-block bootstrap intervals. Across 898 pedestrians in three scenes, the lateral rule missed no dangers on annotated positions but achieved only 5.6-31.9% stop precision. In two scenes with RGB perception, calibrated ground-plane localization achieved 0.59 m and 0.51 m planar RMSE, compared with 1.72 m and 1.39 m for a geometric baseline and 0.81 m and 0.68 m for calibrated Depth Anything V2. Detection recall of 0.43 and 0.26 made missed detections the leading source of missed danger. A two-standard-deviation safety margin with ground-plane localization matched or improved on the lateral rule's missed-danger rate in all eight scene-threshold settings and reduced unnecessary stops in seven. All robot interactions are simulated, and outcomes are offline decision classifications, not demonstrations of collision avoidance.
bullets: Lateral-only distance is a conservative lower bound on planar distance: it missed no dangers with accurate positions but caused many unnecessary stops.
A two-factor Shapley framework attributes decision errors to the safety rule versus perception, separating missed detections from localization errors.
Ground-plane localization outperformed the geometric baseline and calibrated Depth Anything V2 in the reported scenes.
Low detection recall was the leading contributor to missed dangers in RGB-perception experiments.
A two-standard-deviation safety margin matched or improved missed-danger rates in all tested settings and reduced unnecessary stops in seven of eight.

papers.abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at https://umlic.github.io/papers/BGP/.
authors: Junhyeon Bae, Jaebak Hwang, Gwanwoo Choi, Minung Kim, Seungyul Han
bullets: Targets path mirages: spurious successes in offline data that cause agents to commit to unreliable routes.
Represents high-variability points as nodes in a branching graph.
Learns goal-conditioned graph edges with segmentation to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity.
Experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show reliable goal reaching and substantial improvements over prior methods.
Scope: designed for stochastic, long-horizon offline goal-conditioned environments.

papers.abstract: Efficient crowd navigation requires anticipating dynamic collision-free space without relying on fragile object tracking. We propose the Don't Risk It Planner (DRIP), an end-to-end LiDAR-only planning framework that couples occupancy forecasting with trajectory-conditioned clearance and uncertainty estimation. Operating directly on LiDAR-derived occupancy grid histories, DRIP predicts a distribution over minimum robot-obstacle clearance for candidate control sequences to evaluate collision risk. The model is trained using a risk cost that grounds predictive uncertainty directly in empirical collision outcomes rather than geometric regression alone. In closed-loop experiments with up to 45 pedestrians, DRIP achieves higher success rates with fewer collisions and reduced freezing behavior compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Mathai Mathew Pulicken, Laksh Nanwani, Basant Sharma, Phani Teja Singamaneni, Arun Kumar Singh, K. Madhava Krishna
bullets: Addresses safe, efficient navigation in dynamic crowds without relying on fragile object tracking.
Uses LiDAR-derived occupancy-grid histories to forecast occupancy and estimate clearance and uncertainty for candidate control sequences.
Trains risk predictions against empirical collision outcomes, rather than geometric clearance regression alone.
In closed-loop experiments with up to 45 pedestrians, it improves success rates while reducing collisions and freezing versus state-of-the-art baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of DRIP’s LiDAR-only prediction and trajectory-conditioned risk architecture. A history H of pose-warped BEV occupancy maps is encoded independently by a shared-weight spatial CNN, conditioned on ego velocity V through FiLM. Spatiotemporal Transformer blocks then reason over the temporal history and spatial BEV tokens to produce a shared scene representation zscene. Two branches use this representation: the occupancy decoder predicts the future evolution of the scene (Ôk) over a 20-step horizon, while the trajectory-conditioned Distance Head combines scene features with candidate trajectory queries qk to predict a stepwise clearance distribution (µk, σ 2 k) and a trajectory-specific kernel width λ. These predictions are subsequently used to compute the distributional MMD2 risk r̂θ(u) for each candidate trajectory u.

papers.abstract: Humanoids have become increasingly agile and capable in real-world environments. To operate safely in dynamic scenarios, they must rapidly evade fast-moving obstacles while maintaining stability and physically feasible whole-body motion. Learning such behaviors remains challenging due to the high-dimensional dynamics of humanoid systems and the need to jointly balance reactive obstacle avoidance, motion naturalness, and control robustness. In this work, we present Humanoid Dodgeball, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for agile dynamic obstacle avoidance in humanoids. Our method enables highly dynamic whole-body evasive maneuvers against incoming projectiles through threat-aware reward shaping, while multiple direction-specific adversarial motion priors regularize the learned behaviors toward stable and diverse human-like motions. Extensive simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves dynamic obstacle avoidance performance across diverse obstacle speeds and launch distances, while preserving robust and physically plausible humanoid motions.
authors: Aoqian Zhang, Chunzheng Wang, Haoran Chen, Annan Tang, Cheng Xiang, Fan Shi, Shuzhi Sam Ge
bullets: Targets dynamic obstacle avoidance while preserving balance, physical feasibility, and natural motion.
Uses threat-aware reward shaping to encourage agile evasive responses.
Employs direction-specific adversarial motion priors to regularize behavior toward diverse, stable human-like motions.
Simulation and hardware experiments show improved avoidance across varied obstacle speeds and launch distances.
The abstract focuses on projectile evasion and does not specify broader obstacle types or quantitative results.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of Humanoid Dodgeball. During simulation training, predictive and near-field threat for key bodies are computed to characterize incoming projectile hazards and guide threat-aware reward shaping for whole-body evasion. Direction-specific adversarial motion priors, selected according to the root escape direction, regularize the learned behaviors toward diverse and natural human-like dodge motions. When the threat subsides, recovery rewards, including orientation and capture-point objectives, encourage rapid stabilization. During hardware deployment, the trained actor is executed using obstacle positions estimated from the motion-capture system.

papers.abstract: Pretrained generative models, such as diffusion and flow matching models, have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in synthesizing high-quality data. However, steering their generative trajectories to satisfy strict constraints--such as identity preservation in image editing or obstacle avoidance in robotics--remains fundamentally challenging. While recent training-free guidance methods enforce path-safety, they rely heavily on min-norm controllers that only account for immediate constraint satisfaction. These myopic approaches often yield suboptimal trajectories that hover dangerously close to the boundary, severely restricting the model's ability to optimize toward its target. In this paper, we propose AegisFlow, a training-free, non-myopic path-safe guidance framework that recasts guided generation as a safety-critical optimal control problem with global scope. By integrating a time-varying barrier function directly into the global cost functional, AegisFlow naturally enforces constraints along the entire generative path. To compute the global optimal control, we derive a tractable, mathematically grounded approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AegisFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods across text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning, establishing a significantly better trade-off between target alignment and constraint satisfaction. Code is available at https://github.com/LiuKunpeng03/AegisFlow.
authors: Kunpeng Liu, Boshi Zhang, Keyou You
bullets: Addresses the myopic behavior of existing path-safe guidance methods, which may stay near constraint boundaries and limit target optimization.

Experiments on text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning show improved target-alignment/safety trade-offs over prior methods.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots commonly pair a global planner with a local model predictive controller (MPC), but nonconvex obstacle avoidance and a limited horizon can make the robot freeze in complex layouts. Deciding whether to replan, wait, or call for help is a supervisory decision. Recent work queries a large language model (LLM) supervisor on every anomaly, which is slow and costly. We instead distill the LLM online into a decision tree. After each training episode, counterfactual replay labels recoveries as needed, unnecessary, or harmful. These labels retire unhelpful rules. In simulation, on 20 unseen layouts where the MPC alone freezes, the tree handles at least 18 correctly across all seeds, either by reaching the goal or by calling for help when no feasible path exists. The tree matches both an always-query LLM supervisor and expert-designed rules, while issuing no LLM queries at test time. Handwritten rules cannot anticipate the long tail of situations a physical robot will encounter. Online distillation is a promising remedy: the tree handles familiar cases, and the LLM is consulted only for new ones, whose validated recoveries become new rules. Language models can thus also serve as designers of supervisors rather than only as runtime supervisors.
bullets: Targets MPC failures where limited horizons and nonconvex obstacles cause autonomous robots to freeze.
After each episode, counterfactual replay labels recovery actions as needed, unnecessary, or harmful, pruning ineffective rules.

papers.abstract: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) has achieved promising performance, but most methods rely on structured traffic states that must be estimated from sensor observations in real deployments. Visual TSC learns signal decisions directly from images, yet existing methods depend on fixed roadside cameras and remain tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains. UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye-view (BEV) observations that jointly capture intersection topology and traffic dynamics, making them a promising sensing platform for visual TSC. We present BEVLight, a generalizable TSC framework that directly maps BEV observations to signal actions. BEVLight grounds visual features onto individual lanes and composes them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, allowing a shared policy to score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. To train the policy, we develop a web-based virtual teleoperation platform and collect over 5K human control decisions together with their underlying traffic states. Simulator-provided traffic states first supervise lane- and movement-level representations, after which human phase selections and rankings supervise the phase scorer. Re-rendering the recorded trajectories under diverse appearances preserves both forms of supervision and encourages robustness to visual changes. Closed-loop experiments demonstrate zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections: BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7--9\% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or outperforms structured-state RL controllers that receive ground-truth traffic states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study further shows that BEVLight transfers to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.

papers.abstract: Legged robots have demonstrated advanced capabilities across a wide range of real-world tasks, yet much of this progress concerns the robot controlling only itself. Once the robot is coupled to an external object -- particularly an underactuated one -- the dynamics of the combined assembly become more complex. Towing a wagon is a common practical scenario, where coupled dynamics make reliable navigation challenging. This difficulty is amplified in confined spaces, where collision-free navigation requires finding a narrow set of feasible paths under strict real-time constraints. To address this, we propose a navigation framework that combines Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control over a learned Forward Dynamics Model (FDM). The CFM model mitigates the initialization problem of MPPI and accelerates its convergence, while MPPI with the FDM recovers feasible solutions beyond the CFM model's training distribution by iterative refinement. We integrate the framework into a full-stack navigation system for RAIBO-Wagon, a quadruped towing a custom wagon, and validate it in real-world outdoor experiments on 15 m-long courses through confined spaces, with all sensing and computation performed fully onboard. The system achieves an 85% success rate across 40 trials, towing a total load of up to 40 kg -- nearly 100% of RAIBO's body weight.
authors: Insung Yang, Eunchae Kim, Jungwoo Hur, Seunghun Jeon, Donghyuk Choi, Jemin Hwangbo

Validated fully onboard on 15 m outdoor courses through confined spaces, achieving an 85% success rate over 40 trials.
Towed loads up to 40 kg, approximately the robot’s body weight.

papers.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
authors: Peitong Duan, Khashayar Gatmiry, Jeffrey Nichols, Samy Bengio, Emmanuel Abbe
bullets: Addresses brittle trajectory memorization and high inference costs in UI navigation.
Decouples navigation into a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model.
Uses LLM-based dense step rewards plus terminal task-completion rewards, optimized with PPO and step-level advantages.
Introduces GiGPPO, which stabilizes value estimation using rewards from visually similar states in concurrent trajectories.

Evaluations across UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld show stronger performance than SFT and terminal-only RL baselines, including nearly sevenfold OOD improvement for 8B agents on Android and competitive results on real iOS apps.

papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) sensing enables robot ego-motion estimation in darkness, smoke, and fog, yet RF odometry remains challenging because multipath and moving reflectors make cross-frame matching highly ambiguous. Existing methods often rely on auxiliary inertial sensors or ground-truth pose supervision. We present RFWalk, a self-supervised, RF-only odometry framework that models dense correspondences across range-azimuth frames as random walks on a space-time graph and learns them from unlabeled sequences through temporal cycle consistency. To rule out correspondences that are cycle-consistent but physically implausible, we introduce a Doppler consistency loss that constrains correspondence-induced motion using radial velocity measured by the RF sensor itself. Ego-motion is then recovered through robust $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ registration that suppresses uncertain correspondences and those arising from independently moving objects. Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.
authors: Kunzhe Song, Jialuo Du, Jingkai Lin, Huacheng Zeng
bullets: Addresses ambiguous RF frame matching caused by multipath and moving reflectors.
Models dense range-azimuth correspondences as random walks on a space-time graph.
Uses temporal cycle consistency and a Doppler consistency loss without pose labels or auxiliary sensors.
Recovers ego-motion via robust SE(2) registration that downweights unreliable and independently moving-object correspondences.
Remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic pedestrian scenes.

papers.abstract: Anticipating the motion of nearby objects is critical for safe and efficient robot navigation. Without a proper understanding of what may move, a robot may plan overly conservative, inefficient trajectories to guarantee safety, or it may be overly risky, resulting in unacceptable collisions. While tracking and predicting the motion of known objects has seen significant progress, little research addresses how a robot should adapt online to novel objects, including anticipating how one object may move another (e.g., a person operating a forklift to move a pallet). To enable this capability, we propose a meta-learned graph neural network that leverages a semantic, geometric, and relational history of objects to accurately predict, from a few online observations, when objects will begin to move in new environments. We demonstrate that our method, which is trained only in simulation, accurately anticipates the motion of objects unseen at training time, transfers to hardware without any fine-tuning, and outperforms a vision-language model and a class-frequency baseline in both simulation and hardware experiments. Our method's accurate prediction enables collision-free traversals in a closed-loop navigation simulation, while remaining within four seconds of the fastest, collision-prone planner.
authors: Mason Peterson, Gage MacLin, Camilla Tabasso, Jonathan P. How, Joshua Migdal, Tye Brady, Taskin Padir
bullets: Targets open-world motion anticipation, including one object causing another to move.
Uses semantic, geometric, and relational object histories in a graph neural network with meta-learning.
Trained only in simulation, it transfers to hardware and handles objects unseen during training without fine-tuning.
Outperforms a vision-language model and class-frequency baseline in simulation and hardware experiments.
Supports collision-free closed-loop navigation while staying within four seconds of the fastest collision-prone planner.

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe quadrotor flight in unknown environments, yet conventional frame-based cameras remain challenged by motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency under fast motion. Event cameras, with sub-millisecond latency, high dynamic range, and negligible motion blur, offer a promising alternative, but leveraging them for closed-loop control remains difficult. Existing approaches either adopt cascaded architectures that first estimate depth and then map it to control commands, introducing error propagation, or achieve end-to-end control through costly offline pretraining before online fine-tuning can even begin. We address these challenges with a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to render events efficiently within the training loop, integrated into a differentiable simulation pipeline that enables direct gradient backpropagation through the differentiable physics model, improving sample efficiency. This allows us to train an end-to-end policy that maps event frames directly to control commands, without intermediate depth estimation. We validate our approach through zero-shot real-world deployment on a quadrotor, achieving robust obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including under low-light conditions where conventional cameras typically fail.
authors: Chenlu Shou, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency in frame-based obstacle avoidance for fast quadrotor flight.
Uses a CUDA-based event simulator integrated with differentiable physics to backpropagate through the training loop.
Learns an end-to-end policy mapping event frames directly to control commands, avoiding cascaded depth estimation.
Demonstrates zero-shot real-world deployment in odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including low light.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: System Framework Overview. The simulator renders a grayscale frame from each quadrotor state, and two consecutive frames are used to compute the event frame. The differentiable point-mass dynamics model then propagates the current state forward using this action. A loss is computed based on the resulting state and action, and the corresponding gradients are propagated backward through the entire differentiable pipeline to update the policy.

papers.abstract: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a B\'ezier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.
authors: Yuanxiang Yang, Yu Liu, Fabricio Oliveira, Yu Han, Claudio Roncoli
bullets: Addresses safety, lateral comfort, uncertain surrounding-vehicle behavior, and the computational cost of NN-embedded optimization for connected automated vehicles.
Uses ICRNN, FICNN, and PICNN surrogates to model safety from planned trajectories, lane-change duration, and historical traffic states; a separate FICNN models lateral comfort.
Embeds the surrogates through linear programming, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer formulations.

Experiments show competitive surrogate accuracy, substantially better optimization efficiency than conventional MIPs, and lower weighted planning cost than baseline planners in closed-loop simulations.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in off-road terrain is commonly achieved using hierarchical control and planning architectures that rely on explicit cost maps and one-way information flow from a high-level planner to a low-level controller, decoupling planning from the true execution cost experienced during control. We propose a hierarchical planning and control framework in which information flows bidirectionally, allowing the low-level controller to guide trajectory selection at the planning level. The highest level of the hierarchy is a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control-style planner that determines optimal trajectories and passes these waypoints to a pretrained low-level reinforcement learning (RL) controller. Rather than drawing from an explicit cost map, our MPPI planner leverages the value function of the RL controller as an implicit cost representation. In this formulation, MPPI serves as a trajectory exploration mechanism, while the low-level controller's value function guides the search. To account for the distribution shift seen by the value function between training and evaluation, we propose an online policy evaluation process that adapts the value function to unseen driving experiences, and we demonstrate this adaptation in unseen off-road simulation environments. We evaluate our approach in a high-fidelity off-road driving simulator across a range of challenging terrain conditions and compare its performance against a baseline MPPI controller. The results demonstrate that our method achieves safer and more effective navigation to goal locations while eliminating the need for explicit cost maps and enabling tighter coupling between planning and control.
authors: Anoushka Alavilli, Raymond Song, Guanya Shi, Jeff Schneider
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level planning and low-level execution in hierarchical off-road navigation.
Uses MPPI to explore trajectories, with the pretrained controller’s value function guiding trajectory selection.
Applies online policy evaluation to adapt the value function to unseen driving experiences and distribution shift.
Evaluated in a high-fidelity off-road simulator across challenging terrains against a baseline MPPI controller.
Reports safer, more effective goal-directed navigation while removing the need for explicit cost maps.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of our value-guided planning framework. We pre-train RL policies to provide both an actor πθ(s) and a value function Vϕ(s). MPPI samples candidate trajectories and evaluates them using a cost that combines goal progress with the negative value estimate, treating −Vϕ(s) as a control-aware cost. The selected trajectory is executed by the policy, and the resulting experience can be used to update the value function online. This enables planning to be guided by the expected performance of the controller without requiring an explicit cost map.

Fig. 3: Comparison of pitch and vertical jerk violations across all 64 evaluation trajectories for the MPPI baseline ((A), (B)), our algorithm ((C), (D)), and our algorithm with online adaptation ((E), (F)). Panels (A), (C), and (E) show pitch violations exceeding 0.4 rad (22.9◦), while (B), (D), and (F) show vertical jerk violations exceeding 10e−2 m/s3. The violations are colored by their severity and are no more than 0.7 rad. and 2 m/s3 for pitch and jerk respectively. The MPPI baseline includes an explicit pitch cost term, whereas our method is trained with a jerk penalty in the reward function. When divided into equally-spaced buckets of low, medium, and high violation severity, the MPPI baseline recorded 317, 51, and 19 jerk violations and 84, 0, and 0 pitch violations, respectively; ours recorded 22, 1, and 0 jerk violations and 11, 1, and 0 pitch violations; and ours with online adaptation recorded 31, 0, and 0 jerk violations and 1, 1, and 3 pitch violations.

In (A), our method incurs damage midway through the trajectory, while the online adaptation variant avoids this region through online updates alone, without any prior knowledge that this region would cause damage. In (A), (B), and (E), the baseline MPPI algorithm becomes stuck and is unable to complete its planned route. In (C), our algorithm demonstrates its ability to follow existing trails, which provide safer traversal than off-trail terrain. In (D), our algorithm with online adaptation reaches the maximum time limit and does not complete the trajectory.

Fig. 4: (A) Visualization of training data coverage and evaluation start–goal waypoints. papers.abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. papers.abstract: Smart wheelchairs are robotic devices that gather information from the surroundings and allow people to safely drive through various environments. They usually rely on the interpretation of high-level user's intentions, typically decoded through human-robot interface (HRI) or brain-machine interface (BMI). However, navigating in an unknown environment and accurately understanding user commands remain significant challenges. Misinterpretation of commands or the environment can lead to user frustration, distrust of the system, or even unsafe situations. In this paper, we present a novel Multi-Layer Navigation System (MLNS) for a smart wheelchair that enables navigation in unknown environments while interpreting and safely contextualizing user's intentions even in the case of limited and faulty commands. The stack relies on a Virtual Sensors-Driven Potential Fields (ViSPF) method for obstacle detection that accounts for the wheelchair's actual size, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) module for trajectory generation, and an open-vocabulary computer vision algorithm for target identification. Finally, a system based on Priority Queue (PQ) was implemented for target selection. We validated our system on a real smart wheelchair with experiments involving 10 participants without disabilities, including scenarios with faulty input interfaces. The results demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our system in real-world environments, proving its potential for practical applications in assistive technologies.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

On R2R-CE val-unseen, the full system outperforms evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines; removing temporal memory greatly lengthens paths and lowers SR.

papers.abstract: Compositional diffusion planners have demonstrated remarkable success on long-horizon diffusion planning by sampling short trajectories, namely chunks, and composing them into a long trajectory. However, averaging overlapping chunks can induce the mode-averaging problem, resulting in discontinuous trajectories. Several works aim to address this problem, whereas a non-negligible portion of plans remains infeasible. In this work, we propose Selective Compositional Diffuser (SCD), handling this problem by measuring reachability. To this end, we present a self-supervised learning method for the reachability classifier. This is trained on offline data and generated chunks jointly to address potential distributional mismatch, while reducing the bias inherited from the generated data. Based on this, we construct a graph whose edge costs represent whether consecutive chunks are reachable, and traverse the graph to find effective yet efficient routes. Lastly, we generate bridging trajectories and refine the composed trajectory for smooth transitions. We evaluate our method on OGBench stitching tasks. It practically reduces incompatible mode compositions and the mode-averaging problem compared to the studied baselines. Across tasks, SCD improves success rates, reaching state-of-the-art results on HumanoidMaze-Large and Giant tasks.
authors: Chanyoung Park, Youngjoong Kim, Jaesik Park
bullets: Addresses discontinuities from averaging overlapping chunks and infeasible plans in compositional diffusion planners.

papers.abstract: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360{\deg} cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180{\deg} and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180{\deg}, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200{\deg} FIORD and 205{\deg} FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.

papers.abstract: Humans navigate their environment based on their vision system, anticipating how the ground will respond before committing to a step. Self-supervised learning could provide legged robots the same ability, but the supervisory signal is typically chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined. We present Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which proposes a meaningful and consistent footstep instability score, based on the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation. It projects the continuous score into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. We propose two variants, a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. Both metrics are compared against state-of-the-art alternatives in two independent evaluations that share no data or labels. On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 % over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, our metric also trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 % over the strongest alternative, and by a further 25 % when supplemented with onboard context. In a real-world experiment over a 50 m forest trajectory, the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain properties such as mud and vegetation, while stepping around geometric obstacles like fallen branches. Code is available for reproducibility at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/TACOS.
authors: Jean-Michel Fortin, William Larriv\'ee-Hardy, Gabriel Jeanson, Olivier Gamache, Daniele De Martini, Fran\c{c}ois Pomerleau, Philippe Gigu\`ere

Projects the score into preceding camera images to train a dense visual instability predictor.
Provides a hindsight-based hard score and an immediately available causal soft score.
Both variants outperform evaluated alternatives for detecting and ranking contact instability; the best predictor improves rank correlation further with onboard context.
In a 50 m forest test, the predictor responds to mud and vegetation while avoiding geometric obstacles such as fallen branches.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) are becoming increasingly important and useful for embodied intelligence, as they enable robots to anticipate the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with the physical environment. However, underwater robots are usually subject to passive dynamics, such as inertia, buoyancy, hydrodynamic drag, and persistent drift, which can continue to affect the vehicle even after an action is completed. Existing WAMs, which primarily predict action-conditioned visual observations, are not explicitly designed to capture such passive motion dynamics. In this paper, we present AquaWAM, the first World Action Model designed for underwater embodied agents. Instead of predicting future images, AquaWAM models both action-conditioned and passive physical dynamics, including the thruster dead band, the inertial glide that outlasts each command, and ambient currents. Specifically, it senses through the DVL, IMU, pressure sensor and joint encoders, while cameras supply only semantics for understanding goals and target pose. By modeling compact navigation states rather than high-dimensional visual observations, AquaWAM substantially reduces the model size and computational cost compared with conventional WAMs. Experimentally, AquaWAM achieves a 72.6% task success rate across 20 underwater tasks on the USIM benchmark, outperforming existing methods while making action decisions 2.7x faster than U0 on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Our model also remains effective when some onboard sensor measurements are unavailable. For example, without DVL velocity measurements, our method still achieves a 61.6% success rate, compared with 39.4% for U0.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in previously unseen environments requires effective perception, persistent environmental representation, and collision avoidance while maintaining progress toward a goal. Existing perception-based methods often rely on prior maps or short-horizon observations, limiting their ability to exploit previously observed structure. We propose a memory-aware multi-sensor navigation framework that integrates LiDAR and RGB perception, online distance-field representation learning, and a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (MCBF-QP). The framework persistently represents static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles, enabling the MCBF-QP controller to exploit previously observed geometry for obstacle circumvention and adapt its safety constraints and guidance to local conditions. Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor environments demonstrate improved navigation efficiency and goal-reaching performance while maintaining collision avoidance in narrow passages and around dynamic obstacles.
bullets: Targets limitations of prior-map dependence and short-horizon perception in unseen environments.
Fuses LiDAR and RGB data with online distance-field representation learning.
Separately preserves static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles.
Uses a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program for safe, context-aware control.
Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor settings show improved efficiency and goal reaching while avoiding collisions in narrow and dynamic scenarios.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion in confined spaces requires continuous height adaptation across multiple locomotion modes, yet most existing approaches remain limited to height-adjustable bipedal walking. We present REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments through variable-height bipedal walking and crawling. The learned policies regulate body height over complementary command ranges of 1.27--0.50m in bipedal locomotion and 0.50--0.20m in crawling, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. To address contact-rich crawling dynamics, we employ a history-conditioned latent representation that captures terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive observations. A bidirectional transition policy further connects crouched bipedal locomotion and crawling across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. These skills are integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands, including proactive height targets. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, reliable mode transitions and confined-space traversal with the proposed pipeline. Code and videos are available at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/REACH/.
authors: Shengzhang Xu, Yuning Guo, Weiyi Hu, Yifeng Xu, Zhongyu Li, He Kong
bullets: Addresses the limitation of bipedal systems that cannot traverse spaces below crouched-walking clearance.
Uses hierarchical reinforcement learning with history-conditioned latent representations for contact-rich crawling.
Employs a bidirectional transition policy to connect crouched walking and crawling despite major kinematic and contact changes.
Combines learned locomotion skills with LiDAR-based 3D planning and proactive body-height commands.
Real-world experiments show accurate tracking, terrain robustness, reliable mode transitions, and confined-space traversal.

papers.abstract: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.
authors: Riccardo Bianco, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses precise timing, alignment, and collision avoidance when flying through moving narrow gaps.
Uses signed-distance gating to turn sparse traversal success into dense, differentiable pathwise losses.
Trains a visual-feature-to-thrust/body-rate policy in one stage without privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation.
Pathwise gradients outperform score-function gradients in controlled precision-critical benchmarks.
Achieves 99.3% simulation success and 80% success across 10 real-world trials from varied initial conditions.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and milliwatt-level power consumption, making them ideal for agile robots such as tiny drones navigating through cluttered environments. However, existing simulators generally render photorealistic images before converting them into events, making large-scale reinforcement learning prohibitively slow. We propose an analytic event simulator that exploits what event cameras fundamentally measure - moving contrast edges - to synthesize event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion without visual rendering. Our simulator generates a 64x64 event observation in 17 microseconds on a single GPU - over 400x faster than a state-of-the-art rendering pipeline - enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning for goal-directed obstacle avoidance to converge in under 30 minutes - three orders of magnitude faster than training on rendered events. Policies transfer zero-shot to physically based event simulations (ray-traced Isaac Sim). Our policy reaches 83% success in cluttered courses unseen during training (mid-difficulty, traversability probability approx. 0.57), at 2.4 m/s average goal velocity, and retains 70% in a simulated texture-dense indoor hall. Furthermore, we quantized the policy to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie equipped with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera and an OpenMV N6 microcontroller board. Without any fine-tuning, external processing, or positioning, the policy achieves an average success rate of 82% (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) across three real-world obstacle courses of increasing difficulty. authors: Dequan Ou, Austin Lopez, Quentin Missinne, Christophe De Wagter, Guido C. H. E. de Croon

A quantized 1.2 MB policy runs onboard a 56 g Crazyflie, reaching an average 82% success rate across three real-world courses.

papers.abstract: In smart factory environments, passive entities such as humans and movable obstacles may interfere with autonomous robot operations, posing significant safety risks. Detecting potential conflicts between robots and entities outside their field-of-view (FoV) is therefore of paramount importance. However, conventional passive object detection systems rely on sensors such as LiDAR, radar, or cameras, which operate under direct line-of-sight (LoS) and are limited by obstacles and occlusions. To overcome these limitations, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception via the communication infrastructure thanks to cooperation among distributed wireless devices. In this paper, we propose a framework for passive entity sensing beyond the robot's FoV that relies solely on distributed channel measurements from the communication infrastructure to perform risk-aware classification. These measurements are embedded into high-dimensional representations using hyperdimensional computing (HDC), enabling robust and scalable learning without explicit channel reconstruction. Numerical simulations based on a commercial ray tracer and ROS-based validation in realistic smart factory scenarios demonstrate improved safety and enhanced path planning with up to 89% accuracy under severe occlusions, while maintaining low computational complexity.
authors: Placido Mursia, Marco Rossanese, Francesco Devoti, Adrian Lendinez Ibanez, Lanfranco Zanzi, Xi Li, Xavier Costa-Perez
bullets: Addresses robot safety risks from humans and obstacles hidden by occlusions in smart factories.

Maps measurements to high-dimensional representations with hyperdimensional computing for risk-aware classification without reconstructing channels.
Validated through ray-tracing simulations and ROS-based smart-factory scenarios.
Supports safer path planning under severe occlusions, with scope demonstrated in simulated and realistic validation environments.

papers.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
authors: Daan van Hamersveld, Ewoud Smeur, Iurii Kriachko
bullets: Addresses the need for lower-cost, longer-range interception of medium-altitude, long-endurance drones.
Uses a neural network to map filtered monocular-vision observations directly to actuator commands.
Trains the policy with proximal policy optimization in a custom Python environment.
Outperforms two classical guidance controllers under most simulated conditions.
Successfully intercepts maneuvering fixed-wing targets in real-flight tests.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies form structured internal representations of traffic, ego behavior, and road constraints. These representations offer a monitoring interface for anticipating failures, complementing risk signals from trajectories, controls, and manually designed features. We introduce the Structured Representation Probe (SRP), a lightweight monitor that reads actor, ego, and map representations from a frozen policy. SRP learns a separate linear risk direction for each source and aggregates element scores through cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling, retaining sensitivity to salient evidence while reducing dependence on token count. Event-window supervision links the readout to upcoming hard failures, and auxiliary event type heads jointly train the source directions across failure modes. Online alerting uses a single generic score without modifying the driving policy. Bench2Drive experiments on DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD show higher frame-level PR-AUC and ROC-AUC than the evaluated runtime baselines. On DriveTransformer at a horizon of 2 seconds, ROC-AUC reaches 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency, with 2.67% readout runtime overhead. The trained probes also retain the ability to distinguish impending failures on new routes.
authors: Jiawei Liang, Tianrui Lou, Le Yang, Xianghao Jiao, Wei Wang, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Addresses the need for risk monitoring that complements trajectory-, control-, and hand-crafted-feature-based signals.

Uses event-window supervision and auxiliary event-type heads to train a single generic online alert score without changing the driving policy.
On Bench2Drive with DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD, SRP outperforms evaluated runtime baselines; for DriveTransformer at a 2-second horizon, ROC-AUC is 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency.
Adds 2.67% readout runtime overhead and retains failure-discrimination ability on new routes.
